The worldwide seroprevalence of parvovirus B19 has been assessed to be about 40-60%. It has been shown that parvoviruses can also infect new host species, adapt, and co-evolve. A comprehensive genomic surveillance is essential to gain a better insight in the adaptation, evolution, and also epidemics of parvoviruses. In the scope of the large parvovirus B19 epidemic 2023/24 following the SARS-CoV-2 pandemic, we developed a rapid and convenient system to analyze parvovirus B19 genomes directly from patient samples by next-generation sequencing. We utilized this system to study the part of the unusual outbreak in Southern Germany (Central Franconia), comprising the counties Nuremberg, Fuerth, and Erlangen. This detected a certain genetic diversity within the analyzed samples and identified shared mutations in comparison to reference sequences. Here, two phylogenetically distinct groups were observed, compatible with the co-circulation of at least two B19V lineages in the region and a putative new genotype of human parvovirus B19, possibly induced by immunosuppression was identified. We established a new, quick, and convenient surveillance system for human parvovirus B19 that enables the analysis of outbreaks and monitoring of viral genetic changes.

articles.title: Association of Planetary Health Diet with decreased risk of cardiometabolic diseases, multimorbidity, and its progression: a prospective cohort study.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Lifestyle factors account for most of cardiometabolic diseases (CMDs) and progression to cardiometabolic multimorbidity (CMM). Yet, whether adherence to the Planetary Health Diet (PHD) is related to a lower risk of CMDs, CMM, and CMD progression is less known.

METHODS: We used large cohort data that included over 100,000 participants. Adherence to the PHD was measured by the Planetary Health Diet Index (PHDI) and CMDs were ascertained by linkage to national registries through 1 September 2023. Cox proportional hazards models or weighted Cox regression models were employed to analyse the relationship between the PHD and the risk of CMDs. CMD progression in relation to the PHD was estimated by multi-state modelling with Cox regression.

RESULTS: After a median follow-up of 12.5 years, greater adherence to the PHD was associated with a decreased risk of stroke (hazard ratio (HR) = 0.973, 95% confidence interval (CI) = 0.951-0.997) and type 2 diabetes (0.968, 0.952-0.984). The association of the PHDI with type 2 diabetes showed significant nonlinearity (p = 0.04), with the lowest risk occurring when the PHDI reached 84 points. Compliance with the PHD was inversely related to the risk of transitions from baseline separately to first CMD and to death, with an HR (95% CI) of 0.89 (0.84-0.94) and 0.81 (0.73-0.89) among adults in the highest adherence group, respectively.

CONCLUSION: Our findings support the PHD as a modifiable factor for the primary prevention of CMDs and the PHDI at 84 points being linked to the lowest type 2 diabetes risk.

articles.title: Effect of neuromuscular blockade reversal on early postoperative pulmonary function after thoracoscopic lung resection: a multicenter, double-blind, randomized controlled trial protocol.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Pulmonary function decreases immediately after thoracic surgery, a change that is often overlooked and lacks effective intervention strategies. Residual neuromuscular blockade (RNMB) is an important, controllable factor. This study aims to compare the effects of sugammadex versus neostigmine for neuromuscular blockade reversal on pulmonary function recovery at 1 h postoperatively.

PATIENTS AND METHODS: This multicenter, double-blind RCT will enroll 240 patients scheduled for unilateral thoracoscopic partial lung resection (≤ 1 segment). Eligible participants will be randomly assigned in a 1:1 ratio to the sugammadex group (2 mg/kg) or the neostigmine group (0.03 mg/kg co-administered with atropine 0.015 mg/kg). The primary outcome is the percentage decrease in forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1) at 1 h postoperatively relative to the preoperative baseline. Secondary outcomes include the percentage decrease in FEV1 from baseline on postoperative days 1 to 3, and pain scores measured by the verbal response scale (VRS) at multiple postoperative time points. Other outcomes include opioid consumption, recovery time of gastrointestinal function, incidence of postoperative nausea and vomiting (PONV), 15-item Quality of Recovery (QoR-15) scores, and the incidence of postoperative pulmonary complications (PPCs).

DISCUSSION: This study aims to assess the superiority of sugammadex over neostigmine reversal regimens in improving 1-hour postoperative pulmonary function following thoracoscopic lung resection. The findings will provide mechanistic evidence on whether optimized neuromuscular reversal improves early postoperative pulmonary function, and may inform the design of future confirmatory trials with patient-centered outcomes.

CLINICAL TRIAL REGISTRATION: ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT07309393.

articles.title: A multi-dimensional analysis of quality changes in Shandong Junan white tea during storage.
articles.abstract: The chemistry of long-term high-latitude white tea storage remains poorly characterised. This study profiled Junan white tea from newly manufactured tea (Y0) through three years of storage (Y3), using sensory evaluation, colourimetry, electronic-tongue and chemical analyses with multivariate statistics; kinetics were modelled and extrapolated with a physics-informed neural network (PINN). During storage, the made tea turned brownish green and the liquor deepened to dark yellow and orange-red; L* decreased while b* and C* increased; bitterness and astringency attenuated and richness increased. Tea polyphenols and gallic acid, the core markers, changed in opposite directions. Non-esterified catechin C degraded fastest (half-life ≈ 0.98 yr); caffeine showed no detectable change. The PINN offered no accuracy advantage over the kinetic model but extrapolated robustly from sparse data; 5-10-year trajectories await external validation. These results provide an objective basis for year identification and storage management of northern white tea.

articles.title: Continuation of Clopidogrel in Total Knee Arthroplasty: Perioperative Bleeding and Cardiovascular Outcomes in a Consecutive Case Series.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Perioperative clopidogrel management in total knee arthroplasty (TKA) is challenging because interruption may increase thrombotic risk, whereas continuation may increase bleeding. Evidence remains limited.

METHODS: We retrospectively reviewed 31 consecutive patients (35 knees) undergoing primary TKA while continuing clopidogrel 75 mg daily (April 2018-September 2019). A multidisciplinary team involving orthopaedic surgery, cardiology, and anesthesiology determined continuation. One senior surgeon performed all procedures using a tourniquet-free technique with intravenous and intra-articular tranexamic acid. All patients also received low-dose aspirin for at least 2 weeks postoperatively as venous thromboembolism prophylaxis. Outcomes through 90 days included bleeding, transfusion, wound complications, infection, major adverse cardiac and cerebrovascular events, symptomatic venous thromboembolism, and anesthesia-related complications.

RESULTS: Mean age was 69 ± 6.4 years; mean estimated blood loss was 285 ± 95 mL, and mean hemoglobin decrease was 1.8 ± 0.6 g/dL. No transfusions or major bleeding occurred. Minor wound drainage followed 3 procedures (8.6%), and superficial cellulitis occurred in 1 knee (2.9%); no deep infections occurred. Four patients (12.9%) reported mild, nonspecific headaches; none met criteria for post-dural puncture headache. No clinical signs or symptoms suggestive of spinal hematoma or persistent neurologic deficit, and no myocardial infarction, stroke, or cardiovascular death, were observed.

CONCLUSIONS: Clopidogrel continuation during primary TKA may be feasible in carefully selected patients receiving multidisciplinary assessment and multimodal blood management. The small sample, retrospective design, and absence of a control group preclude conclusions about comparative safety.

articles.title: Implementation of scientific evidence into rheumatological care-the viewpoint of the EULAR.
authors: van der Helm van Mil AHM
articles.abstract: The gap between scientific discoveries and bedside application remains one of the most significant challenges in modern healthcare. Implementation science can aid this process by ensuring that health practices evolve alongside scientific progress rather than lagging years behind. This viewpoint focuses on the efforts of the European Alliance of Associations for Rheumatology to foster the implementation process of recommendations for rheumatic and musculoskeletal disease by addressing implementation strategies and by outlining barriers and facilitators for supporting interdisciplinary and patient-centred care.

articles.title: Comparison of [18F]-florbetapir PET visual interpretation and quantitation to detect amyloid pathology at the community level.
articles.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: In research and clinical trial applications, [18F]-florbetapir positron emission tomography (PET) imaging data are commonly evaluated with quantitation-based approaches. In clinical practice, scans are primarily interpreted visually by nuclear medicine physicians or radiologists (community readers), often with varying amyloid PET expertise. This study investigated the concordance between visual reads and quantitation of florbetapir PET scans at the community level.

METHODS: The analysis included 337 florbetapir PET scans from 2 studies: AV45-QP (96 scans each interpreted by 80 community readers, generating 7680 binary reads) and AV45-RTP01 (241 scans and interpretations submitted by 29 community readers, generating 237 binary reads after removing indeterminate or uninterpretable scans). Inter-reader reliability (Fleiss' κ) was assessed in AV45-QP. Area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) analysis evaluated the association between quantitation and visual reads, with optimal thresholds determined by Youden's index and concordance evaluated with Cohen's κ.

RESULTS: There was substantial inter-reader agreement in AV45-QP (Fleiss' κ = 0.71). The median of individual readers' optimal Centiloid (CL) thresholds was 24.7 (range: 12.84-59.44 CL); 91.3% of readers had optimal thresholds between 20 and 50 CL. In AV45-RTP01, the optimal threshold was 22.2 CL. Visual reads, compared with quantitation, showed a median AUC of 0.90 and median Cohen's κ of 0.72 for AV45-QP, and AUC and Cohen's κ of 0.91 and 0.76, respectively, for AV45-RTP01.

CONCLUSIONS: Community readers showed substantial but imperfect inter-reader agreement and concordance with quantitation of florbetapir PET scans. Inter-reader disagreement and visual-quantitative discordance were non-negligible, supporting complementary roles for visual interpretation and quantitation.

articles.title: Aortic plaque morphology and cholesterol crystal release assessed using non-obstructive general angioscopy.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Non-obstructive general angioscopy (NOGA) enables direct visualization and dynamic assessment of aortic plaque morphology and surface disruption, compared with conventional imaging modalities such as computed tomography. Aortic plaque disruption has been implicated in organ injury, potentially through the release of cholesterol crystals (CCs) into the bloodstream and subsequent inflammatory responses in peripheral organs. However, differences in CC detection according to aortic plaque morphologies have not been fully investigated.

METHODS: We prospectively enrolled 144 consecutive patients with coronary artery disease who underwent NOGA between September 2021 and December 2024. A total of 350 aortic plaque sites in the infrarenal abdominal aorta were classified into six morphological types and analyzed. The presence of CCs was assessed using a filter paper rinse method under polarized light microscopy, and detection rates were compared across plaque morphologies.

RESULTS: CCs were detected in 79 of 350 plaque-site samples (22.6%). CC detection differed significantly across plaque morphologies and was highest in puff chandelier ruptures (42.6%), followed by puff ruptures (16.3%), thrombi (2.9%), ulcers/fissures (2.2%), and yellow plaques (1.5%). After accounting for within-patient clustering using a mixed-effects logistic regression model with a patient-specific random intercept, plaque morphology was significantly associated with CC detection (global P < 0.0001). In patient-level multivariable analyses, the number of puff chandelier ruptures remained independently associated with CC detection after adjustment for relevant comorbidities and laboratory parameters.

CONCLUSION: Puff chandelier rupture was associated with the highest rate of CC detection, suggesting that this morphology may represent a biologically active plaque phenotype with greater CC shedding potential. These findings link direct plaque morphology to a functional marker of plaque activity.

articles.title: Exertional syncope caused by acquired obstruction of the pulmonary artery due to an organized thrombus in a dog.
articles.abstract: An 8.5-year-old Boxer was referred for evaluation of frequently occurring exercise-induced seizure-like episodes for 2.5 months. Cardiac auscultation revealed a left basilar systolic murmur with an intensity of IV/VI. Echocardiography showed severe pulmonary arterial obstruction with a pressure gradient of 90 mmHg due to a suspected intraluminal mass. Cardiac catheterization was performed, where a right ventriculogram revealed a large rounded filling defect in the pulmonary artery trunk. No balloon angioplasty, biopsy or stenting were attempted. After euthanasia, post-mortem examination revealed an organized thrombus of unknown etiology attached to the wall of the pulmonary artery trunk. The adjacent arterial wall showed a markedly thickened intimal layer. The etiology remains unclear, primarily due to the chronic nature of the condition. Antemortem blood tests and postmortem examination failed to reveal any prothrombotic conditions. Acquired causes of pulmonary arterial obstruction are extremely rare in dogs, and an organized thrombus has not been reported yet.

articles.title: A composite lymph node-targeting nanoadjuvant NA@DCM integrates TLR9 and mitochondrial metabolic reprogramming for enhanced hepatitis B vaccination.
articles.abstract: Hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection remains a major global public health concern. Although hepatitis B subunit vaccines are safe and effective, improved adjuvants may further enhance their immunogenicity. We developed NA@DCM, an aluminum-based composite nanoadjuvant in which DSPE-PEG2000 nanomicelles incorporating a covalently conjugated DSPE-PEG-CpG 1018 (DC) conjugate are interfacially assembled with nano-aluminum (NA). We evaluated draining lymph node (dLN) biodistribution, immunogenicity, and biosafety in murine models, and examined B-cell activation mechanisms by transcriptomic, Western blot, and pharmacological inhibition analyses. NA@DCM enhanced CpG-associated accumulation in dLNs at 6 h versus free CpG, with sustained retention and component colocalization over 48 h. Compared with its individual components and their physical mixture, NA@DCM increased antigen-specific IgG titers, the IgG2c/IgG1 ratio, IFN-γ+/TNF-α+/IL-2+/IL-4+ CD4+ and CD8+ T cells, and germinal center responses, and matched an AS04-like reference formulation in total IgG. These features are consistent with a Th1-biased antibody profile. Mechanistically, NA@DCM enhanced Toll-like receptor 9 (TLR9)-NF-κB signaling and mitochondrial function, with increased superoxide-associated fluorescence, ATP production, and respiratory chain complex activities. Oligomycin A inhibition of ATP synthase attenuated bioenergetic responses and CD69/CD86 upregulation in human Namalwa and primary murine B cells, indicating mitochondrial ATP synthesis is required for NA@DCM-induced B-cell activation. NA@DCM showed favorable hemocompatibility in vitro and no overt acute toxicity in vivo; repeated immunization induced early cytokine responses and local infiltration without detectable hepatic or renal abnormalities. Collectively, NA@DCM integrates lymph node-targeted delivery, TLR9-associated signaling, and mitochondrial bioenergetic modulation, supporting further preclinical development as a hepatitis B vaccine adjuvant.

articles.title: Network pharmacology-based identification and experimental validation of active compounds from Qingda Granules against Ang II-induced hypertension.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES: Hypertension is a significant global health issue that raises the risk of cardiovascular diseases (CVDs). Qingda Granule (QDG) is a traditional Chinese medicine formula used to treat hypertension, but its active compounds and mechanisms of action remain poorly understood.

METHODS: Network pharmacology identified potential active compounds and KEGG pathways. Four compounds-gastrodin, rhynchophylline, baicalin, and liensinine were selected. Hypertension was induced in mice via Angiotensin II (Ang II) infusion. QDG (1145 mg/kg/day) or each compound (10 mg/kg/day) was administered orally once daily. Outcomes measured included systolic blood pressure (SBP), diastolic blood pressure (DBP), mean arterial pressure (MAP), pulse wave velocity (PWV), and abdominal aortic wall thickness. Histological examination and immunohistochemistry for expression of total myosin light chain (MLC) and phosphorylation of myosin light chain (p-MLC) were performed in exploratory subgroups of three mice per group.

RESULTS: Network pharmacology analysis identified 482 predicted targets overlapping with hypertension-related targets. The compound-target network was constructed and analyzed, and hub nodes were identified using multiple parameters, such as betweenness centrality and degree. These four selected compounds-gastrodin, rhynchophylline, baicalin, and liensinine-ranked among the top 50 nodes in the compound-target network. Consequently, these four compounds were selected for further validation. KEGG enrichment analysis identified vascular smooth muscle contraction as an enriched candidate pathway (18 targets). In vivo, QDG and all four compounds treatment significantly lowered blood pressure, lowered PWV, and reduced abdominal aortic wall thickness. Exploratory subgroup analyses showed attenuated aortic histopathological changes and reduced p-MLC immunoreactivity, with no significant difference in total MLC immunoreactivity in abdominal aortic tissues of Ang II-infused mice.

CONCLUSION: QDG and its four individually administered compounds attenuated blood pressure elevation and were associated with lower PWV and reduced abdominal aortic wall thickening in Ang II-infused mice, as well as reduced p-MLC immunoreactivity. These findings suggest that the QDG and its four compounds contribute to antihypertensive effects.

articles.title: SGLT-2 inhibitors in peritoneal dialysis: A new dawn for cardio-renal protection.
articles.abstract: The rising global incidence of chronic kidney disease has positioned peritoneal dialysis (PD) as a critical renal replacement therapy. However, its long-term efficacy is often compromised by peritoneal fibrosis and encapsulating peritoneal sclerosis, leading to treatment failure in kidney failure patients. Furthermore, this population faces compounded health challenges, including heightened cardiovascular risk and metabolic syndrome. Sodium-glucose co-transporter 2 (SGLT-2) inhibitors, initially developed as anti-diabetic agents, have garnered significant attention for their demonstrated clinical benefits in renal and cardiovascular protection, as well as metabolic improvement. This review aims to comprehensively analyze the mechanisms of action and clinical application prospects of SGLT-2 inhibitors in PD patients, synthesizing evidence from preclinical studies, observational data, and extrapolated findings from trials in chronic kidney disease (CKD) populations. By synthesizing existing literature, we seek to provide insights for clinical practice and illuminate future research directions.

articles.title: Refractory circulatory shock following intentional polypharmacy antihypertensive and NSAID overdose: Clinical recovery temporally associated with sequential intravenous lipid emulsion and methylene blue - A case report.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Calcium channel blocker (CCB) overdose carries substantial mortality without advanced organ support. Ingestion of a fixed-dose antihypertensive combination with a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) is an uncommon polypharmacy toxidrome. The role of intravenous lipid emulsion (ILE) and methylene blue in refractory cases remains poorly defined.

CASE REPORT: A 64-year-old man (135 kg) ingested approximately 300 mg amlodipine, 300 mg perindopril, 75 mg indapamide and 15,000 mg naproxen with ethanol. Despite apparent stability on arrival he deteriorated to 77/47 mmHg, pH 7.20 and lactate 10.5 mmol/L. Seven hours of escalating treatment - noradrenaline (peak 58 mcg/min), vasopressin, calcium and high-dose insulin euglycaemic therapy (HIET) - failed to restore haemodynamic targets. Intralipid 20% was given (total approximately 8.9 mL/kg), followed 35 min later by methylene blue 140 mg (1.0 mg/kg). Lactate fell from 10.5 to 6.1 mmol/L over the subsequent 55 min with the noradrenaline dose unchanged. All vasopressors were stopped within 14 h. HIET was accompanied by concurrent glucose, potassium and phosphate nadirs (1.7, 1.7 and 0.27 mmol/L). KDIGO stage 2 acute kidney injury (peak creatinine 303 µmol/L) required no renal replacement therapy and resolved completely (creatinine 81 µmol/L at 3.5 months). The patient was discharged on day 9.

CONCLUSION: Sequential ILE and methylene blue were temporally associated with rapid metabolic recovery in refractory circulatory shock following polypharmacy antihypertensive overdose. Individual contributions cannot be determined from a single case, and a delayed effect of concurrent HIET cannot be excluded. These agents may represent rescue options when conventional therapy is insufficient.

articles.title: Functional health literacy and medication adherence in atrial fibrillation patients.
articles.journal: American heart journal plus : cardiology research and practice
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Atrial fibrillation (AF) treatment requires strict, long-term adherence to oral anticoagulants (OACs) to decrease associated morbidity risks. Despite its importance, adherence varies widely; nonadherence contributes to life-threatening adverse outcomes and elevated costs. Health literacy (HL)-the ability to acquire, comprehend, evaluate, and apply health information-is an important, yet underestimated factor. Given conflicting evidence on the HL-adherence association in chronic diseases, this study investigated this relationship and influencing demographic/contextual factors in AF patients across Iran.

METHODS: This descriptive-analytical cross-sectional, multicenter study was conducted in 2025 across Tehran, Kurdistan, and Kermanshah provinces on 407 adult AF patients receiving OAC therapy. Functional HL was assessed using the HELIA questionnaire; medication adherence was evaluated via MMAS-8. Analysis involved Pearson correlation, independent-samples t-tests, and multiple linear regression.

RESULTS: Mean total HL score was 108.65 ± 30.96 (moderate); mean MMAS-8 was 2.61 ± 1.54 (relatively high adherence). Total HL demonstrated a significant negative correlation with MMAS-8 scores (r = -0.099, p < 0.05), indicating higher HL associates with improved adherence, driven primarily by the "Information" subscale (r = -0.172, p < 0.01). While males had significantly higher HL scores (p < 0.001), females showed better adherence (p = 0.045). Notably, older age was paradoxically linked to worse adherence in Kurdistan (r = 0.327, p < 0.01). In multiple linear regression adjusting for age, gender, and study site (R2 = 0.214, p < 0.001), total HL emerged as a strong independent predictor of better adherence (β = -0.500, p < 0.001), alongside older age, female gender, and residing in Kurdistan (all p < 0.001).

CONCLUSIONS: Health literacy is a statistically significant, independent and modifiable predictor of medication adherence in Iranian AF populations. Efficacy is specific to functional information application, highlighting the need for interventions focused on practical skills. The complex age-gender interaction demonstrates how regional socioeconomic and cultural contexts affect the HL-adherence relationship.

articles.title: Atypical cryptococcal meningitis in an HIV-negative patient with advanced chronic kidney disease following corticosteroid exposure.
articles.abstract: Cryptococcal meningitis is increasingly recognized outside HIV. We report an HIV-negative man with advanced chronic kidney disease and recent corticosteroid exposure who presented with encephalopathy without headache, meningismus, or elevated intracranial pressure. MRI showed leptomeningeal enhancement; CSF cryptococcal antigen was positive despite negative fungal culture and multiplex PCR. Induction with liposomal amphotericin B and high-dose fluconazole was complicated by renal failure requiring hemodialysis. This case highlights diagnostic discordance and treatment challenges in advanced kidney disease.

articles.title: Atrial Fibrillation During Zanubrutinib Treatment in Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia With a Historical Ibrutinib Control.
articles.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Atrial fibrillation (AF) complicates Bruton tyrosine kinase inhibitor therapy in chronic lymphocytic leukemia.

METHODS: We retrospectively evaluated 679 zanubrutinib-treated patients across 52 Italian centers, with 354 historical ibrutinib-treated controls. Shanafelt AF scores were assessed.

RESULTS: Nine zanubrutinib-treated patients developed AF (1.33%) during median treatment of 15.5 months, versus 42 historical controls (11.9%) over median observation of 25 months. Five zanubrutinib events occurred among patients scoring ≥ 5. No affected patients experienced embolic or bleeding complications.

CONCLUSION: AF was uncommon during zanubrutinib treatment, even in the higher-risk subgroup. Historical comparisons remain limited, and exploratory score findings require confirmation with longer follow-up.

TRIAL REGISTRATION: The authors have confirmed clinical trial registration is not needed for this submission.

articles.title: Apolipoprotein A1 as an emerging cardiovascular biomarker: A systematic review and meta-analysis of its association with cardiovascular outcomes.
articles.journal: American heart journal plus : cardiology research and practice
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Apolipoprotein A1 (ApoA1), the main structural protein of high-density lipoprotein, has been proposed as a non-traditional biomarker for cardiovascular risk. However, its prognostic value beyond conventional lipid measures remains uncertain because available studies differ in population setting, outcome definition, and whether ApoA1 is assessed alone or as part of the ApoB/ApoA1 ratio. This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated the association between ApoA1-related measures and cardiovascular outcomes.

METHODS: This review was conducted in accordance with PRISMA 2020 guidance. PubMed, Embase, Scopus, and Web of Science were searched from database inception to June 2026. Observational studies evaluating ApoA1 or ApoB/ApoA1 ratio in relation to cardiovascular outcomes were eligible. Study selection was performed independently by two reviewers. Risk of bias was assessed using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale, and certainty of evidence was evaluated using GRADE. Random-effects meta-analysis was performed for ApoA1-alone clinical cardiovascular estimates, with additional expanded sensitivity and exploratory ratio-based analyses.

RESULTS: Sixty studies comprising a reported total of 2,213,585 participants were included in the analysis. In the restricted random-effects meta-analysis of four ApoA1 estimates, higher ApoA1 was associated with lower cardiovascular risk (pooled HR = 0.84, 95% CI: 0.81-0.87; p < 0.001; I2 = 15.75%). An expanded exploratory analysis including six estimates yielded a similar inverse association (pooled relative effect = 0.82, 95% CI: 0.77-0.86; p < 0.001; I2 = 34.81%). The expanded synthesis included different relative effect measures and should therefore be interpreted cautiously. ApoB/ApoA1 ratio evidence was evaluated separately.

CONCLUSION: Higher ApoA1 concentrations were associated with lower cardiovascular risk in the quantitative analyses. However, the pooled estimates were derived from a small subset of the available evidence, and differences in study populations, exposure definitions, statistical measures, and lipid-lowering treatment limit their interpretation. Further prospective studies establishing incremental predictive value beyond validated cardiovascular risk models are needed before routine clinical use can be recommended.

articles.title: Candida albicans onychomycosis coexisting with nail scabies: a diagnostic challenge in an elderly woman.
articles.abstract: Nail scabies is rare and may closely mimic onychomycosis, particularly in patients without typical cutaneous lesions. Here we report an 82-year-old Chinese woman initially suspected of having onychomycosis, whereas direct microscopic examination of nail scrapings unexpectedly revealed Sarcoptes scabiei mites together with fungal hyphae in the same microscopic field. Fungal culture yielded yeast subsequently identified as Candida albicans (C. albicans) by matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization time-of-flight mass spectrometry (MALDI-TOF MS). Based on these findings, nail scabies coexisting with C. albicans onychomycosis was diagnosed. The patient was successfully treated with topical crotamiton under occlusion combined with bifonazole cream. This case demonstrates that fungal infection and parasitic infestation may coexist within the same nail unit and highlights the importance of combined parasitological and mycological evaluation in patients with atypical nail dystrophy.

articles.title: Non-Sugar Sweetener Consumption and Glycemic Control in Middle-Aged and Older Adults with Prediabetes: Background, Design, and Methods of a Controlled Feeding Trial.
articles.abstract: Type 2 diabetes (T2D) and prediabetes are rising globally and constitute a significant metabolic disease burden. Development of these conditions involves insulin resistance, declining β-cell function, chronic low-grade inflammation, and gut microbiome disruption. Middle-aged and older adults comprise over one-third of individuals with T2D and 50% of those with prediabetes. Non-sugar sweeteners (NSS) are widely promoted as a strategy to reduce added sugar intake and help manage blood glucose concentrations. Adults with or at risk for T2D are among the highest users of NSS. However, the impact of NSS on glucose homeostasis remains unclear due to heterogeneity across trials, including short duration, inconsistent dosing, predominantly healthy participants, and infrequent assessment of individual NSS, which limits the ability to establish clear intake recommendations. To address these gaps, two three-arm randomized controlled feeding trials were designed to test four NSS. Adults aged ≥40 years with prediabetes will follow a 6-week standardized eucaloric diet reflecting typical U.S. intake, which includes a 2-week lead-in diet followed by a 4-week intervention period. In Trial 1, participants will be randomized to one of two intervention groups (sucralose or aspartame) or a control group receiving no NSS. In Trial 2, participants will be randomized to one of two intervention groups (acesulfame potassium or saccharin) or a control group receiving no NSS. The intervention groups will receive the respective NSS at 25% of the FDA-established acceptable daily intake (ADI), adjusted for body weight (mg/kg). The primary outcome for both trials is 24-h glycemic control and insulin sensitivity in response to intake of specific NSS types compared with an identical control condition. Secondary outcomes include markers of inflammation (e.g., TNF-α and MCP-1) and changes in gut microbiome composition.

articles.title: Musculoskeletal imaging in disseminated fusariosis: A case report with diagnostic imaging challenges.
articles.abstract: Disseminated fusariosis is a life-threatening opportunistic fungal infection that primarily affects immunocompromised patients with hematologic malignancies. Its imaging manifestations are heterogeneous and may evolve during immune recovery, complicating the distinction between active infection and inflammatory response. We report the case of a 31-year-old man with acute myeloid leukemia who developed disseminated Fusarium solani infection involving the skin, soft tissues, paranasal sinuses and bones during induction chemotherapy. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography, ultrasound, magnetic resonance imaging and 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography/computed tomography (18F-FDG PET/CT), demonstrated lesion evolution after neutrophil recovery, including a characteristic ultrasound target sign and corresponding peripheral enhancement and FDG uptake despite clinical improvement. Histopathology and follow-up biopsies supported immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome rather than persistent fungal infection. This case highlights the importance of interpreting imaging findings with clinical and pathological data during immune recovery. Recognition of imaging changes associated with immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome may help avoid misdiagnosing inflammatory lesions as persistent or progressive fungal infection.

articles.title: Integrating Social Determinants of Health Into Emergency Medicine Clerkships: A Qualitative Study of Student Reflections.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Social determinants of health (SDH) significantly influence emergency department (ED) care and patient outcomes, yet experiential learning opportunities in SDH remain inconsistently integrated into clinical education. Prior work has been effective but resource intensive. We sought to explore an adapted SDH-focused clinical experience that built on prior curricula and pre-clerkship SDH instruction while minimizing additional non-clinical resources.

METHODS: We implemented a semi-structured SDH-focused experience within a required emergency medicine (EM) clerkship which sought to integrate prior knowledge from a pre-clerkship SDH curriculum. In the ED, students partnered with care managers or social workers to identify patients affected by SDH, conducted patient interviews, and completed written reflections. De-identified reflections from one academic year (2023-2024) were analyzed using an inductive thematic analysis approach. Two investigators independently coded an initial subset, developed a shared codebook, and applied iterative constant comparison to generate themes with investigator triangulation to enhance trustworthiness.

RESULTS: Students described intersecting barriers to care, including language discordance, financial insecurity, and immigration-related challenges. Reflections also linked these barriers to direct clinical consequences such as delays in care, limited follow-up access, and patients leaving against medical advice. Students described how communication barriers and limited interpreter availability impacted care delivery and safety. Reflections also described structural inequities and the role of interdisciplinary teams in mitigating these challenges. Two additional themes, chronic illness and aging and health systems science, were interpreted as cross-cutting factors that modified how SDH were experienced rather than as determinants themselves.

CONCLUSIONS: A semi-structured, experiential SDH curriculum embedded within the ED clerkship elicited reflections in which students identified and interpreted real-world barriers to care. These findings describe how students applied SDH concepts in the ED rather than demonstrating change attributable to the activity. This approach offers a feasible model for embedding SDH learning within existing clinical workflows.

articles.title: 4D bioprinting of dynamic skin constructs: stimuli-responsive materials for adaptive wound healing.
articles.abstract: Wound healing remains a major clinical challenge, particularly for patients with chronic conditions such as diabetes, where impaired tissue repair contributes to significant morbidity and mortality. Conventional static wound dressings and three-dimensional (3D) bioprinted constructs fail to dynamically adapt to the evolving biochemical and biophysical microenvironment of a healing wound. The emergence of four-dimensional (4D) bioprinting, which incorporates time as a programmable dimension, offers a transformative paradigm by enabling printed scaffolds to undergo controlled shape morphing, drug release, and functional adaptation in response to stimuli, including temperature, pH, reactive oxygen species (ROS), light, magnetic fields, and enzymatic activity. This critical narrative review adopts an operational definition of 4D bioprinting and applies it as an inclusion criterion: additive fabrication that places cells or cell-instructive matrix under spatial control, a transformation programmed into that spatial arrangement during printing, and a measurable post-fabrication change with a defined trigger, threshold and rate. Judged against these criteria, much of the literature presented as 4D bioprinting comprises cast responsive hydrogels, electrospun meshes, microneedle arrays and smart dressings, and every system discussed here is accordingly assigned to one of four evidence tiers. We examine the measurement caveats that qualify wound pH, temperature and reactive oxygen species as design targets; the levers that set the magnitude, direction and rate of morphing; the three ASTM-aligned biofabrication families and how each enables or constrains programmed transformation; cell-generated contractile force as an endogenous actuator; and the failure modes peculiar to 4D systems, including threshold drift in protein-rich exudate, actuation slower than the biology it targets, single-shot chemistry and multi-stimulus cross-talk. Autonomous stimulus-responsive therapeutics are distinguished from genuine closed-loop sense-and-treat platforms. Evidence remains overwhelmingly rodent-based, no 4D bioprinted skin construct has entered a registered clinical trial, and almost no study compares an adaptive construct against a compositionally identical static control-the comparison that will decide whether 4D functionality earns its complexity.

articles.title: Accuracy of different methods for predicting proximity to failure during resistance training.
articles.abstract: Proximity to failure (PTF) is increasingly considered in resistance training (RT). Two common methods used to prescribe PTF are rating of perceived exertion (RPE) and repetitions in reserve (RIR). This study compared the accuracy of RIR and RPE for predicting PTF. In a randomised crossover design, 32 participants (19 trained, 13 untrained) completed machine chest press and leg extension exercises at 75% of one-repetition maximum. Participants completed two experimental sessions, one using RIR and one using Borg-RPE. Experimental session (RIR/RPE) and exercise order were randomised. During each set, participants indicated when they believed they had reached 2 RIR or 8 RPE and then continued to momentary failure. Accuracy was calculated as the difference between actual repetitions remaining to failure and the number predicted at the verbal call. No significant differences in accuracy were observed between RIR and Borg-RPE for either exercise (chest press: mean difference -0.03 repetitions, 95% CI - 0.50 to 0.44, p = 0.893; leg extension: mean difference 0.16 repetitions, 95% CI - 0.39 to 0.71, p = 0.556). Training status did not influence the difference in accuracy between methods. These findings indicate that Borg-RPE and RIR produce similar accuracy when estimating PTF during machine-based RT under the conditions tested.

articles.title: Immune system challenges posed by Brucella: mechanisms of evasion and immune provocation.
articles.abstract: Brucella spp. are stealthy intracellular Gram-negative zoonotic bacteria triggering brucellosis in humans and animals worldwide. These pathogens have evolved robust mechanisms to colonize hosts, withstand immune attack, escape clearance, and sustain long-term survival and transmission. Their full infection cycle depends on dual capacities to evade and reprogramme host immunity, creating a balanced state between host immune control and bacterial persistence. Recent research reveals diverse immune cell populations responding to infection and continuous shifts of bacterial intracellular niches over disease progression. A core pathogenic trait of Brucella spp. is weakly immunogenic pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs), notably its unusual lipopolysaccharide (LPS). Unlike LPS from enteric bacteria, this molecule triggers mild, delayed inflammation, enabling unnoticeable early bacterial proliferation. The VirB type IV secretion system (T4SS) secretes numerous protein and lipid effectors to reshape macrophage physiology and suppress protective immunity. Still, the stage and cell-reservoir-specific functions of these virulence factors remain poorly defined. This review traces the complete Brucella spp. infection cascade: mucosal invasion, early immune camouflage, intracellular compartment remodelling, systemic immune suppression, impaired adaptive immunity, chronic tissue reservoir formation, and disease relapse. We address how concurrent immune evasion and mild inflammatory stimulation support persistent infection, summarize latest research progress and unresolved questions, and translate these mechanistic findings into practical applications. These include refined diagnostic tools, DIVA vaccines, host-targeted therapeutics, combined antibiotic-immunomodulator regimens, and integrated One Health interventions for brucellosis control.

articles.title: Association between empirical antibiotic appropriateness and clinical outcomes in surgically managed diabetic infections of the lower extremities: a retrospective cohort study.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Diabetic foot infections (DFIs) are a leading cause of hospitalization and lower-extremity amputations. Management requires combined surgical and antimicrobial treatment; however, the clinical impact of appropriate empirical antibiotic therapy remains uncertain.

PATIENTS AND METHODS: We conducted a retrospective single-center study of hospitalized patients with DFI who underwent surgical debridement with positive deep tissue cultures. Patients were classified by appropriateness of empirical antimicrobial therapy administered. The primary outcome was a composite adverse outcome of major amputation, all-cause mortality, or ≥3 surgical procedures within 90 days. We also assessed hospitalization and antibiotic burden. Inverse probability of treatment weighting and multivariable regression were used to adjust for baseline differences and identify predictors of outcomes.

RESULTS: We included 190 cases (mean age 64.9 ± 11.8 years; 24.2% female), of whom 57.9% received appropriate empirical therapy. Patients receiving inappropriate therapy had higher comorbidity burden and more prior vascular and diabetic foot complications. The primary outcome at 90 days was similar between groups (23.8% vs 21.8%; adjusted OR 0.64, 95% CI 0.23-1.76). On multivariable analysis, dementia, prior diabetic ulcer, and leukocytosis were associated with adverse outcomes, while empirical therapy appropriateness was not. Inappropriate therapy yielded fewer 30-day hospital-free and antibiotic-free days.

CONCLUSION: In surgically managed DFIs without systemic illness, inappropriate empirical therapy - failing to cover all isolated pathogens - was not associated with worse 90-day clinical outcomes, though it reduced 30-day hospital-free and antibiotic-free days. Our findings support antimicrobial stewardship in DFIs, favoring narrow-spectrum empirical regimens following surgery while awaiting culture results.

articles.title: Sex-Specific Determinants of Noncommunicable Diseases Among Respondents From Wealthier Households in Bangladesh.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Noncommunicable diseases (NCDs), including hypertension and diabetes, have emerged as a major global public health concern in low- and middle-income countries like Bangladesh. In light of this, the current study aims to identify the sociodemographic factors associated with NCDs among Bangladeshi men and women, with a particular focus on those from wealthier households, to gain a deeper understanding of NCD risk in a rapidly evolving health landscape.

METHODS: Data were used from the nationally representative Bangladesh Demographic and Health Survey (BDHS) 2022. A total of 2729 men and 3441 women from wealthier households were included in the analysis. NCD status was defined as the presence of hypertension, diabetes, or both, and the  χ 2   test of independence was used to assess associations between NCDs and background characteristics. Separate binary logistic regression models for both men and women were employed to estimate the effects of sociodemographic factors on NCDs.

RESULTS: This study estimated a higher prevalence rate of NCDs among women (41.3%) compared to men (37.4%). Both adult men and women had a higher association with NCDs, with the effect more noticeable among the age groups 30-44, 45-59, and 60+ years. Secondary and higher levels of education were less likely associated with NCDs among women, whereas men with higher levels of education had an increased association with NCDs. Overweight (aOR = 1.80) and obese (aOR = 4.08) men had a higher likelihood of association with NCDs with respect to normal body mass index (BMI), and a similar trend was found among overweight (aOR = 1.73) and obese (aOR = 3.00) women.

CONCLUSION: This study shed light on the sex-specific higher association with NCDs among rich Bangladeshi people. Increased age and higher BMI are associated with the development of NCDs among both men and women.

articles.title: Health Seeking Behaviour Related to Hypertension Among Adults in Africa: A Scoping Review.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Hypertension is a major public health challenge in Africa, yet evidence on health-seeking behaviour and its determinants remains fragmented. This scoping review aimed to map the available evidence on health-seeking behaviour and its determinants related to hypertension among adults in Africa.

METHODS: The scoping review was conducted in accordance with the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) methodological guidance for scoping reviews and reported in line with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR). Seven electronic databases were searched for peer-reviewed studies published between January 2010 and January 2025. Studies involving adults aged 18 years and older in African countries and addressing health-seeking behaviour or its determinants in relation to hypertension were eligible for inclusion.

RESULTS: Sixteen studies from nine African countries were included. Healthcare-seeking behaviours were influenced by socio-economic status, cultural beliefs, social support, health system factors and knowledge of hypertension. Medical pluralism and delayed healthcare utilization were commonly reported.

CONCLUSION: Hypertension-related health-seeking behaviour in Africa is shaped by individual, social, cultural and health-system factors. Interventions that address these factors are needed to improve hypertension prevention, early detection, treatment uptake and control.

articles.title: Education Research: The Complex Case Conference (CCC): A Multispecialty Conference to Enhance Clinical Collaboration Within Neurology.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES: Clinical neurology is becoming increasingly subspecialized, yet neurologists regularly encounter challenging, undifferentiated cases that span subspecialty boundaries. Few formalized opportunities exist for neurologists to present complex cases to peers with differing expertise, especially in multisite departments. Our study had 2 aims: (1) to assess whether there was a perceived need for a formalized mechanism for cross-specialty case discussion in a single multisite institution and (2) if so, whether a monthly, hybrid, structured case conference could meet this need.

METHODS: To address our first aim, we completed a needs assessment by surveying neurology residents and attendings at a multisite academic medical center. We then addressed our second aim by implementing the Complex Case Conference (CCC); an 18-month follow-up survey was conducted to evaluate its utility and impact. We used a "Plan, Do, Study, Act" quality improvement approach and report changes across cycles. We report descriptive statistics; comparative analyses used the Fisher exact test and Wilcoxon rank-sum tests.

RESULTS: Twelve respondents completed the needs assessment. In the preceding month, 75% (9/12) had at least 1 case where multispecialty input would have been helpful, yet 33% (4/12) reported having a good mechanism to discuss challenging cases with other subspecialties or within their own subspecialty (33% [4/12]). CCC was developed to address these needs. CCC was held monthly for 60 minutes, during protected Grand Rounds time, with 30 minutes dedicated to a preselected case and 30 minutes as an open forum. Twenty responses were included in the postimplementation survey. The proportion of respondents who felt they had a good mechanism to discuss challenging cases significantly increased, with other subspecialties (33% [4/12] to 80% [16/20] [p = 0.036]) and within their own (33% [4/12] to 90% [18/20] [p = 0.002]). Respondents also reported increased knowledge of existing institutional resources (17% [2/12] to 70% [14/20]) [p = 0.009]). There was no significant change in intradepartmental referrals or recognition of cases where multispecialty input would be beneficial.

DISCUSSION: After an institutional needs assessment, CCC was developed to foster multispecialty clinical collaboration within an academic department. It provides a dedicated forum for discussing cases that would benefit from multispecialty input and has proven valuable for complex patient discussion, supporting clinician growth, and sharing institutional knowledge.

articles.title: Socio-ecological dynamics of disease transmission in rewilding landscapes: A case study of the Northern Drakensberg Nature Reserve, South Africa.
articles.abstract: Rewilding is increasingly promoted as a conservation strategy for restoring biodiversity and ecosystem processes. Yet rewilding efforts could involve species (re-)introductions that have implications for infectious disease dynamics. Despite the importance of such socio-ecological dynamics at the human-livestock-wildlife interface, the role of rewilding in disease prevalence remains poorly understood. We conducted semi-structured key informant interviews and focus group discussions with 24 stakeholders in the Northern Drakensberg Nature Reserve, South Africa, to examine how ecological dynamics, livestock management practices, governance conditions, and stakeholder perceptions shape disease transmission risks in a rewilding landscape. We analyzed the data using inductive thematic analysis guided by the One Health framework. Ecological and governance factors revealed that scavenger species, particularly vultures, jackals, and free-roaming dogs, shaped carcass persistence and pathogen exposure pathways, while the absence of coordinated governance across private landowners, conservation authorities, park managers, and community members created major gaps in disease surveillance and response. Disease risks were rarely considered in wildlife introduction decisions. Conservation authorities often assumed that pre-introduction health screening was sufficient, with limited attention given to post-release ecological dynamics. Disease awareness varied considerably across stakeholder groups and was influenced more by livelihood practices, concerns over grazing competition, and human safety than by epidemiological understanding. Historical exclusion from conservation decision-making further reinforced distrust, undermining disease reporting and compliance with interventions. These findings demonstrate that disease risks in rewilding landscapes emerge through interacting ecological, behavioural, and institutional processes rather than wildlife dynamics alone. Integrating diverse stakeholder perspectives into rewilding governance will be critical for operationalizing One Health approaches and anticipating unintended health consequences.

articles.title: Older age and coronary calcification on optical coherence tomography in patients undergoing percutaneous coronary intervention: a single-centre cross-sectional study in southern Vietnam.
articles.journal: International journal of cardiology. Cardiovascular risk and prevention
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND AND AIMS: Plaque phenotype on optical coherence tomography (OCT) is little studied outside East Asian and Western cohorts. We related age to OCT phenotype in a Southeast Asian percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) cohort.

METHODS: We analysed 306 patients (361 lesions) undergoing OCT-guided PCI in southern Vietnam, December 2023 to January 2026. Features were summarised per patient; age was modelled per decade and in three groups (<60, 60-69, ≥70 years). Models were adjusted for sex, clinical presentation and cardiovascular risk factors, with Holm correction across the eight principal features. Eight sensitivity analyses were performed.

RESULTS: Acute coronary syndrome (ACS) accounted for 36.6%. Unadjusted, calcification rose from 56.5% to 79.1% across age groups, lipid-rich plaque fell from 79.3% to 59.1% and red thrombus from 17.4% to 4.3%. After adjustment, only calcification remained associated with age (odds ratio 1.64 per decade, 95% CI 1.25-2.16; Holm-adjusted P = 0.003), as did every calcium subtype (nodules 1.77); no other feature showed an independent association. Angiography showed the calcium in 34.4% versus 57.7% of OCT-calcified lesions (youngest versus oldest group). The association was evident in ACS (2.64, 1.59-4.36) but not in CCS, in which about 80% had calcification at every age (P for interaction = 0.002).

CONCLUSIONS: Older age was independently associated with calcification on OCT, more often superficial, nodular and angiographically visible, particularly in ACS. The lower prevalence of lipid-rich and thrombotic features was not independent of sex and presentation. Being cross-sectional, these data describe differences between age groups, not change within individuals.

articles.title: Burkholderia cepacia complex and Burkholderia gladioli in large animals, dairy products, and livestock ticks: A systematic review of an emerging One Health concern.
articles.abstract: Burkholderia mallei is an established zoonotic pathogen that causes glanders, whereas B. pseudomallei is primarily an environmental pathogen that causes melioidosis in humans and animals. Most other Burkholderia species are environmental or plant-associated organisms; however, members of the Burkholderia cepacia complex (BCC) and B. gladioli are recognized opportunistic pathogens, particularly in susceptible humans. We conducted a PRISMA-guided systematic review of Web of Science, Scopus, and PubMed, supplemented by Google Scholar citation searching, through January 2025. We included eligible primary studies reporting naturally occurring infection, colonization, microbiome detection, or contamination involving large animals, dairy products, or livestock-associated ticks; we excluded animal-model and experimental-infection studies. Forty-eight unique studies met the eligibility criteria: 36 involving large animals, 10 involving dairy products, and two involving livestock-associated ticks. Reported organisms included B. cepacia, B. cenocepacia, B. contaminans, B. vietnamiensis, and B. gladioli, as well as Burkholderia identified only at the genus or complex level. Clinical disease was reported more often in horses and small ruminants, whereas findings in cattle and pigs were more often nonclinical or of uncertain clinical significance. BCC organisms and B. gladioli were also detected in raw milk and other dairy products, although detection frequencies varied substantially among studies and sample types. No study has demonstrated direct transmission from contaminated dairy products to human cases. The evidence was predominantly low-level and heterogeneous, indicating potential One Health relevance but precluding firm causal conclusions. Prospective surveillance, validated species-level identification, and genomic comparisons are needed to clarify pathogenicity, prevalence, and potential transmission pathways.

articles.title: Interventional radiology management of juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma.
articles.abstract: Juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma is a rare, highly vascular tumor that occurs almost exclusively in adolescent and young adult males and is associated with substantial intraoperative bleeding risk during surgical resection. Preoperative intra-arterial embolization is commonly performed to reduce tumor vascularity and improve perioperative safety. We present a case of a 21-year-old male with a history of asthma presenting with persistent unilateral nasal congestion who was found to have a left-sided nasopharyngeal mass. Surgical pathology later confirmed sinonasal angiofibroma. Diagnostic cerebral angiography demonstrated tumor blush supplied by branches of the left sphenopalatine artery arising from the internal maxillary artery of the external carotid circulation without significant contribution from the internal carotid artery or ophthalmic artery anastomoses. Using a microcatheter system, selective catheterization of the left sphenopalatine artery was performed, and embolization was achieved with 200-micrometer polyethylene glycol microspheres until near stasis was observed. Postembolization angiography demonstrated marked reduction of tumor blush, consistent with successful devascularization. The patient subsequently underwent successful surgical resection with remarkably low intraoperative blood loss (estimated 50 mL). This case highlights the role of interventional radiology in targeted preoperative embolization for the management of juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma. Selective embolization of the sphenopalatine arterial supply can significantly reduce tumor vascularity and facilitate safer surgical resection with minimal blood loss. The relatively insidious clinical presentation and use of polyethylene glycol microspheres, which, to our knowledge, have not been previously described in juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma, represent distinctive clinical and technical features of this case.

articles.title: Perforated hepatic flexure adenocarcinoma mimicking pyogenic hepatic abscess: A CT diagnostic pitfall.
articles.abstract: Perforated colorectal carcinoma may present with inflammatory and septic features that obscure the underlying malignancy. Tumors arising at the hepatic flexure are particularly challenging because of their close anatomical relationship with the liver, allowing perforation-related inflammation and necrotic hepatic metastases to mimic pyogenic hepatic abscesses on imaging. A 58-year-old man with hypertension and human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection receiving antiretroviral therapy presented with acute abdominal pain, fever, chills, and systemic inflammatory symptoms. Ultrasound demonstrated hepatic lesions and irregular hepatic flexure wall thickening suspicious for malignancy, while contrast-enhanced CT showed multiple abscess-like hepatic lesions with features of both metastatic disease and perforation-related inflammation. Emergency laparotomy revealed a perforated hepatic flexure tumor densely adherent to the liver, with fibrinopurulent exudate, an inflammatory tract between the hepatic flexure and adjacent liver, multiple hepatic nodules, and peritoneal tumor seeding; histopathology confirmed moderately differentiated adenocarcinoma with hepatic and nodal metastases and central necrosis in the hepatic lesions (pT4N2M1). This case highlights the diagnostic overlap between pyogenic hepatic abscesses and necrotic hepatic metastases associated with perforated colorectal carcinoma. When abscess-like hepatic lesions coexist with irregular colonic wall thickening, regional lymphadenopathy, or loss of normal tissue planes, colorectal malignancy should remain an important consideration despite accompanying inflammatory features.

articles.title: Continuous prediction of prolonged intensive care unit stay from longitudinal electronic health record data: development and external validation.
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVES: To develop and externally validate Prognostic Estimator of RiSk for prolonged ICU STay (PERSIST), a model that continuously updates the probability of an intensive care unit (ICU) stay longer than 7 days during the first week of ICU admission.

MATERIALS AND METHODS: We developed PERSIST, an XGBoost model, on 49 255 adult ICU stays from the Mount Sinai Health System (MSHS; 2021-2025) and externally validated it in 72 156 Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care-IV (MIMIC-IV) stays (2008-2019). Sixty routinely available electronic health record (EHR) features were aggregated hourly, with predictions every 4 hours from preceding data, benchmarked against L2-regularized logistic regression. We assessed discrimination, calibration, net benefit, SHapley Additive exPlanations attributions, and subgroup performance.

RESULTS: Prolonged stay occurred in 16.1% of MSHS and 11.1% of MIMIC-IV admissions. PERSIST achieved macroaveraged areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.80 (95% confidence interval [CI], 0.79-0.81) and 0.78 (0.77-0.78), respectively, compared with 0.75 (0.73-0.76) and 0.74 (0.73-0.74) for logistic regression. Corresponding areas under the precision-recall curve were 0.73 and 0.68. Brier scores were 0.14 and 0.13. Across modeled thresholds, PERSIST provided greater net benefit than treat-all and treat-none strategies. Discrimination was similar across reported age, sex, and racial groups.

DISCUSSION: Prognostic Estimator of RiSk for prolonged ICU STay transported across 2 health systems differing in era, case mix, and outcome prevalence, and outperformed logistic regression under identical conditions. Net benefit was greatest during the early ICU days, when few patients have declared a prolonged trajectory and a risk estimate can still inform planning.

CONCLUSION: Continuously updated, EHR-based prediction of prolonged ICU stay is feasible and generalizable. Prospective evaluation should determine whether it improves ICU care coordination and capacity planning.

articles.title: Morbid Obesity May be Associated With Increased Odds of Prosthetic Joint Infection After Anterior-Based Total Hip Arthroplasty.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Obesity increases perioperative risk after total hip arthroplasty (THA), particularly with anterior-based approaches. However, outcomes among patients with class II versus class III obesity remain poorly defined. This study compared early complications and patient-reported outcomes (PROMs) between these obesity classes.

METHODS: We retrospectively reviewed patients with BMI ≥35 kg/m² undergoing elective anterior-based primary THA from January 2022 to January 2025. Patients were stratified into BMI 35-39.9 kg/m² (Class II) and BMI ≥40 kg/m² (Class III) cohorts. Firth penalized logistic regression evaluated the association between BMI group and prosthetic joint infection (PJI) requiring operative irrigation and debridement (I&D).

RESULTS: 193 patients were included (BMI ≥40: n = 53; BMI 35-39.9: n = 140). The BMI ≥40 kg/m² cohort had a greater proportion of females (77.4% vs 57.1%; P = .015) and higher ASA classification (P = .02). PJI occurred more frequently in the BMI ≥40 cohort (7.5% vs 1.4%; P = .049). Unadjusted odds of PJI were higher with BMI ≥40 kg/m² (OR 5.03, 95% CI 1.08-29.6), but the association was no longer statistically significant after adjustment for age, sex, and surgical approach. Both cohorts demonstrated significant improvement in WOMAC and SF-12 Physical scores at 3 months without between-group differences.

CONCLUSIONS: Patients with BMI ≥40 kg/m² demonstrated higher observed PJI rates after anterior-based THA while achieving comparable early functional improvement. These findings suggest a clinically important risk signal warranting confirmation in larger studies rather than establishing BMI ≥40 kg/m² as an independent risk threshold.

articles.title: UHRF1 promotes epithelial-mesenchymal transition in renal tubular epithelial cells by driving G2/M phase arrest through activating the TGF-β/Smad signaling pathway.
articles.abstract: Diabetic kidney disease is a major cause of chronic kidney disease, and persistent activation of transforming growth factor-β/Smad signaling contributes to tubulointerstitial fibrosis. The epigenetic regulator UHRF1 has been implicated in renal fibrosis, but its role in sustaining transforming growth factor-β signaling remains unclear. To investigate whether UHRF1 promotes transforming growth factor-β1-induced epithelial-mesenchymal transition in tubular epithelial cells through a DNMT1/Smad7-dependent mechanism. Human HK-2 tubular epithelial cells were stimulated with transforming growth factor-β1. UHRF1 was overexpressed or silenced to evaluate effects on viability, apoptosis, migration, cell-cycle distribution, profibrotic mediator secretion, and epithelial-mesenchymal transition marker expression. Rescue experiments were performed using Smad7 overexpression and the transforming growth factor-β receptor inhibitor SB431542. DNMT-family specificity was additionally assessed by co-immunoprecipitation of UHRF1 with DNMT1, DNMT3A, and DNMT3B. UHRF1 overexpression aggravated transforming growth factor-β1-induced epithelial-mesenchymal transition, apoptosis, migration, G2/M phase arrest, and profibrotic mediator production, whereas UHRF1 silencing attenuated these changes. Mechanistically, UHRF1 recruited DNMT1 to the Smad7 promoter, suppressed Smad7 expression, and sustained Smad2/3 phosphorylation. Restoration of Smad7 or inhibition of transforming growth factor-β signaling reversed the effects mediated by UHRF1. In the DNMT-family specificity analysis, DNMT1, but not DNMT3A or DNMT3B, was detected in UHRF1 immunoprecipitates under the tested conditions. UHRF1 promotes epithelial-mesenchymal transition in tubular epithelial cells by sustaining transforming growth factor-β/Smad signaling through epigenetic repression of Smad7. The DNMT-family comparison supports a preferential UHRF1-DNMT1 association in this experimental system. Clinical trial registration: Not applicable.

articles.title: From cardiometabolic risk to kidney protection: extending the dM-HTN-AKI paradigm to critical care in the Philippines.
Accurate 3D brain cross-modality image translation by lesion-aware post-training of latent diffusion models with voxel-space objectives.
articles.abstract: Cross-modality image synthesis offers significant potential for mitigating challenges in medical image acquisition, particularly in acute settings. While latent diffusion models (LDMs) currently represent the state-of-the-art in generative modeling by leveraging compressed latent spaces, this efficiency necessitates a trade-off that often compromises fine structural details. This limitation is particularly critical when reconstructing small but clinically significant structures, such as ischemic lesions, where high-fidelity delineation is essential for diagnostic utility. To address this challenge, we propose a novel post-training framework for LDMs in 3D medical image-to-image translation by incorporating lesion-aware medical voxel-space objectives (LDM-3D-LAPT). Specifically, we convert the pretrained 2D LDM into a 3D volumetric model and post-train the model using a multi-objective loss function incorporating global image reconstruction, focal lesion-specific reconstruction, and auxiliary lesion segmentation guidance. We evaluate this framework on the task of synthesizing diffusion MRI from CT perfusion scans in a cohort of 100 acute ischemic stroke patients. We further evaluate our framework in an independent external cohort of 85 patients. Ablation studies showed that voxel-space post-training improved lesion segmentation. Internal and external evaluations demonstrated gains in ADC lesion fidelity and lesion-detection sensitivity. Our adaptable post-training strategy provides a practical approach to improving lesion-focused medical image translation.

articles.title: Diagnosing diabetes: the earlier the better.
Task Force 11: Additional Cardiac Conditions and Considerations in Competitive Athletes.
articles.journal: Medicine and science in sports and exercise
articles.abstract: The recently updated AHA/ACC Scientific Statement: Clinical Considerations for Competitive Sports Participation for Athletes with Cardiovascular Abnormalities provides a comprehensive framework for guiding clinicians in the evaluation and management of competitive athletes. Divided into 11 Task Forces, it covers a broad range of cardiovascular diseases and clinical scenarios. Task Force 11 was devoted to cardiac conditions and considerations in athletes not included in the other Task Forces. Here, we present the detailed rationale for the clinical considerations covered in this section of the Scientific Statement. These topics include hypertension, commotio cordis, pulmonary embolism, performance-enhancing drugs and supplements, exercise in extreme environments (specifically altitude and scuba diving), and pregnancy.

articles.title: Task Force 10: Clinical Considerations for the Care of Masters Athletes with Underlying Cardiovascular Disease.
articles.journal: Medicine and science in sports and exercise
articles.abstract: Masters athletes are individuals ≥35 yr of age who place a high premium on exercise training and competition. This document details important cardiovascular conditions, risk factors, and data-driven discussion, which serve as the rationale for Section X from the 2025 AHA/ACC Scientific Statement: Clinical Considerations for Competitive Sports Participation for Athletes Cardiovascular Abnormalities. Disease-specific risk stratification and shared decision-making are the cornerstones for Masters athletes when considering competitive sports participation. Coronary artery disease, atrial fibrillation, incidental myocardial fibrosis, aortic enlargement and aneurysms, and valvular heart disease are included in this Task Force document.

articles.title: Task Force 9: Clinical Considerations for the Care of Athletes with Cardiac Channelopathies.
articles.journal: Medicine and science in sports and exercise
articles.abstract: Cardiac channelopathies, including long QT syndrome, catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricular tachycardia, Brugada syndrome, and short QT syndrome, are heterogeneous conditions, which can lead to varying risks in athletes depending on their symptoms, disease severity, genotype, and therapies initiated. Historically, athletes with these conditions were excluded from participation with blanket restrictions, despite an absence of data. More recently, a number of studies have provided more scientific evidence to guide decision making and have been incorporated into these guidelines for athletes with cardiac channelopathies. Many athletes with these conditions may be supported in their decision to return to play as part of a shared decision-making model when they have been assessed, risk stratified, and appropriately treated by a specialist with expertise in these conditions.

articles.title: Task Force 8: Care of Competitive Athletes with Arrhythmias and Sudden Cardiac Arrest: Clinical Considerations and Electrocardiogram Interpretations.
articles.journal: Medicine and science in sports and exercise
articles.abstract: This document outlines recommendations for managing competitive athletes with arrhythmias and risks of sudden cardiac arrest, emphasizing individualized risk assessment, shared decision-making, and return-to-play protocols tailored to each athlete's cardiac profile and sport demands. It provides evaluation strategies for ventricular arrhythmias, implantable cardiac defibrillators, atrial fibrillation, supraventricular tachycardia, Wolff-Parkinson-White pattern/syndrome, and syncope, alongside guidance for electrocardiogram interpretation in athletes. A key focus is placed on differentiating between low-risk and high-risk conditions, with recommendations for treatment strategies and ongoing monitoring to ensure athletes' safety.

articles.title: Task Force 6: Clinical Considerations for the Care of Competitive Athletes with Congenital Heart Disease.
articles.journal: Medicine and science in sports and exercise
articles.abstract: Athletes with congenital heart disease are commonly restricted from competitive sports participation based on limited data regarding exercise-induced sudden cardiac death risk. For most athletes, the myriad of benefits derived from participating in competitive sports outweighs the risk. This document reviews the cardiac assessment that may be considered for children, adolescents, and young adults with congenital heart disease. By utilizing anatomy, physiology, symptoms, and cardiac testing, together with shared decision-making, the authors propose a strategy to help guide medical providers advising their patients on sports participation.

articles.title: Task Force 5: Clinical Considerations for Myocarditis and Selected Cardiovascular Conditions, Including Valvular Heart Disease.
articles.journal: Medicine and science in sports and exercise
articles.abstract: Athletes with myocarditis, pericarditis, valvular heart disease, and other acquired cardiovascular conditions require careful evaluation when considering competitive sports participation. This document outlines key clinical considerations, risk factors, and expert consensus, serving as the rationale for Section V of the recent AHA/ACC Scientific Statement: Clinical Considerations for Competitive Sports Participation for Athletes with Cardiovascular Abnormalities. Disease-specific risk stratification and shared decision-making are essential in determining return-to-play eligibility. This Task Force document addresses myocarditis, pericarditis, the cardiovascular impact of respiratory viral infections, incidental myocardial fibrosis, Kawasaki disease, infiltrative cardiomyopathies, and valvular heart disease.

articles.title: Task Force 1: Sports Classifications.
articles.journal: Medicine and science in sports and exercise
articles.abstract: Competitive sports differ with regards to their physiological demands and risk of collision/impact. With the goal of informing disease-specific recommendations for athletes with cardiovascular disease, we present the sport-specific physiology inherent to the typical practice of common competitive sports. We also classify sports by collision/impact risk, which is particularly relevant to athlete antiplatelet and anticoagulant use. Finally, we discuss how sport-specific cardiovascular adaptations to exercise training manifest on athletes' cardiovascular testing.

articles.title: Erratum: Living liver donor safety: Intraoperative considerations in living liver donation-Guidelines from the ILTS-iLDLT group consensus conference 2025.
articles.journal: Liver transplantation : official publication of the American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases and the International Liver Transplantation Society

articles.title: Predicting Motor Recovery in the Subacute Phase of Stroke: The Role of Passive Motor Task and Electroencephalogram Brain Networks.
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: In stroke rehabilitation, the identification of reliable prognostic factors remains a challenge for effective rehabilitation strategies. This study investigates which motor task has the most predictive utility based on electroencephalogram (EEG) characteristics during the subacute phase of stroke.

METHODS: Data were collected from 10 subacute stroke patients performed different motor tasks (passive, robotic movement; active, voluntary execution; motor imagery [MI]) and a nonmotor task (No-Go) at two time points: T1, approximately 3 weeks after stroke onset, and T2, 2 months after T1. EEG power and network characteristics were extracted for each task, and prognostic models were constructed with nested leave-one-subject-out (LOSO) cross-validation (CV) to avoid information leakage.

RESULTS: Our findings show that the passive task model produced the strongest internal predictive performance across all task conditions (root-mean-square error 5.94; nested LOSO CV-R2, 0.91), with ipsilesional/contralesional motor area event-related desynchronization, characteristic path length, and clustering coefficient emerging as consistent prognostic features. The passive task also showed less overactivation and hyperconnectivity in the early subacute phase relative to the active and MI tasks. This performance advantage was replicated across six analytic procedures (2 feature-selection × 3 regression strategies), supporting the robustness of the task comparison within the present dataset.

CONCLUSIONS: These findings suggest that EEG features obtained during a robot-assisted passive task may provide exploratory prognostic utility for motor recovery prediction in the early subacute phase of stroke.Impact StatementThe passive task may offer a practical approach for assessing neurophysiological markers of recovery potential, supporting the development of more personalized rehabilitation strategies and earlier prognostic evaluation in stroke patients.

articles.title: Effectiveness and sustainability of neonatal resuscitation training programs in reducing neonatal mortality rates in low- and middle-income countries: a systematic review.
articles.abstract: Globally, 75% of neonatal deaths occur in the first week of life. Despite a 52% reduction in the neonatal mortality rate (1990-2022), significant disparities persist in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). This systematic review synthesises evidence on the effectiveness and sustainability of neonatal resuscitation training programs in LMICs, with a focus on training programs, design, provider competency outcomes, and sustainability features. Systematic searches of five electronic databases (Embase, PubMed, MEDLINE (Ovid), Scopus, and CINAHL) were conducted in accordance with PRISMA guidelines to identify studies published between January 2020 and January 2025. Studies evaluating neonatal resuscitation training for healthcare providers in LMICs and reporting competency or mortality outcomes were eligible.
