Primary outcomes were the proportion of women choosing newborn intensive care (IC) versus comfort care, and rates of birth before 25 weeks' gestation. Consultations were stratified by gestation and compared between two eras: 2021-2022 and 2023-2024.

RESULTS: The mean gestational age at consultation was 22 + 5 weeks. For women counselled prior to 23 weeks, where comfort care was recommended, decisions for IC were 35% (14 of 40) in 2021-2022 and 49% (25 of 51) in 2023-2024. Decisions for IC at 23 and 24 weeks, where IC is recommended, remained high, with 92% and 96% opting for IC, respectively. 26% of women counselled went on to birth before 25 weeks.

CONCLUSIONS: Despite lowering the resuscitation threshold from 23 to 22 weeks, just over half of women in a large maternity hospital opted for comfort care in the 22nd week of pregnancy when this was recommended, with weak evidence of a trend towards increasing decisions for IC over time. Importantly, most women who were counselled did not give birth prior to 25 weeks' gestation.

articles.title: The Prevalence of a PFO in the General Population Matching Morphological Dimensions That Are Associated With Cryptogenic Stroke Is Significantly Less Than 25.
articles.journal: Catheterization and cardiovascular interventions : official journal of the Society for Cardiac Angiography & Interventions
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: The prevalence of patent foramen ovale in the general population is, according to several autopsy studies, around 25%. Most patients with a patent foramen ovale remain asymptomatic during their entire life, but some patients experience cryptogenic stroke or transient ischemic attack. Thus, the chance of a bystander-PFO in these patients seems to start at 25%. We hypothesize that patent foramen ovale associated with cryptogenic stroke or transient ischemic attack are different, they are larger in size than patent foramen ovale in asymptomatic individuals.

AIMS: To compare the patent foramen ovale size in patients with cryptogenic stroke and in autopsy patients.

METHODS: We compared the patent foramen ovale size in a large cohort of 418 patients with cryptogenic stroke with the reported size of 263 patients in autopsy studies.

RESULTS: The median patent foramen ovale size was three times larger in our cohort compared to the autopsy patients, with the interquartile ranges not showing any overlap (60.5 mm2 [IQR: 39.3-87.5] vs. 19.6 mm2 [IQR: 7.1-28.3], p < 0.001).

CONCLUSION: Our data showed that patent foramen ovale size in the general population is significantly smaller than in patients with cryptogenic stroke or transient ischemic attack. These findings show that in the general population, the prevalence of patent foramen ovale, similar in size as in patient with stroke or transient ischemic attack, is significantly less than 25%.

articles.title: Dose optimization study of hydroxychloroquine as add-on therapy in patients with uncontrolled type 2 diabetes mellitus.
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Hydroxychloroquine (HCQ) is approved in India as third-line therapy for type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) at a recommended daily dose of 400 mg. However, concerns regarding cumulative retinal toxicity with long-term use highlight the need to identify the lowest effective dose. This study evaluated the efficacy and short-term safety of HCQ 200 mg, 300 mg, and 400 mg once daily in patients with inadequately controlled T2DM.

METHODS: In this randomized, double-blind, multicentre dose-optimization trial, adults with inadequately controlled T2DM despite stable metformin and sulfonylurea therapy were randomized to receive HCQ 200 mg, 300 mg, or 400 mg once daily for 24 weeks. Efficacy endpoints included changes in glycated haemoglobin (HbA1c), fasting, postprandial glucose, and lipid parameters at Weeks 12 and 24. Safety was assessed through adverse-event, laboratory investigations, and ophthalmologic evaluations.

RESULTS: Overall, 218 participants were randomized (mean age 48.22 ± 8.86 years; 58.7% male). At Week 24, mean HbA1c reductions from baseline were -0.64%, -0.78%, and -0.89% in the 200 mg, 300 mg, and 400 mg groups, respectively. Lipid parameters improved across groups. Sixteen participants experienced 23 adverse events; of which 82.6% unrelated to study medication. One serious adverse event, unrelated to HCQ, resolved without sequelae. No retinal abnormalities or ophthalmic adverse events were observed.

CONCLUSION: HCQ 200 mg, 300 mg, and 400 mg demonstrated clinically meaningful glycemic improvements and favorable short-term tolerability over 24 weeks. These findings support dose optimization, particularly using lower doses for individualized treatment, while further studies are needed to establish long-term ophthalmic safety.

REGISTRATION: CTRI/2020/03/023714 [Registered on: 02/03/2020], Clinical Trial Registry-India URL: http://ctri.nic.in.

articles.title: Modulating cognitive reappraisal and hedonic capacity to alleviate depressive symptoms: A randomized controlled fNIRS-based neurofeedback intervention study.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Depression imposes a significant global health burden, with traditional interventions often limited by accessibility and sustained efficacy. This study investigated the efficacy and mechanisms of functional near-infrared spectroscopy neurofeedback training (fNIRS-NFT) in alleviating depressive symptoms.

METHODS: A total of 88 participants were involved in the study (data collected November 2022-June 2024), with 59 completing a one-week fNIRS-NFT protocol targeting right lateral prefrontal cortex (LPFC) activity across 11 sessions, while the remaining 29 served as a no-intervention control group. Based on their neural trajectories across training sessions, participants receiving fNIRS-NFT were further stratified into high-improvement (HI, n = 37) and low-improvement (LI, n = 22) groups. Clinical and behavioral outcomes were assessed at baseline, with depressive symptoms (i.e. BDI score) reassessed at a three-month follow-up. To elucidate the underlying mechanisms, we employed mediation analyses, change-based Spearman's correlation analysis (CSCA), and representational similarity analysis (RSA).

RESULTS: fNIRS-NFT significantly reduced depressive symptoms only in the HI group with effects sustained for three months. Mediation analyses within the HI group revealed that fNIRS-NFT enhanced cognitive reappraisal, which in turn increased hedonic capacity, sequentially reducing depressive symptoms. CSCA and RSA confirmed that fNIRS-NFT-induced LPFC activity changes correlated with improvements in hedonic capacity and cognitive reappraisal.

CONCLUSIONS: The study identifies hedonic drive and cognitive reappraisal as key mechanisms underlying the sustained antidepressant effects of fNIRS-NFT, underscoring its potential as a scalable, noninvasive intervention for depression.

articles.title: Looking Back at Interventions to Improve Patient Safety During Pandemics: A Systematic Review.
articles.abstract: Pandemics threaten patient safety by disrupting health systems and care. The objective was to synthesize the literature on interventions intended to mitigate patient harm caused by Ebola, Influenza A (H1N1), severe acute respiratory syndrome (SARS), and Middle East respiratory syndrome (MERS), impacting 6 patient safety domains: medication safety, diagnostic safety, surgical safety, health care-associated infections, pressure injuries, and falls. This was a systematic review using mixed-methods narrative synthesis, with searches in PubMed, EMBASE, CINAHL, and APA PsycINFO, supplemented by expert input. Studies published through 28 August 2023 were included if they described an intervention addressing a patient safety problem during one of the 4 outbreaks. From 21 unique articles identified that involved 1 or more of the 6 domains, 14 full texts were assessed, and 10 studies were included in the final analysis. Overall, few interventions were reported, and most studies were descriptive with minimal outcome data. Identified strategies included revised triage protocols, targeted infection prevention measures, and modified care pathways to preserve essential diagnostic and treatment services. None of the interventions were designed with patient safety as the primary objective; improvements in safety were secondary effects of broader outbreak responses. Across studies, interventions focused largely on infection control to prevent hospital transmission of the pandemic organism, as well as on system-level adaptations. The findings parallel findings from COVID-19, where triage and operational reorganization, including physical reorganization of units and new pathways to secure resources such as PPE and personnel, were central to maintaining patient care. The review highlights persistent gaps in preparedness and learning systems to ensure patient safety during infectious disease outbreaks, underscoring the need for interventions to reduce patient harm.

articles.title: The degree of facilitation of the spider mite Tetranychus evansi by tomato spotted wilt virus depends on the order of infection.
articles.journal: Philosophical transactions of the Royal Society of London. Series B, Biological sciences
articles.abstract: Priority effects can change the outcome of host-mediated interactions among co-infecting parasites. In a plant-virus-mite system, prior infection with tomato spotted wilt virus (TSWV) increases the number of spider mite (Tetranychus evansi) offspring. This is likely owing to negative immune crosstalk suppressing activation of the jasmonic acid pathway or virus-mediated increase in free amino acid levels in host plants. In this system, we coupled infection order experiments with a mathematical model of virus, mite and plant hormone dynamics to evaluate whether immune- or resource-mediated interactions among parasites might best explain observed priority effects. The model predicted facilitation of mites by the virus in all treatment modalities (i.e. prior inoculation with TSWV, prior exposure to mites and synchronous exposure) via immune-mediated and resource-mediated mechanisms, with the strongest facilitation when TSWV inoculation is first. Our experimental results were broadly consistent with model predictions, exhibiting the greatest facilitation of mites when the virus arrives first. Contrary to model predictions, however, facilitation under simultaneous exposure was only observed when correcting for plant size. Host traits may thus need to be incorporated into appropriate metrics to capture facilitation. This shows that integration of models with experiments can be useful for improving understanding of disease outcomes. This article is part of the theme issue 'Ecological and evolutionary interactions between parasites across scales'.

articles.title: Within-host adaptation in two ectoparasitic mites modifies their likelihood of coexistence via competition-colonization trade-offs.
articles.journal: Philosophical transactions of the Royal Society of London. Series B, Biological sciences
articles.abstract: Adaptation to a novel host can affect coexistence between parasites by modifying traits involved in competition within hosts or transmission between hosts. Here, we test this by performing experimental evolution of the ectoparasitic spider mites Tetranychus urticae or Tetranychus evansi on tomato plants that accumulated cadmium or not, then assessing how such evolution affected their likelihood to coexist in each environment. We found that, in the presence of competitors, the dispersal rate of T. urticae was higher than that of T. evansi, the better competitor, irrespective of the selection regime or the environment. Additionally, the dispersal rate of T. urticae increased when both competitors evolved in the cadmium environment. Moreover, we found a negative correlation between dispersal rate and sensitivity to interspecific competition across populations evolving in the same selection regime, especially in the cadmium environment, indicating a competition-colonization trade-off. Model simulations using this data showed that coexistence was more likely across environments and selection regimes when allowing for extinction-recolonization dynamics, reinforcing the critical role of differences in dispersal between species for coexistence. Our results indicate that adaptation to a novel environment can shape ectoparasite coexistence by modifying both dispersal and sensitivity to competition, thus altering the competition-colonization trade-off. This article is part of the theme issue 'Ecological and evolutionary interactions between parasites across scales'.

articles.title: Estimating strain-strain interactions from co-colonization data under similarity.
articles.journal: Philosophical transactions of the Royal Society of London. Series B, Biological sciences
articles.abstract: Many infection systems are characterized by the possibility of co-infection, the simultaneous presence of two strains, or parasite species in the same host. Although parasite diversity is a key feature of epidemiological dynamics and feedbacks, estimating interactions among parasite strains or species in co-infection scenarios remains difficult. One of the central difficulties stems from the typically limited resolution of co-infection classes in actual real populations, where crucially co-infection by the same strain is hidden, and some pairs of interacting entities may never be seen together. Here, we propose a model-based method to overcome this limitation and its associated biases. We build upon the analytical tractability of an susceptible-infectious-susceptible-replicator model with co-infection and similar interacting strains to propose formal estimators of key interaction and epidemiological parameters from strain co-occurrence and single-occurrence data. We show equivalence of our estimators with maximum likelihood-based estimators. We use simulations to assess method validity in a range of hypothetical parameter combinations, encompassing competition, facilitation, high and low prevalence and variable host population sample sizes. We also illustrate the method's applicability on two real datasets, highlighting that its additional scope could be to test for quasi-neutrality in multi-strain systems. This article is part of the theme issue 'Ecological and evolutionary interactions between parasites across scales'.

articles.title: Subtle changes in cellular immunity interact with microbial co-infection to shape population-level patterns in helminth prevalence and burden.
articles.journal: Philosophical transactions of the Royal Society of London. Series B, Biological sciences
articles.abstract: Processes at the within-host scale, such as feedbacks among immune cells and interactions between the immune system and co-infecting helminths and microbes, influence population-level patterns of parasite distribution and abundance. The magnitude of such influence is historically difficult to estimate owing to difficulties in disentangling cross-scale effects. To understand how changes in cellular immunity cascade into changes in host/parasite populations, we constructed helminth-microbe co-infection simulations using mice as the model host. Within-host processes were parametrized with published and novel empirical data from the mouse-whipworm model system. Using single-dose simulations, we show that classic empirical patterns of immune polarization and parasite expulsion in dose-response and rewilding studies are explained by straightforward immune feedbacks. Increasing the scale of the simulations to spatially explicit host/parasite populations, we show that microbial co-infection permits stable helminth endemicity across a broad range of immunological conditions. Immune-co-infection dynamics shape helminth prevalence and burden. Even without host behavioural variation, our simulations generate aggregated worm burdens from heterogeneity in helminth exposure, microbial exposure and immune function alone. This study demonstrates how alterations to cellular immune function compound with co-infection at the within-host level to cascade into profound population-level effects. This article is part of the theme issue 'Ecological and evolutionary interactions between parasites across scales'.

articles.title: Is within-host viral community assembly shaped by local adaptation?
articles.journal: Philosophical transactions of the Royal Society of London. Series B, Biological sciences
articles.abstract: Host-parasite coevolution describes the continuous reciprocal selection driving host defence and parasite infectivity, with direct consequences for disease dynamics. While abundant evidence exists for coevolution shaping host-parasite dynamics within the 'one host-one parasite' framework, hosts are typically infected by multiple parasites, and the extent to which coevolutionary processes shape within-host parasite communities remains poorly understood. Investigating interactions between parasite communities and their hosts is essential for understanding how coevolution drives parasite diversity, competition and coexistence within hosts. Local adaptation, where parasites perform better on their local hosts compared to other hosts, arises from coevolutionary processes and can be tested using reciprocal transplant experiments. Here, we investigated the effect of coevolution on within-host viral community assembly, by reciprocally transplanting individuals of the host Plantago lanceolata into wild populations during natural viral epidemics. We combined small-RNA sequencing to identify the viral communities and joint species distribution modelling to quantify the effects of local adaptation and host characteristics on viral community assembly. Our results show that host origins vary in the extent to which local adaptation influences within-host viral diversity. Host maternal line and host origin emerged as key factors strongly influencing viral community composition and infection status. The influence of host characteristics varied across virus families, suggesting virus-specific assembly processes and variation in the potential for coevolution to shape these interactions. This article is part of the theme issue 'Ecological and evolutionary interactions between parasites across scales'.

articles.title: Tracking evolutionary costs of pathogen resistance against single versus co-infecting pathogens.
articles.journal: Philosophical transactions of the Royal Society of London. Series B, Biological sciences
articles.abstract: Immunity against pathogens is costly and can adversely affect fitness through resource allocation or physiological trade-offs. Infection by multiple pathogens may further worsen the effects if hosts require the activation of multiple immune responses, which in turn can elevate the overall immunological costs. Poor body condition and stressful environments can also exacerbate these trade-offs. In this study, we experimentally tested these possibilities using Tribolium castaneum populations that were evolving against either a single or a set of co-infecting bacterial pathogens. Contrary to our expectations, none of these evolved beetles showed any measurable trade-offs between pathogen resistance versus major fitness traits, such as reproduction or lifespan. Instead, they appeared to increase reproductive success and resistance to starvation, suggesting improved body condition that could mask underlying fitness costs. However, evolved beetles showed reduced quinone production, an externally secreted antimicrobial defence, indicating trade-offs between internal versus external immunity. Finally, we identified reproductive costs only under limited resource availability, but not under suboptimal resource quality, suggesting that trade-offs can be highly condition-dependent. Overall, this study provides a unique comparison across pathogens and infection types, highlighting the importance of analysing variation in life-history traits within relevant ecological contexts to understand fitness costs of evolving immunity. This article is part of the theme issue 'Ecological and evolutionary interactions between parasites across scales'.

articles.title: Impact of multiple infections and cross-kingdom interactions on rice virus population structure: field and experimental insights from Burkina Faso.
articles.journal: Philosophical transactions of the Royal Society of London. Series B, Biological sciences
articles.abstract: Multiple infections of hosts by various pathogen species or genotypes are common and may affect individual host health, yet their population-scale consequences remain relatively unexplored. Here, we investigate implications for pathogen evolution by testing whether the genetic structure of one pathogen is influenced by another in co-infection. We examined the evolution of an Africa-endemic rice virus of major agricultural importance, building on previous work documenting its genetic diversity and experimental evidence of interactions with a rice-infecting bacterium. We tested whether multiple infections, both within viral species (between viral genetic lineages) and between the two pathogens (virus and bacteria), impacted the structure of viral populations and fitness proxies, by combining field surveys with experimental work. We revealed high local viral diversity, documented multiple infections with distinct viral lineages in the field and detected various past recombination events between lineages. We found that the structure of viral genetic diversity is influenced not only by the location and year, but also by the presence of the bacteria in co-infections. Further, experimental infections show the contrasted performance of some viral lineages when evaluated in single versus multiple infections. Overall, these results suggest that multiple infections contribute to shape the genetic composition of viral populations. This article is part of the theme issue 'Ecological and evolutionary interactions between parasites across scales'.

articles.title: Exploring the consequences of co-infection interactions using within-host resource partitioning models.
articles.journal: Philosophical transactions of the Royal Society of London. Series B, Biological sciences
articles.abstract: Parasites rely on their hosts for resources, while hosts potentially require those same resources for mounting effective immune responses and meeting metabolic and reproductive requirements. Hosts in nature are often infected by more than one parasite strain or species, meaning that co-infecting parasites may also compete for resources. Previous mathematical modelling of single parasite infections showed that the structure of resource flows within a host influences the outcome of infections for both host and parasite. Here, we extend this modelling framework to understand how alternative resource structures, relating to the allocation and usage of host resources among co-infecting parasites and the immune system, influence the outcome of co-infection. Our analysis demonstrates that resource partitioning can produce four distinct co-infection outcomes, ranging from exclusion to coexistence with neutral or asymmetric effects on equilibrium parasite abundances, three of which are possible even when parasites are otherwise identical. These outcomes depend on whether parasites and immune responses share or partition resources, with immune-driven apparent competition and asymmetric access to host resources suppressing one or both parasites. Despite these suppressive effects, we find that total parasite abundance is typically higher in co-infections, implying worse outcomes for hosts. This article is part of the theme issue 'Ecological and evolutionary interactions between parasites across scales.'

articles.title: From low to high transmission: diversity-dependent responses of Plasmodium falciparum population structure to transmission intensity.
articles.journal: Philosophical transactions of the Royal Society of London. Series B, Biological sciences
articles.abstract: Genetic surveillance is increasingly used to characterize malaria transmission, yet genetic patterns can respond nonlinearly to transmission intensity and depend on diversity already present in parasite populations. To isolate these effects from migration, selection, treatment and host immunity, we developed a neutral stochastic agent-based model of a closed human-mosquito transmission system integrating SEIS (susceptible-exposed-infectious-susceptible) epidemiological dynamics with neutral Plasmodium falciparum haplotypes and mosquito-stage recombination, without mutation or de novo allele generation. By independently varying human biting availability (amax) and initial genetic diversity (π0), we examined their joint effects on infection complexity, recombination and parasite population structure across a continuous transmission gradient. Infection prevalence and within-host infection complexity increased rapidly across low-to-intermediate transmission, whereas the effective recombination ratio and the number of recombinant haplotypes continued to increase across a broader range. Higher transmission was also associated with greater retention of human-stage parasite population genetic diversity (πH) and more even haplotype-frequency distributions, while initial genetic diversity constrained attainable genetic outcomes. Similar late-time population structures could be approached through different transient dynamics. Parasite population structure therefore reflects the interaction between transmission intensity and the genetic conditions on which transmission and recombination act, providing mechanistic expectations for interpreting malaria genetic surveillance patterns across heterogeneous transmission settings. This article is part of the theme issue 'Ecological and evolutionary interactions between parasites across scales'.

articles.title: Differing effects of parasite-parasite interaction types on the spatial epidemiology of co-circulating parasites.
articles.journal: Philosophical transactions of the Royal Society of London. Series B, Biological sciences
articles.abstract: Interactions among co-circulating parasite species influence infection risk and disease progression. Interactions can occur within hosts, e.g. altering susceptibility, or indirectly through host demography or movement, potentially affecting landscape-scale transmission. Despite their ubiquity, the spatial implications of these interactions have received limited attention. We combine spatially explicit modelling with laboratory experiments to investigate how parasite-parasite interactions influence disease spread. We model within-host, demographic and dispersal-related interactions across a linear landscape, showing that within-host interactions modifying host susceptibility have the strongest effects on parasite prevalence, spatial heterogeneity and rate of spread. These effects are amplified when parasites invade sequentially, generating pronounced patch-level priority effects. We tested these predictions experimentally using a protist host (Paramecium caudatum) and two bacterial parasites (Holospora undulata and Holospora obtusa). Consistent with model predictions, we found that H. obtusa reduces the overall prevalence and spread of H. undulata across a landscape of interconnected patches, likely through reductions in host susceptibility, and evidence of priority effects, observing reduced H. undulata prevalence when introduced after H. obtusa. Our results highlight that parasite-parasite interactions can have important implications for the landscape-scale epidemiology of co-circulating parasites, but the effect magnitude depends on the interaction type and the timing of invasion. This article is part of the theme issue 'Ecological and evolutionary interactions between parasites across scales'.

articles.title: The impact of co-infection on population stability and chaos.
articles.journal: Philosophical transactions of the Royal Society of London. Series B, Biological sciences
articles.abstract: Parasites play an outsized role in mediating the persistence and stability of host populations. Flour beetles (Tribolium spp.) have long served as classic examples of population dynamics under both disease-free and infected conditions, with elegant combinations of theory and experiments demonstrating, for example, that cannibalism rates can push populations from stability to chaos. As with most organisms in nature, however, flour beetles rarely face just one parasite species, and co-infecting parasites can antagonize or facilitate each other through resources and immunity. To test the prediction that non-neutral interactions would qualitatively alter population stability, we reworked a classic stage-structured discrete-time model to include single and multiple infections and performed sensitivity and bifurcation analyses to identify the most important (co)infection-associated parameters for population stability. The model predicts that stability is highly sensitive to parasite transmission mode regardless of infection multiplicity, but facilitation among parasites rapidly drives populations into oscillations and chaos under effectively realistic conditions. This study identifies an important mechanism for explaining population variability and highlights the importance of within-host mechanisms for driving dynamics at higher levels of biological organization. This article is part of the theme issue 'Ecological and evolutionary interactions between parasites across scales'.

articles.title: Helminth co-infection facilitates gammaherpesvirus infection in the wood mouse Apodemus sylvaticus.
articles.journal: Philosophical transactions of the Royal Society of London. Series B, Biological sciences
articles.abstract: Helminths are widespread parasites that can modulate host immunity, potentially increasing susceptibility to viral infections. However, evidence for these effects varies across systems and environments, and links between laboratory and wild populations remain unclear. We developed a tractable system using wood mice, Heligmosomoides spp. nematodes and wood mouse herpesvirus (WMHV) to bridge this gap. Combining laboratory and field experiments with population modelling, we examined how helminth infection, anthelmintic treatment and diet affect viral dynamics. Across laboratory and field data, helminth infection generally increased susceptibility to WMHV, with stronger effects apparent at higher worm burdens. Furthermore, our field results showed that anthelmintic treatment reduced subsequent viral infection. Our population-level modelling, parameterized from our field data, suggested that helminth burden-dependent facilitation can generate nonlinear effects on viral spread, dependent on helminth virulence. Our findings highlight the potential importance of helminths as facilitators of viral infections and suggest that anthelmintic treatment may provide indirect benefits for viral control. We also show the value of integrating laboratory and field approaches on the same (or closely related) species, in particular the potential offered by the wood mouse-Heligmosomoides-WMHV system, to understand the drivers and consequences of host-helminth-viral interactions. This article is part of the theme issue 'Ecological and evolutionary interactions between parasites across scales'.

articles.title: When two parasites are better than one: interactions between brood parasitism and ectoparasitism across ecological scales.
articles.journal: Philosophical transactions of the Royal Society of London. Series B, Biological sciences
articles.abstract: Parasites rarely occur in isolation, yet the ecological consequences of interactions among co-occurring parasites remain poorly understood in natural systems. Here, we examined the interactions between an ectoparasitic fly (Philornis torquans) and a brood-parasitic bird (the shiny cowbird, Molothrus bonariensis) sharing a common host, the rufous hornero (Furnarius rufus), using seven breeding seasons of field data from central Argentina. At the brood level, the presence of cowbird nestlings increased both the prevalence and abundance of P. torquans larvae, indicating facilitation via enhanced brood attractiveness. However, within parasitized broods, larvae were disproportionately diverted towards cowbird nestlings, substantially reducing the parasitic burden experienced by hornero chicks. In addition, the negative association between parasite burden and hornero survival was weaker in the presence of cowbirds, a pattern consistent with increased tolerance. As a result, coinfection disproportionately harmed the brood parasite and reduced the net impact of both parasites on host survival, yielding lower fitness costs for horneros than infection by either parasite alone. These findings demonstrate that coinfection outcomes emerge from interactions operating across ecological levels, linking individual-level parasite allocation to brood-level survival consequences, and underscore the importance of multi-parasite perspectives for understanding the ecological and evolutionary dynamics of parasitism. This article is part of the theme issue 'Ecological and evolutionary interactions between parasites across scales'.

articles.title: The combined effects of co-exposure and temperature on a planktonic crustacean.
articles.journal: Philosophical transactions of the Royal Society of London. Series B, Biological sciences
articles.abstract: Changes in water temperature that occur seasonally or owing to climate change can strongly influence aquatic ecosystems. Zooplankton are particularly susceptible to such changes owing to their inability to regulate body temperature, which also affects their interactions with endoparasites. While hosts are naturally exposed to multiple parasite species, few studies have explored the joint effects of temperature and multiple parasite exposure on zooplankton-endoparasite interactions. We used the planktonic crustacean Daphnia magna and exposed newborns to four temperatures: 16, 20, 24 and 28°C. At each temperature, groups were exposed to the fungi Australozyma monospora (Am), microsporidium Hamiltosporidium tvaerminnensis (Ht) or both (simultaneously and sequentially). Though we found no evidence for co-infection by both parasite species in a single host, both temperature and the sequence of exposure significantly affected infection traits. Ht prevalence was suppressed by Am across all exposure sequences. Interestingly, this suppression remained even after Am prevalence was reduced by higher temperatures, suggesting that Am's negative effect on Ht does not depend on Am successfully infecting the host. We identified a temperature-dependent priority effect where prior exposure to Ht mitigated the developmental costs of heat stress on Am. While Am spores per degree day generally declined at 28°C, an initial exposure of the host to Ht buffered this reduction, allowing Am to maintain a similar development rate as at lower temperatures. Our results demonstrate that the relationship between environmental conditions and host-multiple parasite interactions may yield unexpected results. In times of climate change, our results highlight the importance of studying the effects of environmental variation and multiple parasite exposure in tandem rather than separately. This article is part of the theme issue 'Ecological and evolutionary interactions between parasites across scales'.

articles.title: Sex Differences in Response to Early Post-Myocardial Infarction Cardiac Rehabilitation.
articles.journal: Catheterization and cardiovascular interventions : official journal of the Society for Cardiac Angiography & Interventions
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Early post-myocardial infarction (MI) cardiac rehabilitation (CR) improves patient outcomes; however, sex-specific patterns of functional recovery and their clinical determinants remain insufficiently characterized.

AIMS: The aim of this study was to compare functional capacity and its change during early post-MI cardiac rehabilitation between women and men, and to identify sex-specific clinical factors associated with functional capacity.

METHODS: This observational study included 173 consecutive post-MI patients referred to early post-MI CR. Patients with paired 6-min walk test (6MWT) assessments at CR initiation and completion were included in the analysis. Within-sex changes and between-sex differences in changes were assessed. Sex-stratified linear and logistic regression models were also performed.

RESULTS: Among patients included in the analysis, 68.9% were men, and the mean age was 61.6 ± 10.7 years. Women were older and had lower functional capacity at baseline and at the program completion (both p < 0.001). 6MWT distance increased in both sexes (women p = 0.001; men p < 0.001). The median increase in 6MWT distance was higher in men than in women (52.50 [26.25; 80.00] vs. 35.00 [3.75; 61.25] m; p = 0.028). CR responder proportions were 62.9% and 32.1%, respectively (p = 0.011). Total and LDL-cholesterol decreased in both sexes, with larger reductions in men in comparisons of changes (p = 0.027 and p = 0.003). Older age was associated with shorter 6MWT distance in both sexes (p < 0.001), and atrial fibrillation was associated with lower capacity in men. Associations for diabetes, coronary disease burden, and renal function in women were not consistently supported by multivariable analyses.

CONCLUSIONS: Early CR was associated with improved functional capacity in both sexes, although women had lower functional capacity at baseline and program completion, and had lower increase of 6MWT distance. Age and atrial fibrillation were associated with reduced functional capacity in men, while observed associations in women require cautious interpretation. These findings need further research on individualized supportive strategies during post-MI CR.

articles.title: Confirmation of Fusion Superiority of P-15 Peptide Enhanced Bone Graft versus Autograft Control in Transforaminal Lumbar Interbody Fusion.
articles.abstract: Study Design: Randomized controlled trial.Objectives: The objective of this supplemental analysis was to confirm superiority of fusion of P-15L (PearlMatrixTM P-15 Peptide Enhanced Bone Graft) compared with local autograft control at 6-, 12-, and 24-months.Methods: Skeletally mature patients with degenerative disc disease were randomized 1:1 to P-15L or the local autograft (control) during single-level transforaminal lumbar interbody fusion with a polyetheretherketone cage and supplemental pedicle screw fixation. The data analysis used a gatekeeping strategy such that fusion rates at 6-, 12-, and 24-months could not be compared unless (1) the primary endpoint demonstrated that P-15L was non-inferior to the control with respect to Composite Clinical Success at Month 24, and (2) Kaplan-Meier (KM) and statistics confirmed the superiority of P-15L relative to control in the time-to-fusion distribution. If the conditions of the gatekeeping strategy were met, fusion rates at the individual timepoints could be analyzed with the Wald z-test.Results: All conditions of the gatekeeping strategy were met; thus, fusion rates at the individual timepoints were analyzed. The Wald z-test for superiority revealed that KM fusion rates of the P-15L group were superior to the control group at 6-, 12-, and 24-months (P<0.0001 at all timepoints). Compared with control, P-15L demonstrated a 30.7%, 27.3%, and 26.2% higher fusion rate at 6-, 12-, and 24-months, respectively.Conclusions: Together, the results from the composite clinical success endpoint, time-to fusion, and the Wald z-tests robustly demonstrate that P-15L was superior to autograft in facilitating fusion at 6-, 12-, and 24-months.

articles.title: EXPRESS: Quantitative Physiological Modelling of Cerebral Blood Flow with an Outflow Model in [18F]FDG and [15O]H2O PET Imaging.
articles.journal: Journal of cerebral blood flow and metabolism : official journal of the International Society of Cerebral Blood Flow and Metabolism
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Conventional PET kinetic models, such as the one-tissue compartment model (1TCM), often aggregate distinct physiological processes- specifically cerebral blood flow (CBF) and permeability- into a single influx constant, K1. Long axial field-of-view (LAFOV) PET scanners provide the high temporal resolution necessary to capture rapid tracer kinetics and isolate these individual parameters.

METHODS: This study evaluated a microvascular compartment model (MCM) using dynamic PET data from 15 healthy subjects. Each subject underwent two [15O]H2O scans and one [18F]FDG scan. The MCM was initially compared with derived K1 values from the standard 1TCM for [15O]H2O. Subsequently, the MCM-derived CBF estimates from the early phase of [18F]FDG scans were compared against gold-standard [15O]H2O CBF measurements.

RESULTS: MCM-derived K1 values for water showed excellent agreement with 1TCM (ICC = 0.998). Crucially, CBF estimates derived from the early phase of [18F]FDG scans (57.6±11.6 ml/100g/min) were highly comparable to gold-standard [15O]H2O values (58.7±11.9 ml/100g/min), with a strong correlation (ICC = 0.92).

CONCLUSION: The MCM effectively leverages LAFOV PET sensitivity to provide a detailed physiological breakdown of tissue transport. This approach enables the extraction of quantitatively accurate CBF measurements from routine [18F]FDG scans, potentially eliminating the need for separate CBF scans in clinical practice.

articles.title: Ultra-processed foods intake and risk of Helicobacter pylori infection: A prospective cohort study.
articles.abstract: Ultra-processed foods (UPFs) are closely associated with gut microbiota diversity and functionality. The gut microbiota plays a role in developing Helicobacter pylori (H. pylori) infection. However, no cohort studies have explored the association between UPFs intake and the risk of H. pylori infection in the general population. In total, 1,769 participants without baseline H. pylori infection were enrolled in this study from the TCLSIH Cohort Study. Information on UPFs intake was obtained from a validated food frequency questionnaire, and H. pylori infection was diagnosed by using the 13C-urea breath test. Multivariable Cox proportional hazards regression models adjusted for potential confounding factors were used to examine the association between UPFs intake and the risk of H. pylori infection. During a median follow-up of 2.0 years, the incidence rate of H. pylori infection was 20.92%. The multivariable-adjusted hazard ratios (HR; 95% confidence intervals) of H. pylori infection across increasing quartiles of UPFs intake were 1.00 (reference), 1.12 (0.79, 1.58), 0.84 (0.57, 1.23) and 0.86 (0.57, 1.29) (P for trend = 0.24) in males, and 1.00 (reference), 1.41 (0.74, 2.69), 1.49 (0.77, 2.88) and 2.72 (1.39, 5.33) (P for trend < 0.01) in females, respectively. This study shows that higher UPFs intake is associated with a higher risk of H. pylori infection in females, while no association was found in males. Further studies are needed to confirm these findings.

articles.title: Metal-Phenolic Nanoplatforms: Zinc-Loaded Mesoporous Catechin Microneedles for Multi-Mechanistic Healing of Diabetic Oral Ulcers.
articles.abstract: Diabetic oral ulcers remain challenging to treat due to persistent inflammation, bacterial infection, and impaired regeneration. Herein, we report mesoporous catechin nanospheres (MCNs) as a versatile platform for multi-metal ion delivery and their integration into a microneedle (MN) patch for ulcer therapy. MCNs, synthesized via interfacial assembly, exhibit high surface area and well-defined mesoporosity, enabling efficient coordination with a broad range of therapeutic metal ions, including but not limited to Zn2 +, Sr2 +, Cu2 +, and Mn2 +. Zinc-coordinated MCNs (Zn@MCNs) demonstrate pH-responsive release, enabling on-demand delivery within the acidic wound microenvironment. When loaded into dissolvable gelatin methacryloyl (GelMA) microneedles (MN-Zn@MCNs), the patch achieves effective mucosal penetration and sustained drug release. In vitro and in vivo studies reveal that MN-Zn@MCNs exhibit immunomodulation by promoting M2 macrophage polarization, broad-spectrum antibacterial activity, and potent reactive oxygen species (ROS) scavenging. In a diabetic rat model, the patch significantly accelerates ulcer closure, re-epithelialization, angiogenesis, and collagen deposition. Transcriptomic analysis implicates regulation of the PI3K-Akt pathway. This work establishes MCNs as a metal-phenolic nanoplatform for multimodal ion delivery, offering a promising strategy for diabetic oral ulcer management and a versatile blueprint for next-generation wound healing materials.

articles.title: From calcium handling to whole-heart function: Insights into diastolic dysfunction across experimental models of heart failure with preserved ejection fraction.
Longitudinal trajectories of plasma biomarkers, amyloid-β burden and cognitive decline in Alzheimer's disease.
authors: for Alzheimer’s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI), Foundation for the National Institutes of Health (FNIH) Biomarkers Consortium Plasma Aβ and Phosphorylated Tau as Predictors of Amyloid and Tau Positivity in Alzheimer's Disease Project Team
articles.abstract: Plasma p-tau217 biomarkers support Alzheimer's diagnosis but most evidence remains cross-sectional. Understanding how these biomarkers change over time, whether assays perform similarly, and how such changes relate to Aβ plaque accumulation and cognitive decline is needed to guide patient care. We analyzed 393 cognitively unimpaired and impaired participants from the ADNI-FNIH consortium (mean age 72.7 years; 49% female; 37% Aβ-PET positive) with longitudinal plasma biomarkers across 14 assays, Aβ-PET and cognitive assessments over a mean follow-up of 5.4 years. Plasma p-tau217 was measured across five assays, and Aβ42/40, p-tau181, GFAP and NfL were examined in secondary analyses. Linear mixed-effects models estimated individual rates of change for plasma biomarkers, Aβ-PET Centiloids, and cognitive performance. Linear regressions related concurrent rates of change in plasma biomarkers, Centiloids and cognition in the whole group, by Aβ-PET status, and by Aβ and tau (AT) PET status in a subsample of 272 participants. For comparison, analogous cross-sectional analyses examined associations between plasma biomarker levels and baseline Centiloids or cognitive performance. Finally, semipartial R² values were calculated across all models to quantify the relative variance explained by plasma biomarker and other covariates. Plasma p-tau217 levels increased across all five assays (standardized β = 0.06-0.08, P < 0.001), whereas Aβ42/40 was largely stable. Among Aβ-PET negative individuals, greater p-tau217 increases were consistently associated with concurrent Aβ accumulation (standardized β = 0.40-0.52, P < 0.001), but not in Aβ-PET positive individuals. Conversely, greater p-tau217 increases were most strongly associated with cognitive decline in Aβ-PET positive individuals (standardized β = 0.41-0.56, P < 0.001). In the tau-PET subsample, p-tau217 change was associated with Aβ accumulation in A-T- and, to a lesser extent, A+T- individuals, but not in A+T+ individuals. P-tau217 was the largest contributor to Aβ-PET variance in longitudinal (20.9-28.8%) and cross-sectional (31.8-47.9%) models. For cognition, however, p-tau217 change was the largest contributor in longitudinal models (22.2-30.6%), whereas cognitive status contributed more than p-tau217 cross-sectionally. Although of lower magnitude than for p-tau217, rates of change in p-tau181 and GFAP showed similar stage-dependent associations. In earlier stages, longitudinal changes in p-tau217 paralleled ongoing Aβ accumulation, whereas once Aβ pathology was established, p-tau217 change was more closely associated with cognitive decline than with further Aβ accumulation. These findings indicate that p-tau217 reflects an early Aβ-associated tau response before aggregated tau pathology, supporting the value of longitudinal p-tau217 for stage-dependent disease monitoring.

articles.title: Reward-based motor learning in post-stroke hemiparesis.
Beyond resection: liver transplantation in biliary malignancies.
articles.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Biliary malignancies comprise a heterogeneous group of tumors with distinct anatomic locations and biologic behaviors. Although surgical resection remains the standard curative-intent treatment, liver transplantation (LT) has emerged in selected settings, making it important to define when transplantation is justified.

AREAS COVERED: PubMed searches for English-language literature, without a lower publication-date restriction, were updated through 22 September 2026, supplemented by reference lists, current society guidelines, consensus statements, and organ-allocation policy documents. This review examines LT for perihilar cholangiocarcinoma (pCCA), intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma (iCCA), combined hepatocellular-cholangiocarcinoma (cHCC-CCA), gallbladder cancer, and distal extrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma. We discuss historical evolution, selection criteria, neoadjuvant strategies, outcomes and pretransplant dropout, technical morbidity after neoadjuvant radiotherapy, allocation policy, living-donor considerations, and future directions.

EXPERT OPINION: The strongest evidence supports LT for highly selected, protocol-compliant pCCA; for iCCA, LT remains an emerging, biology-driven indication limited to two distinct settings: very early incidental tumors in cirrhosis or unresectable liver-confined disease with durable stability after systemic therapy. cHCC-CCA remains selected and controversial, and evidence is insufficient to support routine LT for gallbladder cancer or distal extrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma; expansion should be guided by biologic selection rather than by anatomic considerations alone.

articles.title: Long-term multi-organ trajectories after complete repair of tetralogy of Fallot: a nationwide 22-year cohort study.
articles.journal: European heart journal. Quality of care & clinical outcomes
articles.abstract:
AIMS: Survival after repair of tetralogy of Fallot exceeds 90% at 30 years, but the long-term burden beyond the heart is poorly characterised. We described how complications accumulate across organ systems after complete repair and whether the first complication is prognostic.

METHODS: Using the Korean National Health Insurance Service database (2002-2024), we identified 2,798 patients with complete repair of tetralogy of Fallot without pulmonary atresia or a coded genetic syndrome, applying a 30-day landmark. Cumulative incidence across six organ systems was estimated with death as a competing risk and compared across four surgical eras with era-only and covariate-adjusted Fine-Gray models. Trajectories were analysed from the first complication, excluding the defining event.

RESULTS: Neurological events were most frequent (10-year cumulative incidence 21.0%). A first organ event occurred in 1,086 patients (38.8%). Involvement of a further organ system reached 31.6% at five years after a cardiac-first event versus 20.6% after an extracardiac-first event (sub-distribution hazard ratio 0.72, 95% confidence interval 0.55-0.95), and death occurred in 11.0% versus 1.5% (P<0.001); excluding first-year events attenuated the difference (0.85, 0.57-1.26). Endocrine/metabolic risk rose across eras (adjusted ratios 2.23, 3.65, 4.39) whereas arrhythmia, a comparison outcome, did not. Male sex was associated with cardiac but not extracardiac events.

CONCLUSIONS: After complete repair, most complications arose outside the heart, but an early cardiac first complication marked faster multi-organ involvement and higher mortality. The type and timing of the first complication may help direct lifelong multidisciplinary surveillance.

Domiciliary High-Flow Nasal Cannula in Chronic Respiratory Failure due to COPD: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Evidence for home high-flow nasal cannula (HFNC) in COPD with chronic respiratory failure remains uncertain.

METHODS: We searched PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Web of Science, OpenAlex (from 2010) and ClinicalTrials.gov through 1 August 2026, and CENTRAL on 6 November 2026, for randomized trials in adults with COPD and chronic respiratory failure comparing home HFNC (≥4 weeks) with usual care, long-term oxygen therapy or home non-invasive ventilation (NIV). We used Hartung-Knapp random-effects intervals, RoB 2 and GRADE.

RESULTS: Six trials (588 participants) differed in hypercapnia selection and clinical stability. All pooled estimates favoured HFNC, but confidence intervals included the null. The moderate-to-severe exacerbation rate ratio was 0.51 (Hartung-Knapp 95% CI 0.01-18.35). Mean differences were -8.83 points (-18.56 to 0.89) on the St George's Respiratory Questionnaire, -2.36 mmHg (-6.71 to 1.99) for daytime PaCO2 and -4.05 mmHg (-14.55 to 6.45) for nocturnal transcutaneous CO2. Evidence for admissions (one trial) and mortality (two trials) was inconclusive. In one six-week crossover trial, CO2 change with HFNC was non-inferior to home NIV within a prespecified 5 mmHg margin. Certainty was low to very low.

CONCLUSION: Home HFNC may reduce exacerbations, carbon dioxide and symptom burden in a heterogeneous population with COPD and chronic respiratory failure, but no pooled estimate was statistically robust. Non-inferiority for a physiological surrogate does not establish clinical equivalence with NIV; the review does not establish HFNC as an alternative to NIV and does not support a treatment recommendation. Adequately powered trials in a clearly specified population are needed.

articles.title: Patient Characteristics Associated with Size and Location of Left Atrial Low Voltage Areas in Atrial Fibrillation Patients Undergoing Pulmonary Vein Isolation.
