articles.title: The role of high-dose chemotherapy with autologous stem cell transplantation in adults with mature T-cell lymphomas.
articles.journal: The Cochrane database of systematic reviews
articles.abstract:
RATIONALE: Mature T-cell lymphomas (MTCL) are a rare, heterogeneous group of malignant tumours arising from mature T lymphocytes, generally associated with a poor prognosis. Polychemotherapy has long been the standard treatment for most MTCL subtypes. High-dose therapy followed by autologous stem cell transplantation (autoSCT) and allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplantation (alloSCT) have been investigated to improve overall survival (OS). Given the rarity and poor prognosis of MTCL, an up-to-date systematic review and meta-analysis of the available evidence is warranted.

OBJECTIVES: To assess the benefits and harms of autologous stem cell transplantation in the treatment of mature T-cell lymphoma in adults (≥ 18 years of age) compared to any other treatment, particularly with respect to its efficacy and safety as a consolidation strategy following first-line therapy, and secondarily, for its efficacy as a salvage option.

SEARCH METHODS: We searched CENTRAL Ovid, MEDLINE Ovid, Embase Ovid, conference proceedings, and two trial registries, supplemented by reference checking, citation searching, and contact with study authors, for studies published between January 1990 and October 2025.

ELIGIBILITY CRITERIA: We included prospectively planned trials evaluating autoSCT as first-line or salvage treatment for MTCL. Retrospective studies were excluded because prospective evidence was available. We excluded trials in which fewer than 80% of participants had MTCL, unless subgroup data for these participants were available from the publication or were provided by the trial authors.

OUTCOMES: We analysed overall survival (OS), progression-free survival (PFS), response rate (RR), treatment-related mortality (TRM), adverse events grades 3 and 4 (AE), and quality of life (QoL).

RISK OF BIAS: We assessed risk of bias using the Cochrane RoB 2 tool for randomised controlled trials (RCTs). The certainty of evidence was assessed using the GRADE approach for OS, PFS, RR, TRM, QoL, and grades 3 and 4 AEs.

SYNTHESIS METHODS: We followed standard Cochrane methodology and performed study selection and risk of bias assessment in duplicate by two independent review authors.

INCLUDED STUDIES: We included two RCTs investigating the role of autoSCT as first-line therapy and one retrospective subgroup analysis of an RCT investigating autoSCT in relapsed/refractory (r/r) disease, entailing a total participant number of 190. We identified three ongoing RCTs including participants in first complete remission comparing autoSCT to chemotherapy only, and one ongoing RCT comparing chidamide, carmustin, etoposid, cytarabin melphalan (Chi-BEAM) to BEAM as induction before autoSCT. The overall risk of bias of the included RCTs identified some concerns, due to the small number of participants, heterogeneity of the study populations, and missing outcome data. We rated the evidence for all outcomes as low to very low certainty, due to the very small number of events and study design.

SYNTHESIS OF RESULTS: Meta-analysis was not possible because we only included three RCTs. Therefore, we synthesised the results narratively following the Synthesis Without Meta-analysis (SWiM) reporting guideline. We assessed the certainty of the evidence using the GRADE approach. Three RCTs involving 190 participants with MTCL evaluated autoSCT. One RCT (103 participants) compared autoSCT with alloSCT, one RCT (28 participants) compared autoSCT with chemotherapy alone, and one included a subgroup analysis of 59 participants with peripheral T-cell lymphoma (PTCL) from a larger RCT of 619 participants with relapsed or refractory B-cell and T-cell lymphoma. AutoSCT compared to alloSCT for adults with mature T-cell lymphomas in the first-line setting AutoSCT compared to alloSCT may result in little to no difference in OS (hazard ratio(HR) 0.76, 95% confidence interval (CI) 0.41 to 1.42; 1 RCT, 103 participants; low-certainty evidence), and PFS (HR 1.11, 95% CI 0.70 to 1.88; 1 RCT, 103 participants; low-certainty evidence), at two years. It may be associated with a lower TRM (risk ratio (RR) 0.07, 95% CI 0.00 to 1.21; 1 RCT, 103 participants; low certainty evidence), and shows little to no difference in overall response rate (ORR; RR 0.97, 95% CI 0.69 to 1.37; 1 RCT, 103 participants; low-certainty evidence). There may be little to no difference in the number of adverse events of grades 3 to 5 (RR 0.91; 95% CI 0.57 to 1.44; 1 RCT, 103 participants; low-certainty evidence) between autoSCT and alloSCT. However, the evidence for these outcomes is uncertain. QoL was not reported. AutoSCT compared to chemotherapy alone with mature T-cell lymphoma in the first-line setting The evidence is very uncertain about the effect of autoSCT compared to chemotherapy only on OS (40% versus 45% after 5 years), and PFS (40% versus 38% after 5 years); 1 RCT, 28 participants. TRM, ORR, AE, and QoL were not reported. AutoSCT for adults with mature T-cell lymphoma in the relapsed/refractory setting The evidence is very uncertain about the effect of autoSCT on OS (42% after 2 years) in those with relapsed/refractory MTCL (1 RCT, 59 participants). PFS, TRM, ORR, AE, and QoL were not reported.

AUTHORS' CONCLUSIONS: We included two RCTs evaluating autoSCT in the first-line setting and one evaluating autoSCT as salvage treatment. Data extraction was challenging due to substantial differences in control groups, study designs, intervention details, and reported outcomes. The certainty of the evidence was low to very low, mainly due to the small sample sizes and substantial heterogeneity across study designs and populations. Therefore, we are unable to draw definitive conclusions. Four ongoing RCTs may provide additional evidence, and future updates of this review may allow more robust conclusions. Further RCTs or well-designed comparative studies with similar control groups are needed to clarify the role of autoSCT in MTCL. Standardised reporting of clinically relevant outcomes, particularly overall survival and progression-free survival, would improve future evidence synthesis.

FUNDING: Department of Internal Medicine, Centre for Integrated Oncology Aachen Bonn Cologne Duesseldorf, Faculty of Medicine and University Hospital Cologne, University of Cologne.

REGISTRATION: Protocol available via DOI 10.1002/14651858.CD014671.

articles.title: Intracranial artery stenosis with RNF213 p.Arg4810Lys variant (rs112735431) exhibits less basilar artery bending.
articles.abstract: BackgroundPrevious studies have linked the RNF213 c.14429G>A (p.Arg4810Lys; rs112735431) variant to intracranial arterial stenosis/occlusion, particularly in the anterior circulation, but its association with posterior circulation morphology remains unclear.MethodsIn this retrospective multicenter study, basilar artery (BA) morphology was evaluated using magnetic resonance angiography in 241 Japanese patients with anterior circulation intracranial arterial stenosis (ICAS) without moyamoya disease. BA morphology was classified into three types, and BA bending length (BL) was measured. Multivariable linear regression adjusted for vascular risk factors and other potential confounders. Interobserver and intraobserver reliability were assessed in separate subsets of 40 patients each.ResultsOf 241 patients, 68 (28.2%) carried the RNF213 p.Arg4810Lys variant. Carriers were more frequently female and less likely to have diabetes than non-carriers. Straight or tilted BA morphology was more frequent in carriers (57.4% vs. 22.0%; p < .001). BL was shorter in carriers (median [IQR], 0.00 [0.00-1.77] vs. 2.17 [1.00-3.75] mm; p < .001, Mann-Whitney U test). The mean difference was -1.47 mm (95% CI, -1.87 to -1.08 mm). The association persisted after adjustment (adjusted β, -1.44 mm; 95% CI, -1.94 to -0.94 mm; p < .001). Interobserver and intraobserver agreement was high for BA classification (weighted κ = 0.900 and 0.947, respectively) and BL measurements (ICC = 0.933 and 0.980, respectively).ConclusionsIn Japanese patients with anterior circulation ICAS, the RNF213 p.Arg4810Lys variant was associated with reduced BA bending.

articles.title: Day-15 MRD ≥ 20% Identifies a Very High-Risk Subset in Pediatric T-Cell Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia: A CCLG-ALL 2008 Single-Center Study.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: We evaluated long-term outcomes (median follow-up >12.5 years) of pediatric T-ALL treated via the CCLG-ALL 2008 protocol. Although D33 MRD is an established response marker, it may not fully capture the heterogeneity of early treatment response. We therefore evaluated whether D15 FCM-MRD provides additional prognostic information in children with T-ALL.

METHODS: We retrospectively analyzed 140 T-ALL patients (124 with evaluable flow-cytometric MRD). The optimal D15 MRD cutoff was identified via maximally selected rank statistics. Analyses incorporated multivariable Cox regression, bootstrapping, and competing risk models.

RESULTS: Ten-year event-free (EFS) and overall survival (n = 140) were 69.5% and 83.2%, respectively. The optimal cutoff, D15 MRD ≥ 20%, refined the conventional ≥ 10% high-risk category, predicting inferior 10-year EFS (45.4% vs. 76.8%, p = 0.002). Crucially, among patients achieving D33 MRD < 1%, D15 ≥ 20% still conferred poor outcomes (10-year EFS: 50.0% vs. 77.9%, p = 0.014), whereas D15 10%-19.9% outcomes mirrored those of D15 < 10%. D15 ≥ 20% remained an independent prognosticator (HR = 2.85; 95% CI: 1.38-5.90; p = 0.005) across internal validations. Additionally, D15 ≥ 20% predicted disproportionate treatment-related mortality (TRM; cause-specific HR = 5.49; p = 0.006), with a 10-year incidence of 25.0%. Dual D15 ≥ 20%/D33 ≥ 1% positivity identified extreme risk (HR = 4.41; p = 0.008).

CONCLUSIONS: D15 FCM-MRD ≥ 20% identified a small subgroup of patients with an increased risk of relapse and inferior survival, including patients who subsequently achieved D33 MRD < 1%. These findings require validation in a larger independent cohort.

articles.title: Inter-reader reliability and clinical validity of the MRI grading system for lumbar foraminal stenosis among radiologists and clinicians.
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVES: To assess the interobserver reliability of the Lee system among radiologists and clinicians.

METHODS: A total of 73 patients who underwent MRI of the lumbar spine included. Six interpreters evaluated the degree of lumbar foraminal stenosis (LFS) from the L2-3 to the L5-S1 levels after training the Lee system. A different neurosurgeon assessed the associated clinical manifestations of each patient. The κ statistics were used to analyse the interreader agreement among the radiologists and clinicians. The clinical correlations between stenosis grade and positive clinical manifestations (PCM) were assessed using nonparametric correlation analysis (Spearman's correlation).

RESULTS: There was almost perfect agreement between the trainees (κ = 0.96), radiologists (κ = 0.89), and clinicians (κ = 0.82). The agreements between the radiologist and trainee (κ = 0.78) and between the radiologist and clinician (κ = 0.77) were substantial. Correlation analysis between clinical symptoms and grade for the six readers suggested a moderate correlation, with R ranging from 0.619 to 0.662.

CONCLUSION: The Lee system for LFS demonstrated substantial to almost perfect inter-reader reliability across radiologists, trainees, and clinicians, regardless of differences in reader experience. Furthermore, each group showed a moderate correlation between MRI grades and patients' clinical symptoms.

ADVANCES IN KNOWLEDGE: The Lee system for LFS can be applied with substantial to almost perfect inter-reader reliability not only by radiologists but also by trainees and clinicians without radiologic training, supporting its use where subspecialty expertise is unavailable.

articles.title: Herbal Medicine in Prevention and Treatment of Type 2 Diabetes.
articles.journal: The American journal of Chinese medicine
articles.abstract: Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) is one of the most common chronic diseases, affecting 537 million adults worldwide, a number projected to rise to 783 million by 2045. Single-target agents lower glucose but act weakly on the inflammatory, oxidative and microbial features driving residual complication risk. Chinese herbal medicine addresses this limitation. This review summarizes current evidence on Chinese herbal medicine in the prevention and treatment of T2DM, covering single herbs, active constituents and classic formulas. Herbal medicines and constituents act simultaneously on insulin signaling, inflammation, oxidative stress and the gut microbiota, a profile matching the multifactorial pathophysiology of T2DM and complementing current pharmacotherapy. Added to standard therapy, herbal interventions improve glycemia, insulin resistance and β-cell function, and slow progression from prediabetes to diabetes, with a low incidence of hypoglycemia. Single herbs (Coptis chinensis, Panax ginseng, Pueraria lobata), active constituents (berberine, puerarin, quercetin, baicalin, ginsenoside Rb1), and classic formulas (Ge-Gen-Qin-Lian Decoction, Liu-Wei-Di-Huang Pill) activate AMPK and PI3K/Akt-GLUT4 signaling, preserve β-cell identity and survival, and remodel the gut microbiota and bile acid pool. The gut is a recurrent upstream site of action, so that the low oral bioavailability of several constituents is part of the mechanism rather than a limitation. Mechanistic evidence remains predominantly preclinical, batch variability limits reproducibility, and no trial reviewed here reports cardiovascular or renal hard endpoints. Chinese herbal medicine represents a promising adjunct to standard type 2 diabetes care, offering a mechanistic breadth that addresses residual complication risks. To validate these broader metabolic benefits, future clinical trials must evaluate its efficacy against definitive clinical endpoints.

articles.title: Comorbidity Care Among Older Three-Year Cancer Survivors and Matched Noncancer Controls: Evidence from a Large Japanese Claims Database.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Over 80% of older adults in Japan live with multimorbidity, associated with poor quality of life and increased mortality. US studies report less comorbidity care among cancer survivors than noncancer controls, but evidence from other countries remains limited. This descriptive study compared comorbidity care between older adults with and without cancer using Japanese claims data.

MATERIALS AND METHODS: Using the DeSC Japanese claims database (April 2014-August 2023), we identified patients with gastric, colorectal, lung, breast, or prostate cancer surviving ≥36 months without active malignancy or hospice-care 13-36 months post-diagnosis; chemotherapy or radiotherapy recipients were retained. Noncancer controls were matched 2:1 by age, sex, and region. Condition-related outpatient follow-up was defined as ≥ 2 qualifying outpatient visits during the 24-month assessment period for coronary artery disease, heart failure, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and/or asthma, stroke/transient ischemic attack, and diabetes mellitus.

RESULTS: The study included 79,797 unique cancer survivors across five overlapping cancer-type cohorts, analyzed separately by cancer type. Cancer survivors had lower follow-up rates than controls across all comorbidities and cancer types, with risk differences ranging from -0.9 to - 12.8 percentage points and risk ratios ranging from 0.853 to 0.991. Absolute differences were larger for lung, gastric, and colorectal cancer survivors and smaller for prostate cancer survivors; rankings by risk difference and odds ratio differed for some comorbidities.

CONCLUSION: Older cancer survivors received less comorbidity care than controls, varying by cancer type. Patient-level research should determine whether stronger oncology-primary care collaboration could improve condition-related follow-up.

articles.title: CaV1.3 Ca2+ Channel Regulates Mouse Pancreatic β-Cell Mass, Gene Transcription, Electrical Activity, and Insulin Release in an Age-Dependent Manner.
articles.abstract: High voltage-gated Ca2+ channel 1.3 (CaV1.3) gain-of-function enhances glucose tolerance in mice and humans, while loss-of-function polymorphisms increase the risk of type 2 diabetes. Yet the functional role of CaV1.3 is not fully understood. Here, we investigate whether CaV1.3 deletion alters β-cell glucose-dependent excitability, gene expression, and β-cell mass. We can show that CaV1.3 contributes ∼25% of the β-cell Ca2+ influx, is not compensated by CaV1.2, and that its deletion alters the β-cell gene expression, mass, glucose-dependent excitability, and insulin release in an age-dependent manner. CaV1.3 is functionally expressed in murine β-cells and contributes to β-cell excitability.

articles.title: The "macrofication" of loneliness in public health research: Are there "lonely" societies?
articles.abstract: Loneliness is framed in public health policy as a pressing concern affecting the population. A substantial body of public health research has sought to estimate its prevalence across and within countries. Yet, the methodological constraints of these prevalence estimates are often overlooked. This article details common limitations in the prevailing positivist tradition of public health research and explains how the unproblematized "macrofication" of loneliness can lead to confusion and misleading conclusions. We identify three pervasive sources of bias in population-level loneliness estimates, namely, sampling bias, measurement heterogeneity, and culture-based reporting bias. We argue that widely discussed phenomena, like the "loneliness paradox," may, at least in part, reflect methodological artifacts, such as differential nonresponse, instrument choice, and cultural interpretation, rather than genuine differences in loneliness between macro-contexts. Using evidence from within national contexts, we demonstrate how different measurement approaches (direct vs indirect) shape subgroup patterns in loneliness estimates, including gender differences, thereby altering who is classified as lonely and which risks are inferred. We conclude that current methodological constraints warrant a more cautious interpretation of prevalence estimates and cross-national rankings on loneliness. Therefore, advancing a mixed-method and theory-informed research agenda for the "macrofication" of loneliness research is essential for a nuanced and context-sensitive understanding of loneliness in public health.

articles.title: Associations of High Blood Pressure with Brain Network Functional Connectivity in Healthy Young Adults.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Higher blood pressure (BP) in middle-aged and older adults is associated with altered brain network functional connectivity (FC), but evidence in young adults is limited. This study explored the associations of BP with brain FC in healthy young adults.

METHODS: This cross-sectional study included 1,000 young adults (53.8% women, 22-37 years) from the Human Connectome Project, with no hypertension diagnosis or antihypertensive medication use. Brachial systolic (SBP) and diastolic BP (DBP) were measured using semi-automatic or manual sphygmomanometer. Resting-state functional MRI measured FC within the default-mode (DMN), frontoparietal control (FPN), dorsal attention (DAN), salience/ventral attention (SVN), limbic (LN), somatomotor (SMN), and visual (VN) networks. Linear regression examined associations of SBP and DBP with network FC, adjusting for age, sex, education, body mass index (BMI), smoking history, and alcohol consumption.

RESULTS: Mean (±SD) SBP and DBP were 123.3 ± 13.8 and 76.3 ± 10.5 mmHg. Per 10-mm Hg higher SBP, FC was lower in the SVN (B = -0.0030, 95% CI: -0.0050 to - 0.0010) and higher in the DAN (B = 0.0070, 95% CI: 0.0030 to 0.0100). Per 10-mm Hg higher DBP, FC was lower in the DMN (B = -0.0040, 95% CI: -0.0060 to - 0.0010), SVN (B = -0.0050, 95% CI: -0.0070 to - 0.0020), LN (B = -0.0040, 95% CI: -0.0080 to - 0.0010), SMN (B = -0.0030, 95% CI: -0.0060 to - 0.0005), and higher in the DAN (B = 0.0070; 95% CI, 0.0010 to 0.0100).

CONCLUSIONS: Higher BP is associated with altered brain network FC in early adulthood.

articles.title: A Branched Glucan from Atractylodes macrocephala Alleviates Obese Asthma by Suppressing PAD4-Associated NET Formation.
articles.journal: Journal of agricultural and food chemistry
articles.abstract: Obese asthma is a steroid-insensitive inflammatory phenotype with limited food-derived interventions. AMP2, purified from Atractylodes macrocephala, was identified as a glucose-rich branched glucan with a predominantly (→4)-Glcp-(1→-linked backbone and O-6 substitutions. To evaluate its effects and mechanisms, a high-fat diet (HFD)/house dust mite (HDM)-induced mouse model of obese asthma was established. Oral AMP2 ameliorated airway pathology and dyslipidemia, reduced macrophage infiltration and proinflammatory cytokine levels, and partially restored gut microbial richness and composition. Mechanistically, AMP2 suppressed pulmonary PAD4-associated neutrophil extracellular trap (NET) formation and the NLRP3/caspase-1/GSDMD signaling pathway in obese asthmatic mice. Consistently, AMP2 inhibited PAD4-associated NET formation in primary neutrophils, while GSK484 cotreatment provided no additional inhibition. Furthermore, NET-containing preparations derived from AMP2-treated neutrophils attenuated cell injury and pyroptotic activation in THP-1-derived macrophages. Collectively, these findings suggest that AMP2 alleviates obese asthma by suppressing PAD4-dependent NET formation and subsequent macrophage pyroptosis.

articles.title: Discovery and Engineering of a Shortened Feruloyl Esterase for Enhanced Hydrolysis of PET Degradation Intermediate MHET.
articles.journal: Journal of agricultural and food chemistry
articles.abstract: Enzymatic depolymerization provides a sustainable approach for polyethylene terephthalate (PET) recycling, yet efficient conversion of soluble intermediates remains important for improving overall degradation processes. During PET depolymerization, mono-2-hydroxyethyl terephthalate (MHET) is generated as an important soluble intermediate. Although MHETases hydrolyze MHET into terephthalic acid and ethylene glycol, their limited natural availability and poor heterologous expression restrict broader applications. Here, we identified a novel feruloyl esterase (CbFAE) from Clostridium butyricum as an alternative MHET-hydrolyzing enzyme with a structural scaffold distinct from known MHETases. CbFAE adopts a compact α/β-hydrolase fold with a shortened lid domain and was engineered through a combination of evolutionary and thermodynamic screening. The L186R/V220A variant exhibited a 4.3-fold increase in MHET hydrolysis activity, and molecular dynamics simulations revealed that L186 regulates MHET binding through lid-domain stabilization. These findings underscore the protein engineering potential of this architecture but also offer a high-potential enzymatic toolbox for the biodegradation of MHET.

articles.title: Efficacy of Microvascular Decompression in Idiopathic Trigeminal Neuralgia (Without Vascular Compression): A Long-Term Cohort Study.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES: Trigeminal neuralgia (TN) is a severe facial pain disorder marked by brief, shock-like attacks along the trigeminal nerve distribution. The International Headache Society classifies TN into various subtypes; classical TN (cTN) results from neurovascular compression causing trigeminal nerve root atrophy or displacement, whereas idiopathic TN (iTN) presents without nerve compression or major morphological changes. Although microvascular decompression (MVD) is the first-line surgical treatment for cTN, its efficacy in iTN is poorly understood. Few studies have evaluated outcomes in patients strictly defined by the updated the International Headache Society criteria. This study aims to address these gaps by examining the long-term efficacy of MVD in patients with iTN and identifying predictors of pain freedom.

METHODS: In this retrospective cohort of patients with iTN, adjusted logistic regression evaluated factors associated with long-term MVD outcomes, including age, sex, efficacy of oxcarbazepine/carbamazepine, symptom duration before MVD, and neurovascular conflict.

RESULTS: Between 2013 and 2022, 90 patients undergoing MVD for iTN were included with a median follow-up of 5.1 years (2.2-10.3). Outcomes were as follows: 52 (57.8%) were pain-free without mediation, 6 (6.7%) were pain-free with medication, 7 (7.7%) experienced partial relief, and 25 (27.8%) required subsequent procedures. Long-term outcomes were not significantly associated with age (P = .47), sex (P = .65), symptom duration (P = .19), or medication efficacy (P = .32). Arterial contact was associated with significantly better pain outcomes compared with no arterial contact (P = .037).

CONCLUSION: Patients with iTN may still benefit from MVD, particularly when arterial contact is evident on preoperative imaging. Recognizing distinct iTN subtypes may improve individualized treatment strategies for TN and guide future studies.

articles.title: Antimucoralean prowess of the cyclic lipopeptide (CLiP) from Bacillus sp. against clinically important Mucorales.
articles.abstract: Mucormycosis is a rare opportunistic infection caused by a group of ubiquitous soil saprobic fungi that belong to the Mucorales order. The limited drug options for combating infections caused by Mucoralean species have prompted us to explore a new application of the Bacillus-derived antifungal lead cyclic lipopeptide (CLiP) (AF3) by performing antifungal susceptibility testing (AFST) against 85 clinical Mucoralean isolates, including mainly Rhizopus spp. and Mucor spp. In addition to performing AFST using AF3, which yielded a geometric mean MIC of 4.85 for Rhizopus arrhizus isolates, the germination assays were performed using AF3 against Rhizopus spp., clearly indicating the lipopeptide's ability to prevent the formation of healthy hyphae with sporangia and to cause discernible alterations in the hyphal structures. In the combination study using lipopeptide (AF3) and amphotericin B (AmB), the FICI values against 14 Mucorales isolates/strains indicated synergistic (FICI ≤0.5) and strong additive effects. The synergistic efficacy of the CLiP AF3 and AmB was evidenced by the germination assay followed by bright-field microscopy, thereby significantly lowering the AmB MIC value. The fluorescence and confocal scanning microscopy of the calcofluor white staining of the CLiP-treated R. arrhizus spores provided sound evidence of the CLiP's effect on the germination and hyphal structures. This is the first-ever systematic evaluation of AF3 lipopeptide against clinically important Mucorales and its interaction with amphotericin B. Taken together, the CLiP demonstrated a broad-spectrum antimucoralean potential, which makes AF3 a candidate for combating Mucorales infections.IMPORTANCEMucormycosis, a life-threatening fungal infection with a very high rate of morbidity and mortality, results from a variety of saprophytic fungi that may primarily affect immunocompromised individuals. Individuals with uncontrolled diabetes and hematological malignancies are highly prone to Mucorales infections. The increased frequency of mucormycosis is due to immunosuppression states in the general population owing to extended lifespan in cancer and transplant patients. The major treatment that is available is early and aggressive surgical debridement, combined with high doses of intravenous antifungal therapy. Currently, posaconazole/isavuconazole is the most promising therapeutic alternative to amphotericin B. The present work describes the applications of a novel small lipopeptide lead that has been found to inhibit 85 clinically important Mucorales.

articles.title: Yoda molecules agonize PIEZO2.
articles.abstract: Mammalian PIEZO proteins (PIEZO1 and PIEZO2) act as essential mechanosensitive channels. PIEZO1 is thought to be selectively activated by Yoda molecules (Yoda1 and Yoda2). Although a molecular mechanism for PIEZO1 activation by Yoda1 exists, the origin of Yoda1 selective agonism remains obscure. Here, using electrophysiology and calcium imaging in transfected cells, we show that Yoda1 agonizes PIEZO2, but with a distinct efficacy profile compared to PIEZO1. Yoda1 increases single-channel open probability and macroscopic stretch sensitivity of PIEZO2 currents as efficaciously as reported for PIEZO1, but it elicits weak PIEZO2-dependent calcium influx in the absence of external stimulus, an effect detectable only under non-physiological conditions. Yoda1 slows down inactivation of indentation-evoked PIEZO2 currents, but to a lower extent compared to PIEZO1. The Yoda1 analog Dooku1, which does not modulate PIEZO1, slows down PIEZO2 inactivation similarly to Yoda1. Two PIEZO1 agonists unrelated to Yoda1 but thought to populate the same binding site in PIEZO1 have no effect on PIEZO2 inactivation, suggesting that their PIEZO1 selectivity is better than Yoda1. PIEZO2 inactivation is also modulated by Yoda1's more potent analog Yoda2. Using mutagenesis and molecular dynamics simulations, we show that Yoda2's benzoic acid group forms a transient salt-bridge with a conserved arginine in the Yoda binding site (R1724/R2029 in mouse PIEZO1/PIEZO2), explaining the higher potency of this analog for both channels. Together, our study re-evaluates the PIEZO1 selectivity of Yoda molecules and highlights a complex modulatory landscape toward distinct functional properties of PIEZO channels.

articles.title: Construction of a clinical prediction model for the risk of iatrogenic vertical root fracture using multiple clinical indicators.
articles.abstract: Vertical root fracture (VRF) complicates endodontically treated teeth, often leading to extraction. We developed a diagnostic prediction model for VRF using a retrospective cohort of 80 patients. Three machine learning algorithms (XGBoost, random forest, and LASSO) were used to identify key predictors. As all predictors were ascertained at the evaluation visit, the resulting model is diagnostic rather than prognostic, estimating the probability that a tooth presenting for re-evaluation already harbors a VRF. We evaluated the model via bootstrap internal validation and three-tiered external validation in an independent cohort (n = 130). Intracanal medication, time interval, and the absence of post emerged as consensus predictors. The model demonstrated strong internal discrimination (optimism-corrected AUC = 0.795, 95% confidence interval: 0.703-0.890) and excellent calibration, yielding a risk score ranging from 0 to 5. In the external cohort, locked-model validation achieved an AUC of 0.621, model refit 0.711, and transportability assessment using conceptual proxies 0.756. This model supports risk communication and shared decision-making during re-evaluation for suspected VRF.

articles.title: Telehealth to Support Coordinated Spontaneous Awakening and Breathing Trials in Invasive Ventilation: The TEACH Cluster Randomized Clinical Trial.
articles.abstract:
IMPORTANCE: Coordinated spontaneous awakening trials and spontaneous breathing trials (C-SAT/SBT) improve outcomes for patients receiving invasive mechanical ventilation, but implementation remains inadequate.

OBJECTIVE: To evaluate whether a telehealth intervention added to a standard audit and feedback implementation of C-SAT/SBT increases adherence and improves outcomes compared with standard audit and feedback implementation alone (control).

DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS: A cluster randomized type 2 hybrid effectiveness-implementation clinical trial was conducted in 12 Intermountain Health hospitals in Utah and Idaho. Patients aged 16 years or older who were intubated and mechanically ventilated in the intensive care unit were enrolled from December 1, 2022, until July 31, 2025, with last follow-up on January 23, 2026.

INTERVENTION: Telehealth hospitals received real-time oversight from telecritical care nurses and respiratory therapists for adherence to C-SAT/SBT and a standard audit and feedback implementation. Control hospitals received only standard audit and feedback.

MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES: Co-primary outcome measures were adherence to C-SAT/SBT and ventilator-free days to day 28. C-SAT/SBT was defined as any day that the SAT and SBT were separately adherent, and the SAT followed the SBT within 2 hours or both occurred before noon, or the patient was extubated. Change in adherence from baseline was compared between groups using a mixed-effects logistic model with prespecified 1-sided significance testing. Change in ventilator-free days was compared using a mixed-effects proportional odds model.

RESULTS: There were 4544 patients at telehealth hospitals, 6438 patients at control hospitals, and 1789 preimplementation common baseline patients (median [IQR] age, 62 [47-71] years; 4826 [37.8%] female). The baseline C-SAT/SBT adherence rate of 43.9% increased to 90.3% at telehealth intervention hospitals and to 77.6% at control hospitals (odds ratio for change in telehealth vs change in control, 2.87; 1-sided 95% lower confidence limit, 2.44; P < .001; absolute difference, 11.4%; 95% CI, 8.8%-14.3%). Median (IQR) ventilator-free days from a common baseline of 24 (0-26) increased to 25 (10-27) at telehealth intervention hospitals and 25 (1-27) at control hospitals (odds ratio for change in telehealth vs change in control, 1.21; 95% CI, 1.01-1.45, P = .04; absolute difference, 1.02 days; 95% CI, 0.05-1.96 days).

CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE: Among adults intubated and mechanically ventilated in the intensive care unit, adding real-time telehealth support for C-SAT/SBT improved adherence and increased ventilator-free days more than a standard audit and feedback implementation alone.

TRIAL REGISTRATION: ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT05141396.

articles.title: Association of Alu Insertion Polymorphisms in the Major Histocompatibility Complex Class I Genomic Region With Metabolic Syndrome in Morocco.
articles.abstract: Metabolic syndrome (MetS) is a multifactorial disease resulting from the interaction between environmental and genetic factors. This study investigated the association between five Alu insertion polymorphisms located in the Class I region of the major histocompatibility complex (MHC-I) and susceptibility to MetS and its components in a Moroccan population, as well as to identify any associated haplotype profiles. A case-control study was conducted among 528 unrelated adults, including 239 MetS patients and 289 healthy controls. The five MHC-I Alu polymorphisms (AluyMICB, AluyTF, AluyHJ, AluyHF and AluyHG) were genotyped by PCR amplification. After adjustment for age and sex, the DD genotypes of AluyHJ (odds ratio [OR] adjusted = 1.68; 95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.05-2.71; p = 0.032) and AluyHF (OR adjusted = 1.94; 95% CI: 1.22-3.10; p = 0.0055) were associated with higher odds of MetS. In exploratory analyses of quantitative traits, the DD genotype (AluyHJ) and DD and ID genotypes (AluyHG) were significantly associated with hyperglycemia. The DD genotype of the AluyHF was significantly associated with hypertension, hyperglycemia and dyslipidemia. Haplotype analysis identified 27 haplotypes, three of which were significantly associated with MetS: DDDDD (OR = 1.67; 95% CI: 1.31-2.15; p < 0.0001), DIDID (OR = 5.49; 95% CI: 1.67-18.03; p = 0.0016) and DIIDD (OR = 0.011; 95% CI: 0.001-0.130; p = 0.0003). Furthermore, significant linkage disequilibrium values were observed between certain loci. These findings suggest that certain haplotypic configurations of the MHC-I Alu insertion/deletion markers, as well as the AluyHF and AluyHJ polymorphisms, could constitute genetic markers associated with MetS and its components in the Moroccan population after adjustment for age and sex, possibly by tagging broader MHC-I haplotypic backgrounds rather than through a direct functional effect. They highlight the potential role of this genomic region in susceptibility to cardiometabolic diseases and warrant further validation.

articles.title: Severe Pancreatitis Followed by Posterior Reversible Encephalopathy Syndrome After Pegaspargase in Pediatric Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Asparaginase is essential in the therapy of pediatric acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) but may cause pancreatitis. Posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome (PRES) is a rare neurological complication.

OBSERVATIONS: A 12-year-old boy with T-cell ALL developed severe pancreatitis after pegaspargase, followed by PRES 4 days later. Transient blood pressure elevations during severe abdominal pain were observed before PRES onset, but sustained stage 2 hypertension was absent. Neurological symptoms initially resolved; however, late-onset epilepsy occurred with persistent imaging abnormalities.

CONCLUSIONS: Severe pancreatitis may contribute to the development of PRES in patients receiving asparaginase. Careful neurological monitoring is warranted even when hypertension is transient, and long-term follow-up is necessary due to the risk of epilepsy.

articles.title: Incidence and Clinical Factors Associated with Retreatment after Active Periodontal Therapy in High-risk Stage III-IV Periodontitis: an EMR-based Real-world Retrospective Cohort Study.
articles.abstract:
PURPOSE: Patients with advanced periodontitis may require disease-driven retreatment after active periodontal therapy (APT), but the incidence, clinical composition, and associated baseline factors in routine specialist care remain insufficiently defined. This study aimed to quantify the incidence and timing of first retreatment, characterize the clinical composition of retreatment events, identify baseline clinical factors associated with first and repeated retreatment, and explore the temporal sequence between supportive periodontal therapy initiation and retreatment.

MATERIALS AND METHODS: This electronic medical record (EMR)-based retrospective cohort study included 300 patients with high-risk stage III-IV periodontitis who completed APT at a tertiary hospital in China and were followed through routine specialist care. Baseline was defined as APT completion. The primary outcome was first retreatment for persistent, recurrent, or progressive disease, including repeated subgingival scaling and root planing, local intensive periodontal treatment, periodontal surgery, or periodontal-related tooth extraction. Kaplan-Meier analysis and Cox regression were used for first retreatment, repeated events were analyzed using negative binomial regression, and SPT (supportive periodontal therapy) initiation was evaluated in an exploratory time-dependent Cox model.

RESULTS: During a median follow-up of 24.6 months, 94 of 300 patients experienced first retreatment, corresponding to an absolute risk of 31.3% and an incidence rate of 14.7 per 100 person-years. Among patients with retreatment, the median observed time to first event was 9.8 months, and 55.3% of first events occurred within 12 months. Twelve-month cumulative incidence was 17.3%. In the revised primary Cox model, current smoking, diabetes mellitus, stage IV periodontitis, and residual deep-pocket burden were associated with first retreatment.

CONCLUSION: Disease-driven retreatment after APT was common and often occurred during the early post-treatment period in this selected high-risk stage III-IV periodontitis cohort. Smoking, diabetes mellitus, stage IV disease, and residual deep-pocket burden were associated with subsequent retreatment and may support careful post-APT reassessment in routine specialist care.

articles.title: Intrathecal Cytarabine-Associated Cerebral Vasospasm and Acute Ischemic Stroke in a Young Adult With Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia: A Case Report and Literature Review.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Intrathecal (IT) chemotherapy is standard of care in the management of pediatric acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL). Common toxicities include headache, nausea, and vomiting; cerebral vasospasm is rarely reported.

OBSERVATIONS: A 20-year-old male undergoing induction chemotherapy for B-cell ALL developed cerebral vasospasm of the right posterior cerebral artery, resulting in acute ischemic stroke after receiving IT cytarabine.

CONCLUSIONS: This is the first reported case in the adolescent/young adult (AYA) population, highlighting the importance of recognizing cerebral vasospasm as a potential sequela when AYA patients receiving ALL treatment develop neurological symptoms.

articles.title: Complete genome sequences of Staphylococcus aureus strains FRI-1169 and MN8, two historically related menstrual toxic shock syndrome isolates.
articles.abstract: Staphylococcus aureus strains FRI-1169 and MN8 were originally isolated from known cases of mTSS in the late 1970s. Here, we report the complete genome sequences of these strains.

articles.title: Therapy Performance Predicts Functional Recovery After Stroke.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Early prediction of post-stroke recovery is important for guiding personalized rehabilitation and optimizing care planning. However, existing prediction approaches often overlook therapy intensity and patient engagement during post-stroke rehabilitation.

OBJECTIVE: Deriving therapy performance metrics (TPMs) from clinical notes and evaluate their utility in predicting functional discharge outcomes on the 10-Meter Walk Test (10MWT), 6-Minute Walk Test (6MWT), and Berg Balance Scale (BBS).

METHODS: Electronic medical records from 42 individuals undergoing inpatient stroke rehabilitation were mined to extract TPMs describing therapy exposure, walking distance, treadmill use, and stair practice. TPMs were evaluated across inpatient time-points to compare distributions between participants who met or did not meet established clinical thresholds for each functional outcome and to assess associations with discharge scores. TPMs were integrated into machine learning (ML) models along with patient demographics and sensor-derived gait features collected at IRF admission.

RESULTS: TPMs differentiate patients with clinically meaningful improvements as early as 5-7 days post-admission and were strongly associated with discharge outcomes (R2 = .64-.78, P < .001). Incorporating TPMs into ML models improved 6MWT performance (R2 increased from .30 to .63, reduced prediction error by ~25 m) relative to baseline models without TPMs. Importantly, ML models using TPMs enabled early outcome prediction for non-ambulatory patients, a group often excluded from gait-based predictive approaches.

CONCLUSION: TPMs provide early markers of recovery and enhance the prediction of discharge outcomes, particularly for patients who are non-ambulatory at admission. Leveraging structured information from routine therapy documentation may enable dynamic, near real-time recovery prediction to support data-driven rehabilitation and care planning after stroke.

articles.title: Fecal microbiota transplantation modulates immunosuppressive cells and IgA secretion in a gut microbiota depletion model.
articles.abstract: The relationship between gut dysbiosis and host immune dynamics remains poorly understood. We used an antibiotic-induced gut microbiota depletion model following fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) via co-housing. Mice received an antibiotic cocktail for 4 weeks (Abx group), or for 2 weeks, followed by co-housing with healthy control mice for 2 weeks (CoA group), or kept under conventional housing for 2 weeks (Abx-CH group). The gut microbiota was assessed by 16S rRNA sequencing and Gram staining. Immune cell populations were analyzed via flow cytometry using antibodies for T cells, regulatory T cells (Tregs), IgA-secreting cells, PD-1+ cells, and myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs) in the colon and blood. As a result, α- and β-diversity differed from Control in the Abx and Abx-CH groups, whereas the CoA group resembled Control. Three distinct enterotypes were identified with a recovery pattern (Lactobacillus), a pathobiome pattern (Klebsiella, Escherichia, Proteus), and an expanded pattern (Ruminococcus and Prevotella) through FMT. In the colon, the proportions of Tregs were significantly higher in Abx and CoA groups. IL-10⁺ Tregs tended to increase in the Abx and were significantly lower in the CoA group. IgA-secreting cells and fecal IgA levels in the CoA group were significantly higher than in the Abx group, respectively (6.1% vs. 0.5%, 427.0 vs. 83.7 μg/mL, CoA vs. Abx; p<0.05). In conclusion, FMT could influence the proportion of immune cells in response to gut microbiota modulation. IgA secretion could be upregulated by gut microbiota after FMT.

articles.title: Comparing Heart Rate Variability Upon Admission to Intensive Care Unit Between Moderate-Severe Traumatic Brain Injury and Orthopedic Controls: A Prospective Observational Study.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) is associated with autonomic dysfunction measurable through heart rate variability (HRV). Although reduced HRV during prolonged monitoring has been associated with poor outcomes following TBI, comparisons with other forms of traumatic injury remain limited.

METHODS: We conducted an exploratory prospective cohort study of adults with moderate-severe TBI (msTBI) and isolated severe orthopedic trauma controls enrolled at a single institution from 2020 to 2024. Continuous cardiac telemetry was collected during the first 15 minutes of intensive care unit (ICU) admission. HRV metrics included standard deviation of normal-to-normal intervals (SDNN), root-mean square of successive differences (RMSSD), percentage of successive normal-to-normal intervals differing by >50 ms (pNN50), and low-frequency to high-frequency power ratio (LF/HF). Clinical outcomes including pneumonia, sepsis, infection, acute respiratory distress syndrome, and acute kidney injury were assessed during the first week of hospitalization.

RESULTS: Among 94 patients (51 msTBI; 43 orthopedic controls), time-domain HRV measures were significantly reduced in the majority of msTBI patients compared with published normative values. In adjusted analyses, SDNN was similar across groups (mean difference: 27.0, 95% CI: -3.8 to 57.9, P=0.086). RMSSD, pNN50, and LF/HF were also similar. Within the msTBI cohort, HRV metrics were not associated with first-week clinical outcomes or hospital mortality.

CONCLUSIONS: In this exploratory study, early HRV abnormalities following trauma may reflect autonomic impairment, but measurements immediately upon ICU admission may not capture evolving msTBI-specific dysfunction. Larger longitudinal studies are needed to draw definitive conclusions regarding clinically meaningful autonomic changes and associations with msTBI outcomes.

articles.title: Determinants and Prognostic Impact of Infarct Growth After Endovascular Thrombectomy in Acute Ischemic Stroke.
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Infarct growth (IG) on diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) may predict outcomes after endovascular thrombectomy (EVT); however, its value in real-world consecutive cohorts remains unclear. This study aimed to identify the determinants of IG and evaluate its predictive value for functional outcomes in consecutive EVT patients.

METHODS: We enrolled 262 patients who underwent EVT within 24 hours of stroke onset. Infarct volume was measured on pre-EVT DWI and 5 to 7-day follow-up DWI scans. The IG was defined as a volumetric difference. Multivariable regression and receiver operating characteristic curve analyses were performed to identify the determinants of IG and its predictive value for favorable outcomes.

RESULTS: Of the 262 patients, 133 achieved favorable outcomes. Pre-EVT DWI volume (B=0.414, P<0.001), National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale (NIHSS) on admission (B=0.052, P<0.001), clot retrieval attempts (CRAs) (B=0.221, P<0.001), and successful reperfusion (B=-0.726, P<0.001) were independent determinants of post-EVT infarct volume. IG [odds ratio (OR)=0.015, P<0.001], NIHSS (OR=0.124, P<0.001), and successful reperfusion (OR=2.679, P<0.001) independently predicted favorable outcomes. The IG model [area under the curve (AUC)=0.808] performed comparably to the clinical model (AUC=0.807), and the combined model achieved the highest AUC (0.839).

CONCLUSIONS: Baseline DWI volume, NIHSS on admission, CRAs, and successful reperfusion are independent determinants of IG. The IG is a strong predictor of unfavorable outcomes with incremental value over clinical variables, supporting its use as a practical imaging biomarker for risk stratification after EVT.

articles.title: Community pharmacy interventions in asthma and COPD management in Portugal: an observational study.
articles.journal: European annals of allergy and clinical immunology
articles.abstract: Background. Asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) require long-term management, and community pharmacies play an important role in supporting chronic respiratory disease (CRD) care. However, challenges persist regarding implementation and sustainability of pharmacy-led interventions. This study describes CRD-related services provided in Portuguese community pharmacies, identifies barriers to service delivery, and explores patterns in service provision. Methods. An observational cross-sectional study was conducted among Portuguese community pharmacies using an online questionnaire assessing geographic location, available interventions, and perceived barriers. Descriptive statistics summarized the prevalence of interventions, and a chi-square test was used to assess the representativeness of the sample's geographic distribution relative to the national pharmacy network. Cluster analysis, principal component analysis (PCA), and a Random Forest Classifier were applied as exploratory approaches to identify patterns in service provision and variables more frequently associated with structured pharmaceutical consultations. Results. Only 7.1% of pharmacies reported offering structured pharmaceutical consultations, although among pharmacies without structured pharmaceutical consultations (n = 341), inhaler technique verification (95.3%) and patient referrals (94.7%) were widely implemented. Key barriers included time constraints (67.7%), insufficient funding (58.1%), and limited collaboration with healthcare providers (36.4%). Cluster analysis identified patterns of service provision, with structured pharmaceutical consultations more frequently reported in pharmacies offering a broader range of interventions. Exploratory PCA analyses visualized variability in pharmaceutical intervention practices, while Random Forest modeling highlighted follow-up assessments and respiratory monitoring activities as variables more frequently associated with the availability of structured pharmaceutical consultations. Conclusions. Portuguese community pharmacies contribute to asthma and COPD care through a range of interventions. However, structured pharmaceutical consultations remain limited. The findings highlight variability in service provision and perceived barriers that may influence their implementation. Further research is needed to better understand how these services can be supported and sustainably integrated into routine practice.

articles.title: Minimally Invasive, Endoscopic Atrial Septal Occluder Explantation and Patent Foramen Ovale Closure.
articles.journal: Multimedia manual of cardiothoracic surgery : MMCTS
articles.abstract: A 29-year-old female with posterior circulation transient ischaemic attacks associated with a patent foramen ovale developed persistent central and pleuritic chest pain after percutaneous closure with a 30 mm Gore septal occluder. Allergy testing identified nickel and cobalt hypersensitivity. Echocardiography showed a well-seated device without residual interatrial shunt. The patient underwent minimally invasive surgical explantation of the atrial septal occluder and primary closure of the residual patent foramen ovale. The operation was performed through a 3 cm right anterolateral minithoracotomy port with endoscopic visualization. Cardiopulmonary bypass was established using an 8 mm Dacron side graft to the right common femoral artery, percutaneous superior vena cava cannulation, and direct right femoral venous cannulation. Del Nido cardioplegia was delivered antegrade into the aortic root. A right atriotomy exposed the device. Traction on the retrieval cord (right atrial eyelet) collapsed the device into a linear configuration and allowed removal through the defect. The defect was closed primarily with running 4-0 Prolene suture. Post-bypass transoesophageal echocardiography showed an intact interatrial septum without residual shunt and preserved biventricular function. The patient was discharged on postoperative Day 5 and reported complete resolution of the presenting symptoms at follow-up.

articles.title: Adverse effects of human islet amyloid polypeptide on islet transplantation outcomes.
articles.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Islet transplantation is a promising therapy for diabetes, but mechanisms of graft failure remain unclear. Human islet amyloid polypeptide (hIAPP) contributes to beta-cell dysfunction in Type 2 diabetes; however, its impact on islet transplantation has not been fully defined. We investigated whether physiologically expressed hIAPP affects islet graft function.

MATERIALS AND METHODS: Human IAPP knock-in (hIAPP-KI) mice expressing hIAPP under its native promoter were used as islet donors. Streptozotocin-induced diabetic mice received islet transplants from hIAPP-KI or control donors. Metabolic outcomes, beta-cell apoptosis and proliferation, macrophage infiltration, oxidative stress, and endocrine cell composition were assessed after transplantation.

RESULTS: Before transplantation, islet size and insulin content were comparable between groups. Recipients of hIAPP-KI islets exhibited higher blood glucose and HbA1c levels and lower rates of normoglycemia than recipients of control islets. Insulin content in graft-bearing kidneys was significantly reduced in the hIAPP-KI group, indicating impaired graft function. Histological analyses demonstrated increased beta-cell apoptosis and macrophage infiltration in hIAPP-KI grafts, whereas beta-cell proliferation was unchanged. In vitro, hIAPP-KI islets showed enhanced susceptibility to high glucose-induced oxidative stress, which was attenuated by antioxidant treatment. In addition, pancreatic polypeptide- and somatostatin-positive cell populations were increased in hIAPP-KI grafts.

CONCLUSIONS: Physiological hIAPP expression impairs islet graft function by promoting beta-cell apoptosis, inflammation, and oxidative stress. Targeting hIAPP-associated pathways may improve graft survival and function following islet transplantation.

articles.title: Mifepristone versus other interventions for the prevention of pregnancy in reproductive-age women using emergency contraception.
articles.journal: The Cochrane database of systematic reviews
articles.abstract:
RATIONALE: Emergency contraception uses drugs or intrauterine devices to prevent pregnancy after unprotected intercourse. Understanding the effectiveness, safety, and acceptability of the various methods available is critical for reproductive healthcare providers and their patients.

OBJECTIVES: To evaluate the effectiveness, safety, and acceptability of mifepristone compared to other interventions in reproductive-age women using emergency contraception for the prevention of pregnancy.

SEARCH METHODS: We used CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, two other databases, and two trial registers, together with reference checking and contact with study authors and experts in the field, to identify the studies included in the review. The latest search date was 28 February 2025.

ELIGIBILITY CRITERIA: We included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing mifepristone to oral emergency contraception pills (levonorgestrel, the Yuzpe regimen, and ulipristal acetate) or copper or levonorgestrel intrauterine devices (IUDs). We also planned to include non-randomized studies of interventions (NRSIs) for capturing rare adverse outcomes and detecting minimal clinically important differences (MCIDs). Participants were women seeking emergency contraception within five days of unprotected intercourse.

OUTCOMES: The critical outcome was the number of pregnancies. Important outcomes included any side effects, altered menses, and acceptability, assessed as treatment satisfaction.

RISK OF BIAS: We used Cochrane's RoB 1 tool to assess the risk of bias in the RCTs.

SYNTHESIS METHODS: We synthesized results for each outcome using meta-analysis where possible, using both fixed-effect and random-effects models. We used GRADE to assess the certainty of evidence for each outcome.

INCLUDED STUDIES: We included 87 studies with approximately 36,000 participants. Seventy-nine studies were conducted in China, four in the UK, two in Cuba, and two were multi-country studies. Forty-one studies compared mifepristone with levonorgestrel; three with the Yuzpe regimen (estrogen and progestin); 42 compared two or more doses of mifepristone; and two compared mifepristone with copper IUD. We excluded all relevant NRSIs identified because none reported additional outcome data that were unavailable from the included RCTs.

SYNTHESIS OF RESULTS: Mid-dose mifepristone (25 mg to 50 mg) versus levonorgestrel Compared to levonorgestrel, mid-dose mifepristone likely results in fewer pregnancies (risk ratio (RR) 0.67, 95% confidence interval (CI) 0.49 to 0.91; I2 = 0%; 27 studies, 6052 participants) and likely reduces the occurrence of any side effects (RR 0.55, 95% CI 0.39 to 0.76; I2 = 72%; 17 studies, 4350 participants), both with moderate-certainty evidence. It probably leads to fewer occurrences of early menses (RR 0.71, 95% CI 0.49 to 1.03; 7 studies, 1324 participants), but a higher risk of delayed menses (RR 1.29, 95% CI 1.01 to 1.64; I2 = 25%; 17 studies, 3615 participants), both with moderate-certainty evidence. No studies reported on acceptability. Low-dose mifepristone (< 25 mg) versus levonorgestrel Low-dose mifepristone reduces pregnancy compared to levonorgestrel (RR 0.73, 95% CI 0.59 to 0.90; I2 = 0%; 14 studies, 8752 participants; high-certainty evidence). It likely results in a large reduction in any side effects (RR 0.26, 95% CI 0.17 to 0.38; I2 = 0%; 3 studies, 609 participants; moderate-certainty evidence). Low-dose mifepristone reduces the risk of early menses after treatment (RR 0.45, 95% CI 0.35 to 0.58; I2 = 0%; 6 studies, 1898 participants), but slightly increases the risk of delayed menses (RR 1.52, 95% CI 1.11 to 2.08; I2 = 50%; 10 studies, 7618 participants), both with high-certainty evidence. Low-dose mifepristone probably results in slightly higher treatment satisfaction (RR 1.03, 95% CI 0.99 to 1.07; 1 study, 724 participants; moderate-certainty evidence). Mifepristone versus the Yuzpe regimen Compared to the Yuzpe regimen, mifepristone (any dose) probably results in a reduction in pregnancies (RR 0.14, 95% CI 0.05 to 0.41; I2 = 0%; 3 studies, 2144 participants) and probably results in a large reduction in any side effects (RR 0.89, 95% CI 0.83 to 0.95; I2 = 97%; 2 studies, 1693 participants), both with moderate-certainty evidence. Mifepristone increases the risk of delayed menses (RR 2.83, 95% CI 2.31 to 3.47; I2 = 85%; 3 studies, 1912 participants; high-certainty evidence). It likely increases treatment satisfaction (RR 1.17, 95% CI 1.10 to 1.25; 1 study, 615 participants; moderate-certainty evidence). No studies reported on early menses. Mifepristone versus copper IUD We included two studies. Neither reported data for any side effects nor treatment satisfaction. Evidence for the number of pregnancies and altered menses was of very low certainty due to risk of bias, imprecision, and few events. Mid-dose mifepristone (25 mg to 50 mg) versus low-dose mifepristone (< 25 mg) Mid-dose mifepristone results in a slight reduction in pregnancies (RR 0.77, 95% CI 0.59 to 1.00; I2 = 0%; 26 studies, 12,358 participants) and a slight increase in delayed menses (RR 1.32, 95% CI 1.15 to 1.50; I2 = 53%; 22 studies, 11,733 participants) compared to low-dose mifepristone, both with high-certainty evidence. There may be little to no difference in the occurrence of any side effect or early menses between mid-dose and low-dose mifepristone (both outcomes with low-certainty evidence). No studies reported treatment satisfaction. Certainty and limitations The certainty of evidence ranged from very low to high, with downgrading primarily due to the risk of bias for unclear reporting. Most studies were conducted in China, which may limit the generalizability of findings on side effects and satisfaction. Substantial missing data affected four risk of bias domains: random sequence generation, allocation concealment, blinding, and incomplete outcome data. Sensitivity analyses restricted to studies at low overall risk of bias yielded similar effect estimates.

AUTHORS' CONCLUSIONS: Both mid-dose and low-dose mifepristone are probably more effective than levonorgestrel. Mifepristone is likely more effective than the Yuzpe regimen in preventing pregnancy following unprotected intercourse. Nausea and vomiting are less common with all mifepristone doses than with Yuzpe. A delay in menses is probably the main adverse effect of mifepristone; higher doses of mifepristone seem to lead to increased frequency of delayed menses than lower doses.

FUNDING: This Cochrane review was funded in part by the World Health Organization (WHO).

REGISTRATION: Registration: PROSPERO CRD42024591428.

articles.title: Advance care planning for children with life-limiting and life-threatening conditions.
articles.journal: The Cochrane database of systematic reviews
articles.abstract:
RATIONALE: Children with life-limiting conditions (LLCs) and life-threatening conditions (LTCs) and their families face physical, psychological, and social burdens. This systematic review evaluates advance care planning (ACP) for infants, children, and adolescents with LLCs and LTCs. Paediatric ACP is underutilised, and there is a lack of robust paediatric-specific evidence regarding its benefits and potential harms; thus, this review aims to address this important knowledge gap.

OBJECTIVES: To assess the benefits and harms of advance care planning for children with life-limiting conditions and life-threatening conditions.

SEARCH METHODS: We used the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE, Embase, CINAHL, PsycINFO, ClinicalTrials.gov, and the World Health Organization International Clinical Trials Registry Platform (WHO ICTRP), together with reference checking, citation searching, and contact with study authors, to identify studies included in the review. The latest search date was June 10, 2025.

ELIGIBILITY CRITERIA: We included randomised controlled trials (RCTs) in children with LLCs and LTCs comparing ACP with standard care. We excluded studies in which ACP does not involve children, is limited to parents or caregivers, or focusses on concepts closely related to ACP, such as unstructured communication and shared decision-making.

OUTCOMES: Our outcomes were concordance between children's preferences and end-of-life (EoL) care, decisional regret/conflict, quality of child-family communication, overall well-being, quality of life, satisfaction with care, and family's depression at early term (≤ 3 months).

RISK OF BIAS: For each outcome, we used the revised Cochrane risk-of-bias tool for randomised trials (RoB 2) to assess bias in the RCTs for each outcome.

SYNTHESIS METHODS: We synthesised results for each outcome using a random-effects meta-analysis, conducting pooled analyses when at least two studies met the eligibility criteria for a given outcome. Where meta‑analysis was not possible (e.g. because only one study contributed data for an outcome), we summarised the findings narratively and tabulated key study characteristics and effect estimates. We then described the direction and magnitude of effects, consistency across studies, and the precision and risk of bias of the available evidence. We used the Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development and Evaluation approach to assess the certainty of the evidence for each outcome.

INCLUDED STUDIES: We included a total of five studies with 350 dyads of children, young adults, and their guardians.

SYNTHESIS OF RESULTS: ACP versus standard care at early term (≤ 3 months): Concordance between children's preferences and EoL care Two studies reported individual-level information on children's documented preferences and EoL care among the small number of participants who died. However, these descriptive data did not allow estimation of an intervention effect. One study did not report concordance. Another study noted the difficulty of determining from electronic health records whether the care desired was the care received. Decisional regret/conflict with the Decisional Conflicts Scale One study reported data for this outcome. One study reported lower decisional conflict in the ACP group (P = 0.094). However, there was no description of the specific results (1 study, 38 participants; very low-certainty evidence), and we are therefore uncertain about effects on this outcome. Quality of children - family communication with the Parent-Adolescent Communication Scale One study reported data for this outcome. ACP may result in little to no difference in the quality of children's and families' communication ≤ 3 months (mean difference (MD) 1.4, 95% confidence interval (CI) -4.1 to 6.9; 1 study, 38 participants; low-certainty of evidence). Overall well-being with the Functional Assessment of Chronic Illness Therapy - Spiritual Well-Being Expanded Version 4 and the Spiritual Well-being Scale Two studies reported data for this outcome. The evidence is very uncertain about the effect of ACP on overall well-being ≤ 3 months (2 studies, 156 participants; very low-certainty evidence): one study reported overall well-being (MD 11.00, 95% CI 2.33 to 19.67), and another study did not provide an overall assessment score, but neither the Functional Assessment of Chronic Illness Therapy-Spiritual Well-Being (FACIT-Sp) Meaning nor the FACIT-Sp Faith scores showed clear differences between the ACP group and the standard care group. Quality of life with the Paediatric Quality of Life Inventory and the Patient‑Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System Three studies reported data for this outcome. The evidence is very uncertain about the effect of advance care planning on quality of life ≤ 3 months (standardised mean difference (SMD) -0.07, 95% CI -1.79 to 1.64; I² = 0%; 2 studies, 68 participants; very low-certainty evidence). Another study did not report the numerical data. Satisfaction with care No included studies reported data for this outcome. Family's depression with the Beck Depression Inventory Three studies reported data for this outcome. The evidence is very uncertain about the effect of advance care planning on families' depression ≤ 3 months (MD -1.61, 95% CI -7.12 to 3.90; I² = 31%; 3 studies, 152 participants; very low-certainty evidence).

AUTHORS' CONCLUSIONS: The current evidence is insufficient to determine the benefits or harms of ACP for children with LLCs and LTCs and their families. No studies evaluated satisfaction with care. Overall, our review highlights uncertainty regarding the effects of paediatric ACP on children and their families. Further well-designed studies are needed to assess the benefits and harms of ACP for children with LLCs and LTCs, and their families, and carefully tailor approaches to the child's age and developmental stage. Researchers also need to identify consistent core outcomes and build evidence across high- and lower-income settings.

FUNDING: This Cochrane Review had no dedicated funding.

REGISTRATION: Protocol available via https://doi.org/10.1002/14651858.CD016106.

articles.title: Early Respiratory Mechanics Phenotypes and Stratification of Acute Kidney Injury Severity in Mechanically Ventilated Septic Patients: A Retrospective Cohort Study.
articles.abstract: Structured AbstractBackgroundAmong ventilated septic patients who develop acute kidney injury (AKI), AKI severity may vary according to early respiratory mechanics. We investigated whether multidimensional respiratory mechanics phenotypes were associated with the maximum AKI severity.MethodsThis single-center retrospective cohort study included septic adults who received invasive mechanical ventilation, remained free of AKI during the first 24 h after ventilation initiation, and developed AKI within 72 h. Respiratory mechanics recorded during the first 24 h were used for unsupervised clustering. The primary outcome was the maximum Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes stage reached within 72 h. Associations were evaluated using ordinal and multivariable logistic regression, propensity score matching, and inverse probability of treatment weighting.ResultsAmong 1135 patients, three phenotypes were identified: Cluster 1, characterized by high airway pressures and low compliance; Cluster 2, characterized by low pressures and preserved compliance; Cluster 3, characterized by reduced compliance and relatively higher driving pressure. AKI severity differed across phenotypes. Cluster 1 had the highest proportion of stage 3 AKI, whereas Cluster 2 had the highest proportion of stage 1 AKI. Compared with Cluster 2, Cluster 1 was associated with higher odds of more severe AKI after propensity score matching (odds ratio, 2.01; 95% confidence interval, 1.50-2.69) and inverse probability weighting (odds ratio, 1.82; 95% confidence interval, 1.31-2.51). Respiratory phenotype was not consistently associated with 28-day mortality. Adding phenotype to conventional clinical variables produced only a small, nonsignificant improvement in discrimination for moderate-to-severe AKI.ConclusionsEarly respiratory mechanics phenotypes were associated with AKI severity among mechanically ventilated septic patients who developed AKI. This exploratory, hypothesis-generating study cannot establish prediction of AKI occurrence nor causal effects of ventilator settings. Notably, key hemodynamic variables were unavailable for adjustment, which may introduce unmeasured confounding. Its findings are not suitable to guide clinical decision before external validation.

articles.title: Trajectories of Fasting Blood Glucose and Brain Health in Middle Age.
articles.journal: Journal of the American Heart Association
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Research on associations between long-term fasting blood glucose (FBG) trajectories and brain health in early adulthood is limited. We investigated associations of FBG trajectories with cognition and brain structure.

METHODS: Participants were from the CARDIA (Coronary Artery Risk Development in Young Adults) study, followed for 30 years, who completed ≥1 cognitive test at year 30. Among participants without diabetes with ≥3 FBG measurements from baseline to year 30, we identified FBG trajectories using latent growth mixture models. Participants who developed diabetes after baseline were included for comparison (n=345). Cognition was assessed using tests of processing speed, executive function, memory, fluency, and global cognition. Structural magnetic resonance imaging data from 605 participants included total gray matter volume and white matter lesions. Associations were examined using multivariable linear regression adjusted for demographics and health behaviors.

RESULTS: We included 2808 participants (mean age, 55.2±3.6 years; 56% women; 44% Black individuals). Three FBG trajectories were identified: lower-stable (n=1387), moderate-stable (n=938), and increasing (n=138). Compared with the lower-stable group, increasing FBG and incident diabetes were associated with worse performance in memory, processing speed, executive function, and composite cognition; increasing FBG was also associated with worse global cognition. Incident diabetes was associated with lower total and parietal gray matter volume and greater parietal white matter abnormalities. No consistent sex or race interactions were observed.

CONCLUSIONS: Persistently elevated glucose below the diabetes threshold was associated with worse cognitive performance in midlife, while incident diabetes was associated with structural brain changes.

articles.title: Taste-Testing Nutritious Meals With Youth Experiencing Chemotherapy-Induced Taste Alterations.
articles.abstract: BackgroundYouth undergoing chemotherapy for pediatric cancer can experience taste alterations and household food insecurity that compromise nutritional status and thus clinical outcomes. This paper reports on taste testing nutritious meals in a clinical setting with youth undergoing chemotherapy to inform a future meals program.MethodYouth between ages 12 and 21.9 years, fluent in English or Spanish, and experiencing chemotherapy-related taste alterations were eligible for this cross-sectional study. Consented/assented youth were offered trays with four meal samples, asked to taste each sample, and then rate meal qualities on a 1-5 visual analog scale (5 = very happy face) and provide feedback via an online survey. Researchers also recorded their observations. Quantitative data were analyzed with descriptive statistics and qualitative data with content analysis. The pre-established benchmark for inclusion in the future feasibility study was overall meal rating of 4 or 5 by at least 70% of raters.ResultsSeventeen taste-test sessions were conducted, 32 unique youth provided assent, and eight meal samples were taste-tested in two waves (four meals per wave). Four (4/8; 50%) meals met the benchmark for inclusion in the future feasibility study. Participant ratings and feedback, and researcher observations indicated that how meals looked and felt in the mouth, alongside parental support, were critical to ingestion.DiscussionThe study was well received by youth, parents, and staff at the site. The results will inform adaptation and selection of meals for future feasibility study of an intervention to reduce food insecurity in households of youth undergoing chemotherapy for pediatric cancer.
