Extended T cell phenotyping demonstrated severe depletion of naïve CD4 T cells with relative enrichment of memory CD4 populations. Despite marked clinical improvement and metabolic resolution of disseminated infection on fluorodeoxyglucose-positron emission tomography (FDG-PET) imaging, CD4 and CD8 counts remained severely depleted over 12 months after commencement of anti-mycobacterial therapy.

CONCLUSION: This case highlights persistent profound isolated T cell lymphopenia despite successful treatment of disseminated M. bovis infection. Whether chronic mycobacterial infection contributed to the development of severe T cell depletion or unmasked idiopathic CD4 lymphocytopenia with associated CD8 lymphopenia remains unclear, presenting a significant diagnostic challenge.

articles.title: Storming the Castle Gates: A Case of TAFRO.
articles.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Idiopathic multicentric Castleman disease (iMCD) is a rare inflammatory syndrome, characterised by generalised lymphadenopathy and hyperinflammatory state. Histologically, it has characteristic features that are shared with secondary forms of Castleman disease. It is more common in Polynesian populations, with a prevalence of 28 per million (cf 6-8 per million). More recently, a rare subset of this disease has been identified as thrombocytopenia, anasarca, fever, reticulin fibrosis, organomegaly (TAFRO). Compared to classic MCD, these patients present more acutely with smaller lymphadenopathy, anasarca, and have thrombocytopenia as opposed to thrombocytosis. Recognition of TAFRO is important as it has been shown to have the worst prognosis of any iMCD subtype.

METHOD: We describe the case of a 54-year-old Thai female who presented with three weeks of daily fevers. Blood tests demonstrated thrombocytopenia, while positron emission tomography (PET) revealed small fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG)-avid lymph nodes (∼7 mm longest axis) above and below the diaphragm with splenomegaly. Bone marrow biopsy was unremarkable. Subsequent core lymph node biopsy revealed reactive features without specific features to guide diagnosis. Over the next two months, she developed anasarca and continued to have severe thrombocytopenia with daily fevers. Infectious work-up was negative, and she had trialled extensive antibiotic coverage without improvement.

RESULTS: Multidisciplinary consensus supported excisional lymph node biopsy, despite a technically challenging procedure. This confirmed MCD-like features, which, in conjunction with thrombocytopenia, anasarca, fever, and splenomegaly, supported the diagnosis of TAFRO. Siltuximab was commenced with prompt resolution of clinical syndrome and laboratory abnormalities.

CONCLUSION: This case highlights the importance of multidisciplinary collaboration in reaching a diagnosis of MCD/TAFRO. It emphasises the yield of excisional lymph node biopsy compared to core when this disease is suspected, particularly in ensuring early diagnosis and thus treatment.

articles.title: The Antiphospholipid Patient Who Bleeds: Lupus Anticoagulant-Hypoprothrombinaemia Syndrome (LAHPS) and the Case Against Reflexive Anticoagulation.
articles.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Antiphospholipid syndrome (APS) is reflexively equated with thrombosis and anticoagulation. We present a case of a triple-positive patient whose dominant manifestations were instead bleeding and microvascular, presenting with lupus anticoagulant-hypoprothrombinaemia syndrome (LAHPS) and pulmonary capillaritis, illustrating that APS antibodies can cause bleeding and inflammatory microvascular disease, that treatment is immunosuppression, and that reflexive anticoagulation may harm.

CASE: A 54-year-old man had persistently triple-positive antiphospholipid antibodies since age 28, identified during screening after his father died from APS-associated pulmonary capillaritis. Despite high-risk serology, he had no history of thrombosis. Investigation of prolonged coagulation studies demonstrated acquired factor II deficiency (9-11%) in the presence of a lupus anticoagulant. The prothrombin time was corrected on 1:1 mixing, while the activated partial thromboplastin time remained prolonged, indicating antibody-mediated prothrombin clearance coexisting with a lupus anticoagulant and confirming LAHPS. Years later, he developed bilateral ground-glass pulmonary infiltrates and bronchoscopy-confirmed diffuse alveolar haemorrhage consistent with APS-related pulmonary capillaritis, a manifestation of microvascular APS. He was treated with corticosteroids, hydroxychloroquine, and rituximab rather than anticoagulation, resulting in normalisation of factor II levels (>80%) and complete radiological resolution. After three years of maintenance rituximab, aspirin for primary prophylaxis, and continued avoidance of anticoagulation, he remains free of both bleeding and thrombotic complications.

DISCUSSION: LAHPS is a rare, acquired bleeding disorder, with fewer than 200 cases reported, in which antiprothrombin antibodies accelerate prothrombin clearance, producing bleeding despite persistent antiphospholipid positivity. Recognition depends on identifying the characteristic laboratory pattern of lupus anticoagulant with acquired factor II deficiency. Treatment targets the pathogenic autoantibody through immunosuppression, typically corticosteroids and, in refractory cases, rituximab, rather than anticoagulation. Importantly, restoration of factor II levels may shift haemostasis back towards thrombosis, creating therapeutic challenges throughout the disease course. This case illustrates that APS antibodies can cause bleeding as well as clotting and underscores the need to recognise LAHPS and microvascular APS phenotypes, treat the underlying immune process, and avoid reflexive anticoagulation.

articles.title: Gazing Upon the Great Eye: A Rare Presentation of Behcet's Disease.
articles.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Behcet's disease is a systemic autoimmune condition presenting classically with recurrent and painful mucocutaneous ulcers. It is more prevalent among Mediterranean, Middle Eastern, and Asian populations. Ocular or neurologic involvement is uncommon, but when present, contributes to significant morbidity and mortality (1). Clinical features are variable and often lead to delays in diagnosis (2).

METHOD: We report the case of a 41-year-old female who presented with left-sided pan-uveitis, shifting hypopyon, and retinitis. This followed several months of recurrent oral and genital ulcers, fevers, and constitutional symptoms. Her clinical course was complicated by subacute left lower limb sensory deficits and a new diagnosis of chronic hepatitis B virus infection. Anti-nuclear antibodies and anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies were negative. She was HLA-B*51 positive. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed spinal lesions at the level of T6/T7 involving the right anterior and posterior horns, with possible involvement of the spinothalamic tract.

RESULTS: The patient was initially treated with high-dose topical and systemic corticosteroids alongside entecavir, followed by regular infliximab infusions. Her uveitis and mucocutaneous symptoms significantly improved. A three-month progress MRI scan demonstrated radiological improvement with interval reduction in the size of the spinal lesions, though a degree of lower limb symptoms has persisted.

CONCLUSION: This case illustrates the high morbidity associated with multi-organ manifestations of Behcet's disease. The heterogenous presentation may lead to diagnostic delays, and clinicians are reminded to consider less typical features of this potentially debilitating condition. A cross-disciplinary approach is particularly valuable and paramount to optimizing care for these patients.

articles.title: Better Late than Never? Allogeneic Stem Cell Transplantation for Chronic Granulomatous Disease in Early Adulthood.
articles.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Chronic granulomatous disease (CGD) is an inherited disorder of phagocyte function caused by defective NADPH oxidase activity, resulting in recurrent infection and dysregulated granulomatous inflammation. Although allogeneic stem cell transplantation (alloSCT) is increasingly performed early as definitive therapy, older patients with longstanding CGD present unique challenges due to cumulative infectious and inflammatory complications.

CASE PRESENTATION: We report the case of a 17-year-old patient with CGD diagnosed in South Korea at two months of age who presented to Christchurch Hospital with disseminated aspergillosis with pulmonary and osseous involvement. His disease course prior to this was complicated by recurrent pneumonia, granulomatous osteomyelitis, necrotic lymphadenopathy, colitis, and extended-spectrum β-lactamase (ESBL) Klebsiella pneumoniae infection. Given his significant infectious burden, his case was discussed through Transplantation and Primary Immunodeficiency (TAPID) networks, where international expert opinion suggested he may have been beyond the optimal window and high risk for alloSCT, with initial recommendations to explore emerging gene therapy trials. Following review with the National Institutes of Health (NIH), Bethesda, he underwent matched unrelated donor peripheral blood alloSCT through a clinical trial (D0 = December 20, 2024). Conditioning included busulfan, alemtuzumab, low-dose total body irradiation (300 cGy), posttransplant cyclophosphamide, and tocilizumab, with sirolimus-based graft-versus-host disease (GVHD) prophylaxis. His posttransplant course was complicated by engraftment syndrome, COVID-19 with secondary bacterial infection, persistent fungal osteomyelitis, cytopenias, mild cutaneous GVHD, and immune thrombocytopenia requiring corticosteroids, intravenous immunoglobulin, and rituximab.

CONCLUSION: This case highlights the evolving boundaries of alloSCT for CGD in patients with established infectious complications. It demonstrates that successful transplantation can be achieved in patients with longstanding CGD complications through coordinated international collaboration across transplant haematology, infectious diseases, and clinical immunology specialties.

articles.title: A Machine Learning-Based Prognostic Risk Scoring Model for Patients with Coronary Artery Disease Admitted to the Intensive Care Unit Using Multi-Source Structured Clinical Data From the Information Mart for Intensive Care IV Database.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Critical coronary artery disease (CAD) exhibits significant prognostic heterogeneity. Traditional scoring has limited efficacy in the early identification of high-risk patients. To develop a validated machine learning (ML)-based prognostic risk scoring model for critical CAD to predict adverse outcome risk based on multi-source structured clinical data from the medical information mart for intensive care IV (MIMIC-IV) database.

METHODS: A total of 5472 critically ill patients with CAD meeting the operational definitions of this study were retrospectively enrolled from the MIMIC-IV database and randomly divided into a training set and a test set at a 7 : 3 ratio. Fifty-two structured clinical indicators collected within the time window from 6 hours before intensive care unit (ICU) admission to 24 hours after admission were extracted. Least absolute shrinkage and selection operator regression was applied in the training set to screen core variables based on 1-year all-cause mortality. Multiple ML algorithms were utilized to construct prognostic prediction models, with 1-year all-cause mortality as the primary outcome and 28-day in-hospital mortality as well as CAD-related ICU readmission rate as secondary outcomes. All model parameters and classification thresholds were predefined before performance evaluation in the test set. The test set was excluded from feature screening, parameter tuning, and threshold optimization procedures. Model performance was assessed via the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC of ROC), paired DeLong test, calibration curves, Brier score, calibration intercept, calibration slope, and decision curve analysis. The light gradient boosting machine (LightGBM) model with the highest AUC value was interpreted using SHapley additive exPlanations (SHAP). Additionally, sensitivity analysis with 5 sets of multiple imputations was performed.

RESULTS: The 1-year all-cause mortality, 28-day in-hospital mortality, and CAD-related ICU readmission rate of the study population were 14.2%, 5.6%, and 9.1%, respectively. In the test set, the LightGBM model yielded AUC values of 0.896 and 0.898 for predicting 1-year all-cause mortality and 28-day in-hospital mortality, which were higher than those of other models. Nevertheless, paired DeLong tests revealed no statistically significant differences when compared with the logistic regression model (P = .062 and P = .642, respectively). The LightGBM model exhibited limited predictive performance for CAD-related ICU readmission rate (AUC = 0.690), with no significant difference in AUC relative to the logistic regression model (P = .238). SHapley additive exPlanations analysis identified the Charlson comorbidity index, history of coronary artery bypass grafting, and blood urea nitrogen as the top contributing variables of the LightGBM model. Thresholds derived from SHAP dependence plots were only interpreted as exploratory and model-dependent findings.

CONCLUSION: The LightGBM model established in this study exhibited favorable performance for predicting mortality risk among critically ill patients with CAD in internal validation and was interpretable via the SHAP approach. It can provide quantitative references for early risk stratification and individualized clinical management of critically ill CAD patients in the ICU. However, only internal validation was conducted in the present study, and the model demonstrated suboptimal predictive efficacy and calibration for CAD-related ICU readmission. Therefore, external, multicenter, and prospective validations are required prior to its clinical implementation.

articles.title: Self-reported sleep problems and associated factors among older adults in Malaysia: An ethnic subgroup analysis.
articles.journal: Cranio : the journal of craniomandibular practice
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: This study examines factors associated with self-reported sleep problems within a large sample of older Malaysian adults from diverse ethnic groups.

METHODS: Cross-sectional data from the South East Asia Community Observatory Health Survey 2018 and ordered probit models were used for analysis.

RESULTS: Malay females were more likely to report mild-to-severe sleep problems than males. Malays and Chinese who were older were more likely to report mild-to-severe sleep problems compared to younger ones. Among Malays, smoking was associated with the likelihood of reporting mild-to-severe sleep problems. Higher income, physically active and obese older Chinese adults were less likely to report sleep problems than others. Being diagnosed with hypertension among Chinese and diabetes among Indians was associated with a higher probability of reporting mild-to-severe sleep problems.

CONCLUSION: Sociodemographic characteristics, lifestyles and health profiles are key factors associated with self-reported sleep problems among various ethnic groups of Malaysian older adults.

articles.title: Born preterm, not former anything: Qualitative exploration of health experiences of adults born preterm.
articles.journal: Journal of the American Association of Nurse Practitioners
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Approximately 10% of births worldwide begin preterm, and those with the benefit of modern neonatal care survive into adulthood. In the past 10 years, a call for increased understanding of the health care experience of adults born preterm has been advanced by researchers and advocacy groups.

PURPOSE: This study explored the health experiences of an international sample of adults born preterm spanning a range of gestational ages and birth years.

METHODOLOGY: Data collection was conducted using an electronic survey with convenience, snowballing recruitment. Reflexive thematic analyses of the open-ended question responses were conducted, generating themes that reflected the health experiences of participants.

RESULTS: The final sample included an international group of 80 participants with a mean age of 40 years. Participants described the experience sharing preterm birth status with providers, generating the following themes: Shock/Surprise then Ambivalence, Hypochondriac/Negative Response and Provider-dependent Receptivity. Analysis of responses describing what participants wanted health care teams to know generated additional themes: Achievements, Lifelong Impact, Uncertainty, Trauma, Social/Emotional/Behavioral, Unique Presentations and Recommendations for Education and Practice.

CONCLUSIONS: Adults who were born prematurely are individuals whose life is affected every day by the experience of being born early. Adults born preterm report feeling unheard and misunderstood by providers.

IMPLICATIONS: To maximize future health, it is essential that health care teams, across all specialties, recognize preterm birth history as a risk, similar to family history of heart disease or diabetes. Nurse practitioners have a unique opportunity to fill this much-needed gap in care.

articles.title: Genetic variability of the pneumococcal wciZ-gene and how it relates to capsule-type prediction.
articles.abstract:
UNLABELLED: Streptococcus pneumoniae serotypes 15B and 15C differ solely in the O-acetylation state of their capsular polysaccharides, determined by the activity of the wciZ-encoded O-acetyltransferase. Variation in the number of thymine-adenine (TA) repeats within the wciZ reading frame can induce frameshift events, resulting in either functional (15B) or non-functional (15C) enzyme variants. To characterize wciZ diversity and assess the accuracy of genome-based capsule-type prediction models, the wciZ TA repeat regions of all serotype 15B and 15C isolates from Germany's national invasive pneumococcal disease (IPD) surveillance 2022-2024 were analyzed. A total of 364 wciZ genes were partially sequenced, revealing 19 distinct TA repeat variants. In addition to known repeat counts, previously unreported variants with 2, 12, 13, 14, and 15 repeats were identified. Two novel mutational mechanisms influencing serotype expression emerged: (i) a single thymine deletion upstream of the repeat region, potentially abolishing enzyme activity even when the reading frame is restored, and (ii) a 13-nucleotide deletion downstream of the repeats, causing premature translational termination despite eight TA repeats normally associated with serotype 15B. The distribution of repeat numbers showed a steep, right-skewed, unimodal profile with eight repeats predominating, suggesting a mutational hotspot, and a three-repeat expansion consistently resulting in a 15B phenotype. The SeroBA version currently implemented in the PathogenWatch pipeline correctly predicted most identified variants; however, rare mutations outside the TA repeat region, particularly mutations restoring the reading frame while potentially impairing enzyme function, can compromise prediction accuracy and should be considered in future genome-based serotyping frameworks.

IMPORTANCE: Streptococcus pneumoniae is a major cause of invasive infections, including pneumonia, sepsis, and meningitis. This makes the accurate surveillance and characterization of circulating strains essential for the development of effective prevention strategies. Among pneumococci, serotypes 15B and 15C are a notable example of how subtle genetic changes can result in different capsule phenotypes, which can have significant diagnostic and epidemiological implications. This study reveals that the molecular basis of the 15B/15C switch is more complex than previously assumed, demonstrating unexpected genetic diversity and novel mutational mechanisms within the wciZ gene that distinguish the serotypes. The study demonstrates that serotype assignment based solely on thymine-adenine repeat counts can result in systematic misclassification. By improving our understanding of capsule variation between serotypes 15B and 15C, this study provides valuable insights into genome-based serotyping, enhances the interpretation of surveillance data, and emphasizes the necessity of continuously reassessing molecular prediction.

articles.title: Deriving an Expected Range for Early-Pregnancy Fasting Glucose: A Meta-Regression.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: FPG is widely used for early GDM screening due to low cost and availability, but no consensus normal range exists before routine 24-28 week screening, causing wide variation in reported prevalence. We quantified the relationship between early-pregnancy FPG thresholds and reported prevalence to derive a model-based expected range, testing whether study-level BMI and gestational age contributed additional variation.

METHODS: We searched databases from inception to February 2026 for studies reporting FPG-based prevalence of early dysglycemia or GDM before 20 weeks' gestation, retaining threshold-specific estimates from multi-threshold cohorts. Logit-transformed prevalence was analyzed via inverse-variance weighted meta-regression with minimum FPG threshold (mmol/L) as predictor; exploratory models added study-level BMI and gestational age. Predictions were back-transformed, and thresholds at ∼90% and 10% predicted prevalence bounded the expected range.

RESULTS: Twenty-eight studies contributed 41 threshold-specific estimates (thresholds 4.19-5.60 mmol/L; prevalence 0.7%-90.0%). The FPG threshold showed a strong inverse association with logit-prevalence (β = -4.65, 95% CI -4.98 to -4.31; P < 0.001), explaining 93.8% of variance (R2 = 0.938); the threshold alone predicts prevalence with high accuracy. Prevalence declined from ∼90%(88%) at 4.2 mmol/L to 10% at 5.1 mmol/L (50% at 4.6 mmol/L). BMI and gestational age did not materially alter this, supporting applicability beyond eligibility criteria.

CONCLUSIONS: Reported prevalence of early GDM is very strongly and reproducibly predicted by the FPG threshold alone. We propose 4.2-5.1 mmol/L as a model-derived expected (normal) range for early-pregnancy FPG, reconciling disparate threshold proposals in the literature. Outcome-linked studies are needed before this range informs diagnostic use. Linking early FPG values with maternal and neonatal outcomes is needed before diagnostic thresholds for early GDM can be established.

articles.title: Metabolic Syndrome at 12 Weeks Postpartum in Women with a History of Gestational Diabetes Mellitus: An Analytic Cross-Sectional Study in Mexico.
articles.abstract:
PURPOSE: Gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) increases the risk of developing metabolic syndrome (MetS) postpartum. This study aimed to determine the frequency of MetS at 12 weeks postpartum in women with a history of GDM and to identify associated factors.

METHODS: This descriptive, analytic, cross-sectional study included 126 women diagnosed with GDM (IADPSG criteria) with a singleton live birth, evaluated at 12 weeks postpartum at the Hospital Civil de Guadalajara "Dr. Juan I. Menchaca" of Guadalajara, México, between January 2019 and December 2023. MetS was diagnosed using NCEP-ATP III criteria (≥3 of waist circumference >88 cm, triglycerides ≥150 mg/dL, fasting glucose ≥ 100 mg/dL, blood pressure ≥130/85 mmHg, HDL-C <50 mg/dL. The triglyceride-glucose index (TyG index) was calculated as an indirect marker of insulin resistance. A binary logistic regression model was used to identify associated factors of MetS.

RESULTS: MetS was present in 58.7% (n = 74) of participants. The TyG index showed the strongest association with MetS (85.1% vs. 15.4%, [aOR = 102.6, 95% CI: 11.5-916.4, P < 0.001]). BMI remained an associated factor (aOR = 1.32, 95% CI: 1.14-1.54). Type of GDM treatment during the pregnancy (diet vs. pharmacologic) was not significantly associated with MetS.

CONCLUSION: MetS is highly prevalent at 12 weeks postpartum among women with GDM. The TyG index showed a strong association with MetS, while BMI was also associated with its presence. Both may help identify women who warrant further cardiometabolic assessment, particularly in resource-limited settings.

articles.title: Federated Generation of Synthetic RNA-Seq Data.
articles.journal: Journal of computational biology : a journal of computational molecular cell biology
articles.abstract: Access to genomic data is highly regulated due to its sensitive nature. While safeguards are essential, cumbersome data access processes pose a significant barrier to the development of AI methods for genomics. Synthetic data generation can mitigate this tension by enabling broader data sharing without exposing sensitive information. Synthetic genomic data are produced by training generative models on real data and subsequently sampling artificial data that preserves relevant statistics while limiting disclosures about the underlying individuals. In some settings, a single data holder may have sufficient data to train such generative models; however, in many applications, data must be combined across multiple sites to achieve adequate scale. This need arises, for example, in rare disease studies, where individual hospitals typically hold data for only a small number of patients. The solution we present in this article enables multiple data holders to jointly train a synthetic data generator without revealing their raw data. Our approach combines secure multiparty computation (MPC) to ensure input privacy, so that no party ever discloses its data in unencrypted form, with differential privacy (DP) to provide output privacy by mitigating information leakage from the released synthetic data. We empirically demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method by generating high-utility synthetic datasets from multiple real RNA-seq cohorts in federated settings, showing that our approach enables privacy-preserving data synthesis even when data are distributed across institutions.

articles.title: Proposal for Preference-Informed Win Statistics and Use to Re-Analyze Seven Heart Failure Pharmacotherapy Trials.
articles.abstract:
AIMS: Win ratios (WRs) allow simultaneous evaluation of multiple outcomes using hierarchical composite endpoints, but outcome hierarchies are typically determined by researchers without patient input.We sought to develop a patient preference-informed approach to constructing hierarchical composite endpoints for WR analysis and use it to re-analyze heart failure (HF) pharmacotherapy trials.

METHODS: We synthesized patient preference data from multiple sources to derive two preference-informed hierarchical composite endpoints: tolerability-over-quality of life (QoL) (in descending order, primary: death, HF hospitalization, side-effects, QoL) and QoL-prioritized (QoL, death, HF hospitalization, side-effects). We then re-analyzed individual participant-level data from seven RCTs (n=15,357) using these preference-informed hierarchies and, for comparison, a conventional hierarchy (death, HF hospitalization, QoL, side-effects) with two to four components.

RESULTS: Of seven re-analyzed trials, five showed consistent results across preference-informed and conventional WRs, indicating preference insensitivity. Two trials exhibited preference-sensitive findings. In TOPCAT-Americas, benefit with spironolactone over placebo was attenuated in the tolerability-over-QoL hierarchy (WR 1.03 [95% confidence interval 0.92-1.15] versus conventional four-component WR 1.13 [1.01-1.26]), reflecting large between-group differences in side-effects. In BEST, the benefit of bucindolol over placebo was attenuated and no longer statistically significant with the QoL-prioritized hierarchy (WR 1.07 [0.98-1.16] versus conventional four-component WR 1.15 [1.05-1.26]), despite favorable effects on all four components.

CONCLUSIONS: Integrating empirically-derived patient preferences into hierarchical composite endpoints provides a pragmatic and generalizable approach to evaluating the net clinical benefit of HF pharmacotherapy using WRs. These results highlight the value of incorporating patient priorities into trial design and interpretation, and in therapeutic decision-making.

articles.title: Association of Stressful Life Events With Prenatal Care Adequacy Among Women in Mississippi: A Secondary Analysis of PRAMS Data.
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Prenatal stress is a public health concern associated with adverse maternal and infant health outcomes. Although Mississippi meets national benchmarks for prenatal care (PNC) use, persistent disparities in maternal and infant mortality suggest that utilization alone is insufficient to capture care adequacy. Stressful life events (SLEs) may interfere with engagement in PNC. This study examined the association between SLEs and PNC adequacy among women in Mississippi.

METHODS: We conducted a secondary analysis of 2016-2021 Mississippi Pregnancy Risk Assessment Monitoring System data (N = 6552). Fourteen items assessed SLEs occurring in the 12 months before birth. We operationalized SLEs as aggregated SLEs, type of stressor (financial, relational, traumatic, emotional), and cumulative stressors (0, 1 or 2, ≥3). We assessed PNC adequacy using the Kessner Index. We performed weighted descriptive statistics, Pearson χ2 tests, and multivariable logistic regression models accounting for the complex survey design.

RESULTS: Financial stress and cumulative SLEs were significantly associated with lower odds of receiving adequate PNC. Women reporting no financial stress were more likely to receive adequate PNC than women reporting financial stress (adjusted odds ratio [AOR] = 1.29 [95% CI, 1.07-1.55]; P = .009). Women reporting no SLEs were more likely than women receiving ≥1 SLE to receive adequate PNC (AOR = 1.35 [95% CI, 1.08-1.70]; P = .009). Education, marital status, and health insurance coverage were consistent predictors of PNC adequacy.

CONCLUSIONS: Our findings highlight the need for PNC approaches that address social and economic barriers through social risk screening and supportive care strategies. Future research should evaluate whether interventions targeting financial and social stressors can improve PNC engagement and reduce disparities in maternal and infant health outcomes.

articles.title: Clinical profiles and associated outcomes of distinct inflammatory phenotypes in patients with acute heart failure.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Elevated levels of inflammatory biomarkers are common in acute decompensated heart failure (ADHF) and have been associated with disease progression, diminished diuretic response and adverse outcomes, but a comprehesive understanding of specific inflammatory phenotypes remains elusive. We aimed to identify clinical characteristics, decongestion trajectories and outcomes across inflammatory profiles.

METHODS: Plasma levels of 34 cytokines were measured in 270 patients hospitalized for ADHF enrolled in PUSH-AHF. Unsupervised clustering analyses were performed on cytokine levels to identify patient subgroups based on their inflammatory phenotype. Clinical characteristics, diuresis, natriuresis and clinical outcomes were compared among clusters. We validated our findings in the Japanese JEDI-AHF cohort (n=301) using Random Forest-based cluster projection derived from cytokine levels.

RESULTS: Four distinct inflammatory clusters were identified: a low-inflammation cluster, a low-grade eotaxin-dominant cluster, and two NF-κB-related inflammatory clusters characterized by IFN-γ/Th1 and Th17/IL-17-dominant responses, respectively. Patients in the low-inflammation and eotaxin-dominant-clusters had the most favourable outcomes. Patients within the IFN-γ/Th1-dominant cluster more often had pre-existing heart failure and reduced kidney function. Patients in the Th17/IL-17-dominant cluster predominantly presented with new-onset heart failure, preserved kidney function, the highest NT-proBNP levels and the most impaired natriuresis and diuresis. The IFN-γ/Th1-dominant cluster was associated with an increased risk of 180-day all-cause mortality (HR=2.59 95%CI [1.22-5.49]) compared to the low-inflammation cluster. External validation in JEDI-AHF showed similar findings.

CONCLUSION: Distinct inflammatory phenotypes are present in patients with ADHF and associate with distinctly different clinical profiles, decongestion trajectories and outcomes. This underscores the heterogeneity of inflammation in ADHF and suggests a potential for personalized anti-inflammatory interventions.

articles.title: The challenges with add-on trials in transthyretin amyloid cardiomyopathy.
Adenine Phosphoribosyltransferase Deficiency Masquerading as Chronic Tubulointerstitial Nephritis: Striking Black Speckles in a Fresh Kidney Allograft Biopsy.
articles.abstract: Adenine phosphoribosyltransferase (APRT) deficiency is a rare inherited disorder of purine metabolism causing 2,8-dihydroxyadenine crystal nephropathy, which may progress to kidney failure if unrecognized. We report a 40-year-old woman with rapidly progressive chronic kidney disease whose two consecutive native kidney biopsies were interpreted as chronic tubulointerstitial nephritis without an identifiable etiology. Despite repeated investigations, she progressed to kidney failure requiring peritoneal dialysis and subsequently underwent living-donor kidney transplantation. Persistent allograft dysfunction prompted a biopsy, which revealed striking dark brown-black speckles in the fresh tissue specimen. Histopathological examination demonstrated extensive intratubular crystalline deposits accompanied by acute tubular injury, chronic tubulointerstitial damage, and concurrent acute rejection. Genetic testing identified a homozygous pathogenic APRT frameshift variant (c.280_286del; p.Gly94LeufsTer41). Retrospective reassessment of the second native kidney biopsy revealed previously overlooked crystalline deposits, confirming that the underlying disease had remained unrecognized before transplantation. Following treatment of acute rejection, allopurinol was initiated, resulting in a marked reduction in urinary crystalluria and stable allograft function during six months of follow-up. This case highlights that chronic tubulointerstitial nephritis is a histopathological pattern rather than a definitive diagnosis. Careful histopathological reassessment and timely genetic testing are essential for recognizing treatable crystalline nephropathies before irreversible kidney damage and disease recurrence after transplantation.

articles.title: Living with chronic heart failure in a digital era: Exploring patients' lived experiences of telemedicine and self-management.
articles.abstract: IntroductionChronic heart failure (CHF) affects patients' emotional, physical and social lives. As healthcare systems face rising demand and workforce shortages, telemedicine has become increasingly important as a way to support person-centred care. This study explored lived experiences of patients with heart failure and how they perceive and integrate telemedicine into everyday life.MethodsA qualitative study was conducted using semistructured interviews with 15 patients receiving outpatient CHF care in Denmark between December 2022 and May 2023. A phenomenological-hermeneutic approach guided the study, and data were analysed using Interpretative Phenomenological Analysis to capture how participants made sense of living with heart failure and engaging with telemedicine.ResultsFour themes were identified: (1) the emotional impact of receiving the diagnosis, (2) navigating everyday life with CHF, (3) adjusting future expectations and (4) integrating technology into the treatment experience. Telemedicine enhanced participants' sense of control, safety, flexibility and continuity of care. However, challenges emerged related to emotional communication, self-assessment tasks and limited digital literacy, particularly among those in vulnerable positions.DiscussionTelemedicine supported involvement and self-management, but its benefits were shaped by individual circumstances, digital skills and the extent to which emotional, relational and clinical needs could be addressed digitally. To ensure equitable access and effective engagement, telemedicine must be tailored to patients' needs. These findings highlight that telemedicine can improve continuity but may widen inequities if digital competencies are not addressed and can guide healthcare professionals and policymakers in designing accessible, person-centred telemedicine solutions.

articles.title: Prevalence and associated factors of peripheral arterial disease in hemodialysis patients: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Peripheral arterial disease (PAD) is common in hemodialysis patients and associated with adverse outcomes, but its prevalence and associated factors remain heterogeneous.

METHODS: PubMed, Web of Science, Embase, Cochrane Library, Scopus, CINAHL, CNKI, and Wanfang were searched from inception to April 8, 2026. Cross-sectional and cohort studies reporting PAD prevalence or associated factors were included. Random-effects models were used. Heterogeneity was explored using subgroup, meta-regression, and sensitivity analyses.

RESULTS: The pooled prevalence was 23% (95%Confidence Intervals [CI], 20%∼26%) based on ankle brachial index ≤ 0.9, 42% (95%CI, 29%∼56%) based on ultrasonography or other imaging, and 19% (95%CI, 11%∼33%) based on clinical criteria. Both research regions and proportion of male were associated with heterogeneity. Factors associated with PAD included abdominal obesity (Odds Ratio [OR]=5.41), diabetes mellitus (OR=2.90), cardiovascular disease (OR=2.01), cerebrovascular disease (OR=1.91), male sex (OR=1.70), smoking (OR=1.64), hypertension (OR=1.34), C-reactive protein (OR=1.06), age (OR=1.04), low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (OR=1.02), dialysis vintage (OR=1.01), albumin (OR=0.97), high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (OR=0.94), Black race (OR=0.78), and serum creatinine (OR=0.75). Associations varied by diagnostic criteria.

CONCLUSIONS: PAD is common in hemodialysis patients, with prevalence varying substantially by diagnostic criteria and study settings. Several demographic and clinical characteristics were associated with PAD; however, most evidence was derived from cross-sectional studies and was of low or very low certainty. These findings should not be interpreted causally. Standardized diagnostic criteria and well-designed prospective studies are needed to improve the certainty and comparability of future evidence.

articles.title: Pathogen-reduced platelets for the prevention of bleeding.
articles.journal: The Cochrane database of systematic reviews
articles.abstract:
RATIONALE: Platelet transfusions are used to prevent and treat bleeding in people who are thrombocytopenic (they have a low blood platelet count). Despite improvements in donor screening and laboratory testing, a small risk of viral, bacterial, or protozoal contamination of platelets remains. There is also an ongoing risk from newly emerging blood transfusion-transmitted infections (TTIs), for which laboratory tests may not be available at the initial outbreak. The risk of blood TTIs from platelet transfusion may be reduced by photochemical pathogen reduction. Pathogens are either inactivated or significantly depleted in number, thereby reducing the chance of transmission. Although current pathogen-reduction technologies have been proven to reduce pathogen load in platelet concentrates, some published clinical studies have raised concerns about the effectiveness of pathogen-reduced platelets for post-transfusion platelet count recovery and the prevention of bleeding compared with standard platelets. This is an update of a Cochrane review first published in 2013 and updated in 2017.

OBJECTIVES: To assess the benefits and harms of pathogen-reduced platelets for the prevention of bleeding in people of any age requiring platelet transfusions.

SEARCH METHODS: We searched for randomised controlled trials (RCTs) in CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, CINAHL, the Transfusion Evidence Library, and ongoing trial databases. The latest search date was 14 January 2025.

ELIGIBILITY CRITERIA: We included RCTs that compared the transfusion of pathogen-reduced platelets (PRP) with standard platelets, or that compared different types of PRP.

OUTCOMES: Our outcomes were post-transfusion bleeding, mortality, serious adverse events, platelet refractoriness and mean number of transfusions required per participant.

RISK OF BIAS: We used the Cochrane Risk of bias tool (ROB 1) to assess RCTs.

SYNTHESIS METHODS: We performed meta-analyses using the Mantel-Haenszel method with the fixed-effect model to avoid over-weighting small studies, and assessed the certainty of the evidence using GRADE.

INCLUDED STUDIES: We identified four new trials in this update, with a total of 18 trials eligible for inclusion (one is awaiting classification, and one study of two people was terminated early and not included in our analyses). We included 16 RCTs with 2964 participants in the meta-analyses comparing PRP to standard platelets stored in either plasma (or unknown solution) or platelet additive solution (PAS). Twelve of the 16 completed trials were included in the previous review. Methods of pathogen reduction assessed included Intercept (11 RCTs), Mirasol (5 RCTs), and Theraflex (1 RCT). One study assessed both Intercept and Mirasol, though they did not directly compare the methods (instead, each was randomised with their own control group). No RCTs compared the transfusion of one type of PRP with another.

SYNTHESIS OF RESULTS: We grouped the data into two comparisons based on the storage solution of the untreated platelets. Two studies included more than one control group: one control stored in plasma, and one control stored in PAS. Comparison 1. PRP versus standard (untreated) platelets stored in plasma (or unknown solution) (11 RCTs) There is an increased risk of developing platelet refractoriness (risk ratio (RR) 2.04, 95% confidence interval (CI) 1.74 to 2.39; 8 RCTs, 1937 participants, high-certainty evidence) as a result of using PRP compared to standard platelets. There is probably an increase in clinically significant bleeding (WHO grade 2+) (RR 1.08, 95% CI 0.99 to 1.18; 7 RCTs, 2272 participants, moderate-certainty evidence), and the mean number of platelet transfusions required per participant (mean difference (MD) 1.09, 95% CI 0.68 to 1.50; 7 RCTs, 2079 participants, moderate-certainty evidence). There may be an increase in any bleeding (WHO grade 1+) (RR 1.09, 95% CI 1.04 to 1.14, 8 RCTs, 2122 participants, low-certainty evidence). There is probably no difference in serious adverse events (RR 0.96, 95% CI 0.79 to 1.17, 8 RCTs, 1956 participants, moderate-certainty evidence), and may be no difference in all-cause mortality (RR 0.74, 95% CI 0.46 to 1.20, 8 RCTs, 2381 participants, low-certainty evidence). Comparison 2. PRP versus standard (untreated) platelets stored in PAS (7 RCTs) There is probably an increased risk of developing platelet refractoriness (RR 1.47, 95% CI 1.28 to 1.70; 4 RCTs, 1288 participants, moderate-certainty evidence), and an increased mean number of platelet transfusions required per participant (MD 0.94, 95% CI 0.55 to 1.33; 4 RCTs, 1302 participants, moderate-certainty evidence), as a result of using PRP compared to standard platelets. There may also be an increased risk of clinically significant bleeding (WHO grade 2+) (RR 1.16, 95% CI 0.98 to 1.38; 5 RCTs, 1348 participants, low-certainty evidence) and any bleeding (WHO grade 1+) (RR 1.10, 95% CI 0.99 to 1.21; 4 RCTs, 938 participants, low-certainty evidence). There may be no difference in all-cause mortality (Peto odds ratio 0.77, 95% CI 0.41 to 1.47; 7 RCTs, 1548 participants, low-certainty evidence). We are uncertain about the impact on serious adverse events. There were no credible subgroup differences for any of our outcomes, in either comparison, between methods of pathogen-reduction (Theraflex, Intercept, Mirasol). The most common source of bias was trial funding, with some trials directly funded by the PRP technology being assessed. Blinding of personnel (performance bias) was often not reported, or was described as open-label, though this would not have impacted objective measures such as mortality and laboratory tests. Small sample sizes impacted the width of the confidence intervals, leading to lower certainty for imprecision. None of the studies reported quality of life. We did not evaluate any economic outcomes.

AUTHORS' CONCLUSIONS: Findings from this review were based on 16 trials of 2964 participants; only 44 participants (1 RCT) did not have a haematological or oncological diagnosis. In people with haematological or oncological disorders who are thrombocytopenic due to their disease or its treatment, we found high-certainty evidence that PRP transfusions increase the risk of platelet refractoriness and the platelet transfusion requirement, moderate-certainty evidence of increased risk of clinically significant bleeding (WHO 2+), and low-certainty evidence that it increases the risk of any bleeding (WHO 1+). There was insufficient evidence for people with other diagnoses.

FUNDING: This review had no dedicated funding.

REGISTRATION: Protocol and previous versions available at DOI 10.1002/14651858.CD009072.

articles.title: Functional-food modulation across vascular states in acute mesenteric ischaemia: from thromboinflammatory restraint to perfusion-aligned recovery.
articles.abstract: Reports of rapid deterioration or death following apparently routine gastrointestinal symptoms have prompted patients to ask frontline clinicians why such events occur and whether dietary measures could help prevent them. Such presentations have many possible causes; acute mesenteric ischaemia (AMI) is one rapidly progressive vascular emergency that may evade timely diagnosis. In a Finnish population-based study of acute occlusive arterial AMI, 137 of 470 patients (29%) were diagnosed only after death, underscoring the challenge of timely recognition. Since 2020, observations of infection-associated intestinal endothelial inflammation, microvascular thrombi and ischaemic injury have raised questions about immune-vascular mechanisms, without establishing a population-level increase in AMI incidence. This critical narrative review considers AMI epidemiology, infection-related pathology and immunothrombosis to examine whether an inflammatory, potentially NET-associated vascular susceptibility state could precede clinically apparent thrombosis and an indication for antithrombotic treatment. This proposed interval has not been validated in humans. Broad corticosteroid exposure is limited by a lack of mechanistic selectivity and systemic risks; anticoagulant treatment faces indication and bleeding constraints in individuals without an established antithrombotic indication. We evaluate food-derived bioactives as candidates for research across pre-event susceptibility, reperfusion injury and recovery, while distinguishing experimental activities from effects achievable through ordinary dietary intake. Oral dose, metabolism, human exposure, target engagement and haemostatic safety remain unresolved. This review offers a vascular-state-informed research framework rather than a claim that any food prevents AMI.

articles.title: A potentially fatal complication of post-obstructive diuresis: Torsades de pointes.
articles.abstract: Post-obstructive diuresis can cause electrolyte disturbances with a potentially life-threatening cardiac complication of 'Torsades de pointes' requiring cardiopulmonary resuscitation and electrical defibrillation. Electrolyte replacement brought complete recovery underlining the importance of serial electrolyte measurements and close urine-output monitoring.

articles.title: Caste as a Social Determinant of Diabetes in India: A Scoping Review.
articles.journal: International journal of social determinants of health and health services
articles.abstract: The caste system, a social hierarchy in India, continues to influence health outcomes, including diabetes mellitus (T2DM). Despite policy efforts toward equity, caste still influences access to healthcare, nutrition, and lifestyle exposures, thereby affecting diabetes risk. This scoping review examined how caste has been studied in relation to T2DM in India, focusing on prevalence, risk factors, complications, and healthcare access. We searched PubMed, Cochrane Library, and Web of Science (2015 onwards) for studies on "diabetes mellitus" and "caste." Of 676 records, 59 studies met the criteria. Most (55) focused on Scheduled Tribe (ST) populations. T2DM prevalence was reported in 39 studies, but only 16 analysed caste-specific differences. The pooled prevalence of T2DM across all caste categories was 7.8% (95% CI 5.9-9.6%). Caste-specific analysis of risk factors was also limited, mainly among STs. Few studies examined complications or healthcare-seeking behaviour, again mainly among STs. Evidence on caste and diabetes in India remains fragmented and skewed toward the ST population, with minimal research on other caste categories. Existing studies rarely conceptualize caste as a structural determinant. Future research must adopt an interdisciplinary approach that integrates structural, sociocultural, and biological pathways to understand and address caste-based inequities in diabetes risk, care, and outcomes.

articles.title: Comparing Orthodontic Airway Plate Therapy Between Infants with Isolated and Non-Isolated Robin Sequence.
articles.journal: The Cleft palate-craniofacial journal : official publication of the American Cleft Palate-Craniofacial Association
articles.abstract: ObjectiveCompare orthodontic airway plate (OAP) treatment of infants with isolated and non-isolated Robin Sequence (RS).DesignRetrospective series of infants treated with OAP.SettingNeonatal intensive care and inpatient units of a pediatric hospital.Patients/Participants23 neonates with RS and severe upper airway obstruction with diverse etiologies (isolated RS (n = 7), Stickler (n = 5), RS+ (n = 4), Fetal Fentanyl Exposure[FFE] (n = 3), Campomelic dysplasia (n = 2), Van der Woude (n = 1), Treacher Collins Syndrome [TCS] (n = 1)).InterventionsOAP therapy.Main Outcome Measure(s)Respiratory measures and clinical course.ResultsMean pre-OAP obstructive Apnea-Hypopnea Index (oAHI) was 55 events/hour, highest in FFE (164 events/hour). Following OAP delivery, mean admission duration was 28 days, longest in TCS (50 days). The mean oAHI at completion of therapy was 6 events/hour at a mean age of 5 months, longest in FFE 6 months.ConclusionsOAP therapy is effective for infants with RS+/- syndromes and complex presentations.

articles.title: A marginal structural proportional rates model for recurrent event data.
articles.abstract: In observational studies with time-varying treatments and time-varying confounders, earlier confounders can affect subsequent treatments and earlier treatments can affect subsequent confounders. Marginal structural failure time models have been used to account for this time-dependent confounding to estimate causal treatment effects on time-to-event outcomes. However, the event of interest is often recurrent (e.g. hospitalizations and infections) in clinical and epidemiologic studies. Analyses which ignore recurrences (e.g. time to first event) generally suffer considerable efficiency losses. Very few methods exist for estimating the causal effect of a treatment when the event of interest is recurrent. We therefore propose a marginal structural proportional rates model (MSPRM) to estimate the effect of a binary, time-varying treatment on recurrent event outcomes in the presence of time-dependent confounding. We derive estimation and inference procedures which are shown to have good finite-sample properties using a series of simulations. We then illustrate use of the MSPRM to estimate the effect of time-varying steroid use on the rate of recurrent infection-related hospitalizations accounting for proteinuria over time in Cure GlomeruloNephropathy, an observational cohort study of patients with glomerular disease.

articles.title: The 'Quiet' Effect: A Prospective Study of Superstitious Language and Hospital Code Activations.
articles.abstract: BackgroundSuperstitious beliefs surrounding language are common in high-stress clinical environments. The word 'quiet' is often believed to precipitate increased workload or emergencies, yet prior studies have generally found no measurable effect. Whether broader categories of clinical language are associated with objective hospital escalation events remains unknown.ObjectivesTo evaluate whether the connotation of words announced during intensive care unit (ICU) rounds was associated with same-day hospital code activations or ICU admissions.MethodsWe conducted a single-center prospective study with randomized assignment of a daily word exposure at an academic Level I trauma center. Words were categorized as high-activity, neutral, or low-activity. Days with incomplete word exposure were excluded. The primary outcome was daily total codes; ICU admissions were analyzed as a secondary outcome. Differences across word categories were assessed using the Kruskal-Wallis H test. A secondary quiet-specific analysis compared quiet days with all other study days using Mann-Whitney U testing and negative binomial regression adjusted for day of week and month.ResultsA total of 320 study days were analyzed, including 129 high-activity, 63 neutral, and 128 low-activity word days. Median total codes were 10 (interquartile range [IQR], 8-13), 11 (IQR, 8-13), and 10 (IQR, 8-12), respectively (P = .498). ICU admissions were also similar across groups (P = .364). In secondary analysis, quiet days (n = 12) were not associated with increased total codes compared with non-quiet days (n = 308; median, 10 vs 10; P = .739). After adjustment for day of week and month, quiet-day status was not associated with total codes (incidence rate ratio, 0.941; 95% CI, 0.772-1.147; P = .548).ConclusionsIn this single-center study, the assigned word category during morning ICU rounds was not associated with same-day institutional code activations or ICU admissions.

articles.title: Risk assessment of non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug major toxicities in hospitalized cancer patients receiving palliative care.
articles.journal: Journal of oncology pharmacy practice : official publication of the International Society of Oncology Pharmacy Practitioners
articles.abstract: IntroductionThe Non-Steroidal Anti-Inflammatory Drug Major Toxicity Risk Score (NSAID-MTRS) is a prediction model that provides an individualized 1-year toxicity risk estimate. This study utilized the NSAID-MTRS to identify predictive factors, to estimate risk and to determine major toxicity events in hospitalized cancer patients receiving palliative care.MethodsManual data collection and International Classification of Disease, 10th revision (ICD-10) codes confirmed NSAID-MTRS predictive factors and major toxicity events. A major toxicity event was a major adverse cardiovascular event (MACE), a clinically significant gastrointestinal (GI) event, acute kidney injury (AKI) and death.ResultsOne-hundred and fifty-eight patients were on a NSAID and 375 patients were not on a NSAID. The majority of patients had metastatic disease (58-65%). For patients on a NSAID, the predictive factors of a past or current history of cardiovascular disease was 27%, (n = 42) and current statin medication use was 46% (n = 72). For patients on a NSAID, low, moderate, and high-risk severities were 33% (n = 52), 47% (n = 74), and 20% (n = 32). The 1-year risk estimate (mean ± SD) was 2.6 ± 3.1% and correlated with moderate risk. A MACE, a clinically significant GI event, and AKI frequencies were 5% (n = 8), 9% (n = 14), and 13% (n = 21). Risk severities, 1-year risk estimates, and major events, with the exception of death, were similar between groups (p > 0.05).ConclusionThe utilization of the NSAID-MTRS identified toxicity predictive factors in hospitalized cancer patients estimated to be at moderate risk. Although the NSAID-MTRS provided an evidence-based, patient-specific quantitative estimate of major toxicity risk, additional research is warranted prior to implementation in a cancer patient population.

articles.title: Using Lactate as a Prognostic Marker in Pulmonary Embolism-A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
articles.abstract: BackgroundPulmonary embolism (PE) is a life-threatening condition that requires accurate risk stratification. Although established tools such as PESI and sPESI are widely used, they may not fully capture disease severity. Elevated lactate has emerged as a potential prognostic biomarker, yet its role in routine risk assessment remains uncertain. This meta-analysis evaluates the association between lactate levels and mortality in PE and examines whether lactate may enhance current risk stratification strategies.MethodsWe performed a systematic review and meta-analysis in accordance with PRISMA 2020 guidelines and prospectively registered the protocol on PROSPERO (CRD420251170232). PubMed, EMBASE, and Cochrane Library were searched from inception through January 2026. Prospective and retrospective cohort studies including adults with PE and reporting mortality stratified by lactate levels were eligible. Study quality was assessed using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale. Pooled odds ratios (ORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated using a random-effects (DerSimonian-Laird) model. Heterogeneity was evaluated using I2 and Cochrane Q statistics. Prespecified subgroup analyses were conducted by lactate source (arterial vs venous), study design, and hemodynamic status. Analyses were performed using Stata 18.0, with p < 0.05 considered statistically significant.ResultsEight studies including 2102 patients met inclusion criteria. Elevated lactate was significantly associated with overall mortality (OR 3.57) and short-term PE-related mortality (OR 7.69). Both arterial and venous lactate measurements were independently associated with increased mortality. Elevated lactate predicted all-cause mortality in all-comer PE patients (OR 4.31) and remained significant among normotensive patients (OR 3.39). Associations were consistent across prospective (OR 5.27) and retrospective (OR 3.44) studies.ConclusionsElevated lactate is strongly associated with mortality in PE. These findings support the incorporation of lactate into risk stratification models, consistent with the recent 2026 AHA/ACC/ACCP/ACEP/CHEST/SCAI/SHM/SIR/SVM/SVN guidelines, which include a Class I recommendation for lactate measurement in PE risk stratification.

articles.title: Hypoglycemia is independently associated with higher red cell distribution width in adults with type 1 diabetes.
articles.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Red cell distribution width coefficient of variation (RDW-CV) is associated with cardiovascular risk, but its relationship with glycemia remains inconsistent. No previous study has examined RDW-CV across metrics defined by continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) in adults with type 1 diabetes.

OBJECTIVES: We aimed to assess the associations between RDW-CV and CGM metrics.

PATIENTS AND METHODS: This cross-sectional study included adults with type 1 diabetes without established cardiovascular disease, anemia, or active inflammation. RDW-CV was measured in fasting blood samples within 2 hours of collection. Glucose profiles were assessed using CGM over a 30-day window, and CGM metrics were calculated with GlyCulator 3.0.

RESULTS: The participants had a median age of 34.1 (24.4-41.1) years and a median diabetes duration of 12.0 (7.0-20.0) years; 55.6% were men. Median glycated hemoglobin was 7.7% (6.9%-8.4%), and median RDW-CV was 12.1% (11.8%-12.5%). RDW-CV correlated with the number of hypoglycemia episodes below 54 mg/dl (3.0 mmol/l) lasting longer than 15 minutes (R = 0.21; P <0.001) and with the low blood glucose index (R = 0.20; P <0.001). After adjustment for age, sex, diabetes duration, hemoglobin, mean corpuscular volume, C-reactive protein, body mass index, and smoking status, hypoglycemia episode frequency remained independently associated with RDW-CV (standardized β = 0.19; 95% CI, 0.08-0.30; P = 0.001), including after separate adjustment for time above range, mean glucose, or coefficient of variation (β = 0.17-0.18; all P <0.006), whereas these competing metrics were not associated with RDW-CV.

CONCLUSIONS: Greater hypoglycemia exposure, rather than hyperglycemia or glycemic variability, was independently associated with higher RDW-CV.

articles.title: Five-year outcomes of the Coordinated Care Program after Myocardial Infarction in a cardiac intensive care unit cohort: a propensity score-matched analysis.
Intra-arterial tenecteplase without mechanical thrombectomy and regional cerebral perfusion in acute ischemic stroke with medium- and distal-vessel occlusions.
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the safety and efficacy of intra-arterial tenecteplase (IA-TNK) without mechanical thrombectomy for acute ischemic stroke due to medium-vessel occlusions (MeVOs) and distal-vessel occlusions (DiVOs).

METHODS: We retrospectively reviewed patients with MeVO or DiVO treated with IA-TNK at doses of 2.5 to 10 mg. Computed tomography perfusion (CTP) was performed at baseline and immediately after treatment, with hypoperfused tissue volume defined as Tmax > 6 seconds and processed using RAPID software. Neurological status was assessed using the National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale (NIHSS) at baseline, 24 hours, 7 days, and discharge; functional outcome using the modified Rankin Scale (mRS) at 30 days.

RESULTS: Ten patients considered unsuitable for mechanical thrombectomy received IA-TNK (mean age 64.3 ± 12.3 years). Mean baseline NIHSS was 10.2 ± 4.7, and mean baseline ASPECTS was 9.1 ± 0.7. Angiographic improvement (≥1 mTICI grade) occurred in 4 of 10 patients, and tissue-level reperfusion (≥50% reduction in Tmax > 6-second volume) in 7 of 9 patients with paired CTP. Among 9 patients with paired CTP, median Tmax > 6-second volume decreased significantly from 48.0 mL to 17.0 mL (p = 0.02, Wilcoxon signed-rank test). Early neurological improvement at 24 hours occurred in 7 of 9 evaluable patients. Functional independence (mRS ≤ 2) at 30 days was achieved in 6 of 9 patients with follow-up. No intracranial hemorrhage of any Heidelberg class was observed.

CONCLUSION: IA-TNK without thrombectomy in selected MeVO/DiVO patients was associated with a significant reduction in CTP-defined hypoperfusion, encouraging early neurological improvement, and no symptomatic hemorrhage, supporting further prospective evaluation.

articles.title: Hepatic EPHX1 potentiates liver fibrosis by decreasing eicosatrienoic acids.
articles.abstract: Changes in polyunsaturated fatty acid metabolites are thought to contribute to pathogeneses of metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) and liver fibrosis. This study demonstrated that hepatic microsomal epoxide hydrolase (EPHX1) promotes liver fibrosis by decreasing hepatic eicosatrienoic acid (EET) levels, suggesting that elevation of serum dihydroxyeicosatrienoic acid (DHET) levels is an indicator of advanced fibrosis. Serum lipidomic analysis of 102 patients with MASLD and 121 with chronic hepatitis C, combined with multivariate logistic regression, confirmed elevation of serum 11,12-DHET levels as a predictor of advanced fibrosis. The expression of hepatic EPHX1, which hydrolyzes EET to DHET, increased in patients with advanced fibrosis. MASLD mouse model showed increased hepatic EPHX1 levels and decreased hepatic EET levels. Ephx1-null mice showed suppressed hepatic fibrogenesis and oxidative stress with increasing EET levels. In hepatic stellate cells (HSCs), treatment with 11,12-EET reduced COL1A1 expression, but not 11,12-DHET, attenuated intracellular oxidative stress, and suppressed TGF-β-induced HSC activation. Furthermore, it alleviated liver fibrosis by attenuating hepatic oxidative stress and suppressing HSC activation in mice with thioacetamide-induced liver fibrosis. This study provides evidence that EPHX1 contributes to EET hydrolysis in the liver and participates in liver fibrogenesis, suggesting its potential as a therapeutic target.

articles.title: Targeting KCa3.1 channels in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma impairs disease progression.
articles.abstract: This study explores the therapeutic potential of the calcium-activated potassium channel KCa3.1 in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC). Increased KCa3.1 expression correlates with poor overall survival of patients with PDAC. Using the immunocompetent KPfC (KrasWT/LSL-G12D Tp53fl/+ Pdx1-Cre) mouse model, we evaluated the therapeutic efficacy of KCa3.1 inhibition with TRAM-34 and maurotoxin alone or in combination with gemcitabine. Mechanistic insights were obtained in vitro from KCa3.1 CRISPR knockout pancreatic cancer cells (PANC-1KCNN4-/-) and a three-dimensional mixed spheroid model composed of pancreatic cancer and stellate cells. In vivo, KCa3.1 inhibition combined with gemcitabine decreased growth of tumor nodes and counteracted gemcitabine-induced fibrosis. Consistently, in vitro and ex vivo data showed that KCa3.1 inhibition induced tumor cell death and altered the invasive phenotype. Here, maurotoxin outperformed TRAM-34. On a molecular level, KCa3.1 inhibition diminished epithelial-mesenchymal transition, reduced T cell exhaustion markers and TGF-β1 secretion, and downregulated the G2-M checkpoint. These findings can mechanistically account for the therapeutic benefits of targeting KCa3.1 channels in PDAC.

articles.title: Efficacy and safety of once-daily single-inhaler triple therapy (FF/UMEC/VI) versus FF/VI in Chinese patients with inadequately controlled asthma (TRIUMPH): a randomized, double-blind, controlled, phase 3 trial using Bayesian dynamic borrowing.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Single-inhaler triple therapy fluticasone furoate/umeclidinium bromide/vilanterol (FF/UMEC/VI) improves lung function and asthma control in patients with uncontrolled asthma but lacks data in a Chinese population. This phase 3 trial (NCT04937387) assessed its efficacy and safety in Chinese asthma patients by bridging to global data from CAPTAIN.

METHODS: Patients with uncontrolled asthma on medium- or high-dose inhaled corticosteroids/long-acting beta-2 agonist (ICS/LABA) were randomized (1:1:1:1) to receive double-blind FF/UMEC/VI (100/62.5/25 or 200/62.5/25 µg) or FF/VI (100/25 or 200/25 µg) once daily for 12 weeks. The primary endpoint was change from baseline (CFB) in trough forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1) at Week 12 (FF/UMEC/VI vs FF/VI 100 µg). Secondary endpoints were CFBs in trough FEV1 (FF/UMEC/VI vs FF/VI 200 µg) and asthma control questionnaire-7 (ACQ-7) (both strengths) at Week 12. Trough FEV1 results were supplemented with CAPTAIN data using a Bayesian dynamic borrowing (BDB) method.

RESULTS: Between 29 July 2021 and 9 April 2024, 359 patients were randomized, of whom 358 comprised the intent-to-treat population after excluding one randomized in error. These patients were assigned to FF/VI 100/25 μg (N = 91), FF/UMEC/VI 100/62.5/25 μg (N = 90), FF/VI 200/25 μg (N = 89), or FF/UMEC/VI 200/62.5/25 μg (N = 88). Of these, 357 received study treatment and comprised the safety population. At Week 12, FF/UMEC/VI 100/62.5/25 µg improved trough FEV1 from baseline vs FF/VI 100/25 µg; using BDB, the posterior probability of the treatment difference being >0 was 97.9%, meeting the BDB-predefined success criterion of ≥95%; and the mixed model repeated measures (MMRM)-estimated least-squares (LS) mean treatment difference was 59 mL (95% confidence interval [CI] = -30 to 147). The LS mean treatment difference in change from baseline in ACQ-7 score was -0.028 (95% CI = -0.190 to 0.134). However, the success criterion was not met in trough FEV1 when adding UMEC 62.5 µg to FF/VI 200/25 µg; the LS mean treatment difference in change from baseline in trough FEV1 was -5 mL (95% CI = -94 to 84), and the LS mean treatment difference in change from baseline in ACQ-7 score was 0.112 (95% CI = -0.052 to 0.276). In both FF/UMEC/VI arms, clinically meaningful CFBs in FEV1 were observed at Week 4 and sustained at Week 12. FF/UMEC/VI and FF/VI had similar safety profiles.

CONCLUSION: Adding UMEC 62.5 µg to FF/VI 100/25 µg improved lung function and asthma control at Week 12 in Chinese asthma patients. Such improvements were not observed when UMEC 62.5 µg was added to FF/VI 200/25 µg.

articles.title: Editorial: Clinical Outcomes After Percutaneous Coronary Intervention in Patients With Cirrhosis.
Regaining control of the narrative: UK adults' experiences of managing and resisting type 1 diabetes stigma.
articles.journal: Diabetic medicine : a journal of the British Diabetic Association
articles.abstract:
AIMS: Type 1 diabetes (T1D) stigma is associated with poorer psychosocial well-being and suboptimal diabetes self-management. While it is not the responsibility of people living with type 1 diabetes to address T1D stigma, it is important to understand strategies they use to respond to stigma, and how these might vary over time and across contexts to support interventions.

METHODS: Adults (≥18 years) with T1D completed a survey, including the T1D Stigma Assessment Scale (DSAS-1). Participants scoring in the top quartile on the DSAS-1 were invited to join a co-produced focus group (N = 23, 70% women, 83% white, 60% insulin pump users, median diabetes duration 11 years), the transcripts of which were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis.

RESULTS: Three themes and 10 subthemes were developed. An initial sense of 'lack of control over the narrative' surrounding the condition led to more reactive approaches to managing T1D stigma. Participants described a process of then '(re-)reclaiming control of the narrative', gaining new perspectives and strategies for deciding how to deal with T1D stigma. Thirdly, they reported how T1D stigma management and resistance were affected by 'peer support, advances in diabetes equipment, and societal shifts'. Experiences of T1D stigma appear heightened at the point of diagnosis and when stigma is enacted by individuals expected to 'know better'.

CONCLUSIONS: The findings highlight the importance of greater support around diagnosis and further training for healthcare professionals to reduce stigmatising encounters. Connecting with the T1D community was highly valued and efforts to increase such opportunities should be prioritised.

articles.title: Under-ascertainment of leptospirosis mortality in Peru: ICD-10 versus free-text identification.
articles.journal: Health information management : journal of the Health Information Management Association of Australia
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Mortality surveillance systems rely heavily on ICD-10 coding, yet narrative cause-of-death fields often contain clinically relevant information that is not fully captured in structured codes.

OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the extent to which an ICD-10-only strategy underestimates leptospirosis mortality in Peru compared with an approach that incorporates free-text review.

METHOD: In this study all death certificates registered in the Peruvian national mortality system (SINADEF) from 2017 to 2025 were analysed, in which leptospirosis was identified through ICD-10 coding or narrative fields. Leptospirosis deaths were classified using three mutually exclusive categories: identified by both ICD-10 and free-text, by ICD-10 only, or by free-text only. The study involved assessing concordance, estimating the relative sensitivity of each strategy using a composite definition (ICD-10 and/or free-text), conducting a semantic analysis of narrative expressions, and fitting penalised logistic regression models to explore factors associated with discordant identification.

RESULTS: Among 238 certificates with evidence of leptospirosis, 205 (86.1%) were identified through ICD-10 codes and 229 (96.2%) through free-text review; 196 (82.4%) were captured by both sources. Using the composite definition, ICD-10 alone missed 13.9% of leptospirosis deaths. Free-text-only cases (n = 33) outnumbered ICD-10-only cases (n = 9) by more than three to one. Discordant identification was concentrated in high-burden Amazonian regions and was strongly associated with text-based confirmation categories. Semantic analysis revealed substantial lexical variability, including modified clinical expressions, Weil-related terminology, and orthographic variants. Regression models indicated that discordance was driven primarily by documentation and classification processes rather than geographic or institutional differences.

CONCLUSION: An ICD-10-only strategy substantially underestimates leptospirosis mortality in Peru. Narrative cause-of-death fields contain essential diagnostic information that is not consistently translated into ICD-10 codes. Integrating periodic free-text review into mortality surveillance workflows, including its use to continuously update automated coding dictionaries, can improve completeness, reduce misclassification, and strengthen the accuracy of vital statistics. These findings emphasise the necessity of enhanced coding practices and text-based analytic tools in mortality surveillance systems.Implications for health information management practice:Mortality surveillance programmes in Peru and similar settings should incorporate periodic free-text review to update automated coding dictionaries and reduce under-ascertainment of zoonotic disease deaths.

articles.title: Gallic acid ameliorates depressive-like behaviour associated with type-2 diabetes mellitus by mitigating oxidative stress.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Diabetes is linked with depression due to insulin resistance. Gallic acid, a natural polyphenol, has been demonstrated to have benefits against experimental hyperglycemia. In the present study, we investigated the antidepressant effect of gallic acid on depression-like behaviour in hyperglycaemic rats.

METHODS: Hyperglycemia was induced in rats using dexamethasone (2 mg/kg i.p.) for 7 days, followed by exposure to chronic unpredictable mild stressors to produce depression-like phenotypes. Animals were subjected to daily oral administration for 21 days. Behavioural paradigms like the sucrose preference test, forced swim test, locomotor activity, novelty-suppressed feeding, and novel object recognition were performed. Biochemical estimations, including glucose levels, oxidative stress parameters, and neurotransmitter levels, were performed.

RESULTS: The findings indicated that administration of gallic acid attenuated depressive-like behaviour. Furthermore, treatment with gallic acid also demonstrated better cognitive ability and amelioration of behavioural abnormalities. Gallic acid treatment normalized the elevated blood glucose in diabetic rats. A significant improvement in antioxidant parameters was noticed after treatment with gallic acid. Additionally, altered levels of neurotransmitters like serotonin and dopamine were also improved by gallic acid treatment. Histopathological evaluation of the brain demonstrated increased neural density and restoration of normal neural morphology.

CONCLUSION: Gallic acid may ameliorate depression associated with hyperglycemia by mitigating oxidative stress and neurological dysfunction in the brain. Therefore, the current study provides evidence that gallic acid may exert antidepressant-like effects in the experimental model of hyperglycemia and depression.

articles.title: Efficiency, Efficacy, and Energy-Specific Safety of Pulsed Field Versus Thermal Ablation in Paroxysmal Atrial Fibrillation: Insights From Contemporary Randomized Data (the E3-PFA Collaboration).
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Pulsed field ablation (PFA) is an increasingly adopted, minimally thermal modality for the ablation of atrial fibrillation, but its comparative performance versus contemporary thermal ablation strategies remains incompletely defined. We conducted an aggregate-data meta-analysis of contemporary randomized trials to compare procedural performance, safety, and clinical outcomes of PFA versus cryoballoon ablation and radiofrequency ablation in paroxysmal atrial fibrillation.

METHODS: A systematic search identified 6 contemporary randomized controlled trials enrolling 2015 patients with paroxysmal atrial fibrillation. Study-level random-effects meta-analyses were performed to compare procedural performance, peri-procedural safety, and atrial arrhythmia recurrence, with predefined subgroup analyses according to thermal ablation modality.

RESULTS: PFA was associated with significantly shorter procedure time, left atrial dwell time, and total ablation time than thermal ablation (all P<0.001), whereas fluoroscopy time and anesthetic strategy were comparable between groups. PFA was associated with a significantly lower risk of peri-procedural serious adverse events than thermal ablation (risk ratio, 0.58 [95% CI, 0.35-0.96]; P=0.036). Persistent phrenic nerve palsy and pulmonary vein stenosis occurred exclusively after thermal ablation. Overall, PFA was associated with a lower risk of atrial arrhythmia recurrence than pooled thermal ablation (risk ratio, 0.86 [95% CI, 0.75-0.99]; P=0.03). Subgroup analyses demonstrated a significant reduction in recurrence compared with cryoballoon ablation (risk ratio, 0.80 [95% CI, 0.65-0.97]; P=0.03), whereas outcomes were comparable between PFA and contemporary radiofrequency (risk ratio, 0.93 [95% CI, 0.77-1.13]; P=0.48).

CONCLUSIONS: PFA provides greater procedural efficiency, improved peri-procedural safety, and a lower risk of atrial arrhythmia recurrence than pooled thermal ablation in patients with paroxysmal atrial fibrillation. The efficacy advantage was primarily driven by comparisons with cryoballoon ablation, whereas outcomes were comparable between PFA and contemporary RFA.

articles.title: Delay in insulin treatment of patients with diabetic ketoacidosis due to sample hemolysis: justification for reporting a corrected potassium concentration?
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVES: Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) is a life-threatening complication of diabetes and warrants an emergency department (ED) admission. To reduce morbidity and mortality, insulin should be administered as soon as possible. The treatment, however, should be delayed for patients who initially present with hypokalemia, as insulin reduces K+ levels and potassium replacement should be given priority. The situation is complicated if the initial potassium sample sent for testing is hemolyzed.

METHODS: The medical records for 99 separate encounters of patients who presented to the ED with DKA or hyperosmotic hyperglycemic non-ketotic coma (HHNC) were reviewed. There were 9 who were hypokalemic (<3.5 mmol/L), 45 were eukalemic (3.5-5.0 mmol/L), and 31 were hyperkalemic (>5.0 mmol/L). Fourteen other patients encounters (1 eukalemic and 13 hyperkalemic not included in the above totals) had an ED presentation sample that was hemolyzed (rate 14.1 %).
