These findings describe changes in prescribing patterns during the COVID-19 pandemic, though factors underlying these changes and their clinical implications remain uncertain.

articles.title: Digital intervention to improve adherence to prescribed inhaled therapy among rural Chinese patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease: a pre-post feasibility study protocol.
articles.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) poses a substantial and growing public health burden worldwide. In China, rural patients with COPD experience a disproportionately higher disease burden than their urban counterparts, including higher mortality, limited access to healthcare resources and poor adherence to prescribed inhaled therapy. However, digital interventions specifically tailored to the needs of rural older adults remain limited. This study describes a theory-guided digital intervention based on the Fogg Behaviour Model and aims to evaluate its feasibility, safety, system usability and preliminary effectiveness.

METHODS AND ANALYSIS: This study is a single-arm pre-post feasibility study. A theory-guided digital intervention, delivered through a WeChat Mini Program, will be evaluated among 30 rural Chinese patients with COPD recruited from a tertiary Grade A teaching hospital in Sichuan Province, China. The intervention will be delivered over 4 weeks. Data will be collected at baseline (T0) and immediately after the intervention at 4 weeks (T1). Demographic data (eg, age, gender and education) will be gathered only at baseline.

ETHICS AND DISSEMINATION: Ethical approval was granted by the Affiliated Hospital of Southwest Medical University (approval number: KY2026247). The study has been registered in the ClinicalTrials.gov (ChiCTR2600127028). Results from this feasibility trial will be disseminated through peer-reviewed publications and presentations at domestic and international academic conferences, with the aim of informing the design of a subsequent large-scale randomised controlled trial.

TRIAL REGISTRATION NUMBER: ChiCTR2600127028.

articles.title: Feasibility and acceptability of a structured consultation-based palliative care intervention in a tertiary ICU: a prospective single-arm study.
Electroacupuncture as an adjunctive treatment for non-dipper hypertension: study protocol for a multicentre, randomised, sham-controlled trial.
articles.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Blood pressure normally follows a circadian rhythm, with a 10%–20% nocturnal decline relative to daytime levels; a decline of <10% is defined as a non-dipper pattern and is associated with a higher risk of hypertension-related target-organ damage. Although long-acting antihypertensive medications can reduce nighttime blood pressure, their effectiveness remains limited. Electroacupuncture (EA), as an adjunctive therapy, may improve circadian blood pressure rhythms; however, evidence from large, multicentre trials remains insufficient and its underlying mechanisms remain unclear. This study, therefore, aims to further evaluate the efficacy of adjunctive EA for non-dipper hypertension and explore its potential mechanisms.

METHODS AND ANALYSIS: This multicentre, randomised, sham acupuncture-controlled, patient-blinded clinical trial will recruit 404 patients with non-dipper hypertension, who will be randomly assigned (1:1) to EA or sham SA three times weekly for 8 weeks, followed by a 3-month follow-up. The primary outcome is the proportion of participants converting from a non-dipper to a dipper blood pressure pattern at week 8. Secondary outcomes include nocturnal blood pressure decline, 24-hour mean blood pressure, Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index and 36-Item Short Form Health Survey scores. Exploratory metabolomic and transcriptomic analyses will be performed using serum and whole-blood samples collected at baseline and after treatment.

ETHICS AND DISSEMINATION: This study protocol (V.2.0, 20 December 2023) involves human participants and was approved by the ethics committee of the Affiliated Hospital of Nanjing University of Chinese Medicine (no. 2023NL-278-02). The study findings will be disseminated through presentations at scientific conferences and publications in peer-reviewed journals.

TRIAL REGISTRATION NUMBER: ITMCTR2025000815.

articles.title: Interpreting Unanchored Matching-Adjusted Indirect Comparisons: Where Comparative Evidence Ends and Causal Inference Begins.
articles.journal: Value in health : the journal of the International Society for Pharmacoeconomics and Outcomes Research
articles.abstract: Unanchored matching-adjusted indirect comparisons (MAICs) are increasingly used when head-to-head randomized trials are unavailable or infeasible. By reweighting individual patient data to match aggregate characteristics from an external study, MAICs can improve comparability across populations, but successful covariate balance should not be mistaken for causal identification. Causal interpretation depends on strong assumptions regarding population overlap, the completeness and consistency of measured prognostic factors and effect modifiers, and the absence of relevant unmeasured confounding. Effective sample size, extreme weights, endpoint and eligibility heterogeneity, and post-baseline treatment differences provide additional sources of uncertainty. Using targeted oncology as a clinically relevant example, this Commentary distinguishes measured covariate balance, population overlap, and conditional exchangeability as separate questions for health technology assessment. It also outlines practical approaches to prespecification, sensitivity assessment, and communication of structural uncertainty beyond confidence intervals.

articles.title: Association of Preoperative Sodium-Glucose Cotransporter-2 Inhibitor Use with Postoperative Acute Kidney Injury and Recovery Outcomes Following Major Gastrointestinal Surgery.
articles.journal: Journal of gastrointestinal surgery : official journal of the Society for Surgery of the Alimentary Tract
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 (SGLT2) inhibitors are increasingly used in patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) and may have established cardiovascular and renal benefits. However, the association with postoperative kidney injury and other surgical outcomes remains uncertain. We evaluated the association between preoperative SGLT2 inhibitor use and postoperative outcomes among patients with T2DM undergoing major gastrointestinal (GI) surgery.

METHODS: Epic Cosmos, a multicenter electronic health record database, was used to identify adults with T2DM who underwent major GI surgical procedure between 2018 and 2024. Preoperative SGLT2 inhibitor exposure was defined as continuous use during the 6 months before surgery, allowing interruptions of less than 5 days. The primary outcome was AKI within 7 days after surgery, identified using ICD-10 diagnosis codes, with creatinine-based AKI assessed as a complementary outcome. Entropy balancing and weighted regression models were used to evaluate associations between SGLT2 inhibitor use and postoperative outcomes.

RESULTS: Among 201,123 patients, 11,750 had qualifying preoperative SGLT2 inhibitor exposure and 189,373 did not. ICD-10-based AKI occurred in 17.4% of SGLT2 inhibitor users and 21.2% of nonusers. After entropy balancing, SGLT2 inhibitor use was associated with lower odds of ICD-10-based AKI (OR, 0.85; 95% CI, 0.81-0.89) and creatinine-based AKI (OR, 0.87; 95% CI, 0.82-0.92). SGLT2 inhibitor use was also associated with lower odds of prolonged length of stay (OR, 0.77; 95% CI, 0.73-0.81), ICU stay (OR, 0.90; 95% CI, 0.85-0.95), 30-day mortality (OR, 0.42; 95% CI, 0.35-0.49), and 90-day mortality (OR, 0.50; 95% CI, 0.44-0.56), and higher odds of discharge home (OR, 1.38; 95% CI, 1.32-1.44). In contrast, SGLT2 inhibitor use was associated with higher odds of DKA within 7 days after surgery (OR, 3.59; 95% CI, 300.07-4.18).

CONCLUSIONS: Among patients with T2DM undergoing a major GI surgical procedure, preoperative SGLT2 inhibitor use was associated with lower postoperative AKI but higher DKA. These data may help inform perioperative use SGLT2 inhibitors among patients undergoing GI surgery.

articles.title: Established replicative senescence alters cellular homeostasis and reduces susceptibility to uremic toxin-induced cytotoxicity in renal tubular epithelial cells.
articles.abstract: Population aging has become a major global health challenge, accompanied by a growing burden of age-related chronic diseases, including chronic kidney disease (CKD). Cellular senescence is a hallmark of renal aging and contributes to CKD progression. Although uremic toxins promote tubular injury and cellular senescence, how established senescent renal tubular epithelial cells respond to subsequent uremic stress remains unclear. Here, we established replicative senescence models in two normal renal tubular cell lines NRK-52E (rat) and HK-2 (human) and investigated their responses to the uremic toxins indoxyl sulfate (IS) and p-cresyl sulfate (PCS). Replicatively senescent cells exhibited increased senescence-associated β-galactosidase activity and p53/p21 expression, accompanied by disrupted autophagic homeostasis, enhanced NLRP3 inflammasome-associated inflammatory signaling, and altered expression of iron metabolism-related proteins. IS and PCS induced several of these molecular alterations in young cells, whereas their additional effects were limited in senescent cells. Notably, concentration-response analyses revealed significantly higher IC50 values in senescent cells following IS or PCS exposure, indicating reduced susceptibility to uremic toxin-induced cytotoxicity. Thus, established replicative senescence is associated with substantial basal molecular dysfunction but reduced susceptibility to subsequent uremic toxin-induced cytotoxicity. These findings reveal a dissociation between cellular dysfunction and cytotoxic susceptibility and suggest that this altered stress-response phenotype may favor the persistence of dysfunctional senescent tubular cells under chronic uremic conditions.

articles.title: First-day clinical phenotyping in acute-on-chronic liver failure: a 24-hour landmark analysis with preliminary external reproducibility.
articles.abstract:
INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Acute-on-chronic liver failure (ACLF) is heterogeneous in the intensive care unit (ICU), and severity scores may not capture first-day physiology. This study aimed to derive first-day ACLF phenotypes in a 24-hour landmark cohort, characterize their clinical profiles, examine mortality associations, and assess preliminary external reproducibility.

PATIENTS AND METHODS: Adults with cirrhosis meeting a database-specific operational CLIF-C OF-based definition of ACLF were identified in MIMIC-IV and eICU-CRD. In MIMIC-IV, each patient's first cirrhosis-associated ICU stay was selected before exclusions; patients alive and in the ICU at 24 h entered the landmark cohort. Fifteen variables collected during 0-24 h were clustered separately in 20 imputed datasets using partitioning around medoids, followed by label alignment and consensus assignment. Cox models assessed 30-day mortality, and Fine-Gray models assessed in-hospital death with discharge alive as a competing event. External assignment used MIMIC-IV-derived scaling parameters and phenotype centroids.

RESULTS: Among candidate solutions, K = 2 showed the most favorable stability profile despite overlap in the principal-component projection. Phenotype 2 showed greater metabolic-renal disturbance and multiorgan dysfunction. After CLIF-C ACLF adjustment, Phenotype 2 was associated with 30-day mortality (hazard ratio, 1.72; 95% confidence interval, 1.35-2.17) and in-hospital death (subdistribution hazard ratio, 1.99; 95% confidence interval, 1.58-2.49). In eICU-CRD (n = 765), all 15 feature differences were concordant, and in-hospital mortality was 56.7% in Phenotype 2 versus 23.1% in Phenotype 1.

CONCLUSIONS: Two first-day clinical patterns differed in physiology, organ-failure burden, and mortality after the 24-hour landmark. External concordance supports preliminary reproducibility; validation is required.

articles.title: International expert Delphi consensus on the management of metabolic dysfunction- and alcohol-associated liver disease (MetALD).
articles.abstract:
INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Metabolic dysfunction- and alcohol-associated liver disease (MetALD) describes steatotic liver disease in individuals with cardiometabolic dysfunction and alcohol consumption. As MetALD-specific evidence remains limited, practical guidance is needed for diagnosis, fibrosis assessment, alcohol use disorder management, cardiometabolic treatment, and transplant evaluation.

MATERIALS AND METHODS: We conducted a two-round modified Delphi study with an international multidisciplinary expert panel. Statements were developed after a targeted literature review and organized into four domains: diagnosis and disease stratification, alcohol use assessment and alcohol use disorder treatment, metabolic and cardiometabolic management, and liver transplant assessment. Statements were rated on a five-point Likert scale. Consensus agreement was predefined as a median score ≥4, ≥70% of ratings in the 4-5 range, and interquartile range ≤1.

RESULTS: All 30 experts from 10 countries participated in round 1, and 29 (97%) in round 2. In round 1, 31 of 33 statements met agreement criteria; two were revised and re-evaluated. After round 2, consensus was achieved for all statements. The panel recognized MetALD as having dual metabolic and alcohol-related drivers and endorsed systematic cardiometabolic assessment, longitudinal quantification of alcohol intake, selective use of direct alcohol biomarkers, and stepwise noninvasive fibrosis risk stratification. Recommended care integrates individualized goals for alcohol reduction or abstinence, evidence-based alcohol use disorder treatment, structured lifestyle intervention, weight loss, physical activity, and optimization of diabetes, dyslipidemia, and hypertension. Transplant assessment should be individualized and multidisciplinary.

CONCLUSIONS: This consensus provides practical recommendations for integrated MetALD care and identifies priorities for future clinical research and external validation.

articles.title: Prior Clostridioides difficile Infection Is Associated with Infectious Complications Following Total Shoulder Arthroplasty.
articles.journal: Journal of shoulder and elbow surgery
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Clostridioides difficile infection (CDI) has been associated with postoperative complications and periprosthetic joint infection (PJI) after hip and knee arthroplasty but has not been studied in total shoulder arthroplasty (TSA). This study evaluated the association between CDI within two years before TSA and postoperative infectious complications. We hypothesized that prior CDI would be associated with increased odds of PJI, with the greatest odds when CDI occurred closest to surgery.

METHODS: Patients undergoing TSA were identified in a national claims database. Patients with CDI within two years before surgery (n = 782) were propensity score-matched 1:4 to controls (n = 3,098) on demographics, comorbidities, insurance, surgical year, and care setting. The primary outcome was two-year PJI. The CDI cohort was stratified by timing before TSA (0 to 3, 3 to 6, 6 to 12, and 12 to 24 months). Outcomes were compared using chi-square testing and logistic regression.

RESULTS: Two-year PJI rates were higher in patients with prior CDI (4.6% versus 2.8%; odds ratio [OR] 1.7 [95% CI 1.1 to 2.5]; P = .016), with the greatest odds when CDI occurred within three months before surgery (8.9%; OR 3.4 [1.7 to 6.6]; adjusted P = .002). Prior CDI was also associated with higher odds of subsequent CDI within two years (16.1% versus 1.9%; OR 10.1 [7.3 to 13.9]; adjusted P < .005), with higher odds across all time intervals. After correction for multiple comparisons, differences in pneumonia, sepsis, urinary tract infection, and hospital admission were not significant in the overall analysis.

CONCLUSION: Prior CDI is associated with increased odds of PJI following TSA, particularly when CDI occurs within three months of surgery, as well as with subsequent CDI. These findings suggest that CDI history may help identify higher-risk patients, and surgeons may consider CDI history and timing during preoperative planning.

articles.title: International Expert Consensus Statement on Contemporary Prevention and Management of Postoperative Delirium in Cardiac Surgery.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Postoperative delirium is among the most frequent neurocognitive complications of cardiac surgery, with reported incidence ranging from 14% to more than 50% depending on patient population and operative complexity. It is independently associated with prolonged mechanical ventilation, extended intensive care unit and hospital stay, long-term cognitive decline, and increased mortality. Despite this burden, prevention and management strategies remain inconsistent across institutions worldwide.

METHODS: An international multidisciplinary expert panel applied a structured PICOT (Population, Intervention, Comparison, Outcome, Timing) framework to predefined clinical questions spanning four perioperative phases: preoperative, intraoperative, postoperative and intensive care, and recovery after intensive care. Designated expert groups synthesized available evidence through structured literature reviews, and consensus recommendations were developed using a modified Delphi methodology.

RESULTS: The panel developed 14 consensus statements. Preoperatively, routine screening with the Montreal Cognitive Assessment and Clinical Frailty Scale, and multicomponent optimization are recommended. Opioid-sparing multimodal analgesia is recommended, whereas perioperative dexmedetomidine in place of benzodiazepines, cerebral oximetry, processed electroencephalography-guided anesthesia depth monitoring, and optimized oxygen delivery may be considered. In intensive care, validated delirium screening paired with sedation assessment, daily awakening and breathing trials, structured multicomponent care bundles, correction of reversible precipitants, and circadian-supportive environments are central. After transfer from intensive care, continued ward screening and structured post-discharge cognitive follow-up are recommended.

CONCLUSIONS: These statements provide a framework for preventing and managing postoperative delirium after cardiac surgery and advocate a coordinated multimodal approach. Standardizing screening, prevention bundles, and long-term follow-up within routine clinical pathways is recommended as a core institutional priority.

articles.title: SMOC1 and SMOC2 in organ fibrosis: The direction of the effect is set by the responding cell and its ionic environment, not by the ligand alone.
articles.abstract: Organ fibrosis is the shared terminal phenotype of chronic injury, and is usually treated as a target for inhibition. In the heart that assumption fails. The scar formed during the first week after acute myocardial infarction (MI) prevents the wall from giving way, and its load-bearing capacity is not a function of how much collagen it contains: fibroblast-specific deletion of CCN1 leaves collagen content and myofibroblast conversion unchanged, yet disorganises the fibril network and markedly increases post-MI rupture and mortality. Secreted modular calcium-binding proteins SMOC1 and SMOC2, members of the SPARC family, were long confined to skeletal and ocular development and to cancer, entering fibrosis biology only in the past decade. Evidence places SMOC2 on the profibrotic side in five organs, yet the same protein protects the renal tubule during acute kidney injury through integrin β3 and the CCND1-CDK4/6 axis. Conversely, SMOC1 is secreted transiently by cardiomyocytes after MI; cardiomyocyte-specific deletion doubles the incidence of rupture and AAV9-mediated overexpression reduces it. The same protein inhibits ALK5/SMAD2 signalling in endothelium through endoglin while activating it in fibroblasts through a complex containing the glutamyl-prolyl-tRNA synthetase EPRS. We argue, therefore, that their output is a property of the responding cell and its ionic environment, not of the ligand alone: it is set by the auxiliary-receptor repertoire the cell displays, the calcium concentration its EF-hand pair reads in calcifying tissue, and the phase of injury. Therapy should accordingly target scar quality locally and transiently rather than SMOC signalling globally.

articles.title: A Transgenic Pig Model for human Metabolic Disorders Defines the relationship between the colon pathological phenotype of metabolic disease, the microbiota and the intestinal barrier.
articles.abstract: Metabolic disorders are increasingly associated with intestinal dysfunction and colorectal diseases, yet the pathological characteristics and underlying mechanisms of intestinal injury under metabolic stress remain poorly understood. Here, we established a transgenic (TG) Bama pig model by CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knock-in of three humanized susceptibility genes and subjected the pigs to a high-fat, high-sugar diet (HFHSD) for 4, 8, or 12 months to investigate metabolic disorder-associated colonic dysfunction. HFHSD intervention induced marked alterations in serum biochemical parameters and disrupted colonic mucosal architecture, characterized by glandular disorganization and crypt distortion. Colonic tissues from TG pigs exhibited reduced populations of goblet cells, CD8⁺ T cells, and CD79A⁺ B cells, accompanied by pronounced activation of mitophagy, indicating impaired epithelial barrier integrity and mucosal immune homeostasis. In parallel, microbial diversity and IgA levels were reduced in the colonic contents of TG pigs, accompanied by an increased abundance of potentially pathogenic bacteria, particularly Escherichia-Shigella. Metabolomic profiling of colonic contents further revealed significant alterations in the intestinal metabolic landscape, including decreased levels of isobutyric acid and isovaleric acid and an increased level of myristic acid, a metabolite associated with autophagy-related processes. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that metabolic disorders are associated with coordinated alterations in colonic mucosal integrity, mucosal immunity, mitochondrial quality control, gut microbiota, and intestinal metabolism. The humanized TG Bama pig model provides a clinically relevant large-animal platform for investigating the pathophysiology of metabolic disorder-associated colonic diseases and may facilitate the development and preclinical evaluation of therapeutic strategies targeting intestinal dysfunction.

articles.title: Chronic hypoxia drives coronary artery pathology via TRPC3/4-mediated Ca²⁺ influx and phase separation-dependent cGAS-STING activation.
articles.abstract:
AIMS: Pulmonary hypertension (PH) is frequently complicated by coronary artery remodeling and dysfunction, yet the underlying mechanisms remain poorly defined. This study investigated whether and how chronic hypoxia drives coronary artery dysfunction through TRPC3/4-mediated Ca²⁺ influx and cGAS-STING activation in smooth muscle cells (SMCs).

METHODS AND RESULTS: A rat model of PH was established by exposure to chronic hypoxia. Coronary artery structure and function were assessed by histology and wire myography. In vitro experiments were performed using cultured SMCs, with molecular and cellular analyses including qPCR, western blotting, immunofluorescence, live-cell imaging, mitochondrial assays, and cell-free phase separation assays. PH rats exhibited increased coronary TRPC3/4 expression, enhanced Ca²⁺ influx, and coronary hypercontractility. In cultured SMCs, hypoxia induced mitochondrial dysfunction, mtDNA release, and cGAS condensate formation. TRPC3/4-mediated Ca²⁺ overload promoted mitochondrial damage and cGAS phase separation, while STIM1/ORAI1-mediated store-operated Ca²⁺ entry (SOCE) further contributed to STING activation. Cell-free assays demonstrated that Ca²⁺ promoted cGAS phase separation in both the presence and absence of dsDNA, and this effect was dependent on the cGAS intrinsically disordered region (IDR). Importantly, CIP3 attenuated cGAS phase separation and downstream STING signaling, thereby mitigating hypoxia-induced SMC proliferation, migration, and phenotypic switching. In PH rats, short-term treatment with VAPG-targeted CIP3 reduced right ventricular systolic pressure, attenuated pulmonary and coronary vascular remodeling, and improved coronary contractile responses.

CONCLUSION: Our findings establish a novel mechanistic axis wherein chronic hypoxia drives coronary artery dysfunction via TRPC3/4-mediated Ca²⁺ influx and phase separation-dependent cGAS-STING activation. In our experimental models, targeting cGAS phase separation, particularly through IDR-directed intervention, may represent a promising therapeutic strategy for PH-associated vascular pathology.

articles.title: Outcomes of Endovascular Repair for Stanford Type B Aortic Dissection with Concurrent Retrograde Intramural Hematoma Involving the Aortic Arch and/or Ascending Aorta (Zone 0-2) in a Chinese Population: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the outcomes of thoracic endovascular aortic repair (TEVAR) for type B aortic dissection (TBAD) with concurrent retrograde intramural hematoma (RTIMH) involving the aortic arch, with or without further extension into the ascending aorta.

METHODS: A systematic search of MEDLINE and EMBASE to June 2026 was performed. Studies reporting TEVAR outcomes in adults with TBAD-associated RTIMH, defined as a primary intimal tear at or distal to Ishimaru zone 3 with retrograde intramural hematoma extension into zones 0-2, were included. Co-primary outcomes were technical success and post-TEVAR retrograde type A aortic dissection (RTAD), defined as the new development of a communicating dissection flap within the previously non-flow intramural hematoma. Secondary outcomes included early mortality, stroke, type I endoleak, reintervention, survival, aortic rupture, and aortic remodelling. Proportions were pooled using single-arm random-effects meta-analysis following logit transformation; remaining findings were synthesised narratively.

RESULTS: Seven retrospective cohort studies comprising 342 patients, all from mainland Chinese institutions, were included. The pooled technical success rate was 99% (95% CI 97-99%; I2 = 0.0%). The pooled post-TEVAR RTAD rate was 3% (95% CI 1-8%; I2 = 7.6%), with all events preceded by proximal stent-graft-induced new entry. Secondary outcomes included pooled 30-day mortality of 2% (95% CI 1-4%; I2 = 0.0%), aortic rupture of 2% (95% CI 1-4%; I2 = 0.0%), reintervention of 7% (95% CI 5-11%; I2 = 0.0%), late all-cause mortality of 4% (95% CI 3-6%; I2 = 0.0%), and type I endoleak of 4% (95% CI 2-7%; I2 = 0.0%). All studies reporting pre- and post-procedural imaging demonstrated reductions in ascending aortic diameter and hematoma thickness, with complete ascending IMH resolution in 52.5-100% of patients.

CONCLUSIONS: TEVAR is technically feasible with low perioperative mortality and consistent aortic remodelling in selected patients with TBAD-associated RTIMH. Post-TEVAR RTAD and type I endoleak represent the principal procedure-specific risks. Contemporary evidence remains limited to small retrospective cohorts from a single geographic region.

articles.title: One-Year Outcomes of Surgical Versus Endovascular Revascularization for Acute Limb Ischemia in the SAPLING-ALI Registry.
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Despite the increasing use of endovascular therapy as an alternative to surgery for acute limb ischemia, individualized treatment selection remains challenging. We compared outcomes of endovascular therapy versus surgery and sought to identify patient characteristics favoring either strategy.

METHODS: This multicenter retrospective study included consecutive patients with acute limb ischemia (Rutherford category 1-2b) who underwent revascularization at 13 Japanese institutions between July 2011 and March 2025; patients with thrombosed popliteal artery aneurysm were excluded. The primary outcome was amputation-free survival, defined as freedom from major amputation or death from any cause. The primary analysis was a Cox model adjusted for 13 baseline covariates with hospital as a categorical covariate; propensity score weighting was used as a sensitivity analysis. Subgroup analyses were performed to identify characteristics favoring either strategy.

RESULTS: Of 978 patients (endovascular therapy, n = 607; surgery, n = 371), those treated with endovascular therapy more often had diabetes, hemodialysis, dementia, and non-ambulatory status. Unadjusted 1-year amputation-free survival was lower with endovascular therapy than with surgery (68.7% vs 76.3%; log-rank P = .001), but the adjusted hazard ratio for death or major amputation was 1.03 (95% confidence interval, 0.77-1.38; P = .84). Results were consistent with overlap weighting (hazard ratio 1.15; 95% confidence interval, 0.93-1.42) and across other sensitivity analyses. Thirty-day mortality was 13.1% after endovascular therapy and 8.9% after surgery (P = .05), and the difference was attenuated after weighting. No subgroup favoring either strategy was identified (all P for interaction ≥ .18).

CONCLUSIONS: Unadjusted amputation-free survival was lower after endovascular therapy than after surgery, but the difference disappeared after adjustment for patient characteristics and hospital, and no subgroup favoring either strategy was identified. Endovascular therapy, being less invasive, may be a reasonable alternative to surgery for acute limb ischemia.

articles.title: Secondary analysis of the FIELD randomized trial evaluated the performance of GFR slope in a non-glomerular model of estimated GFR decline.
articles.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Glomerular Filtration Rate (GFR) decline is a recent surrogate kidney endpoint for trials. Estimated GFR (eGFR) decline has been modelled using GFR slope, correlating total and chronic GFR slopes with composite kidney endpoints. Several included interventions caused an initial eGFR decline mediated by glomerular hemodynamics. We tested the association of GFR slopes with clinical endpoints for fenofibrate, an agent with an acute, non-glomerular eGFR decline (i.e. no effect on inulin clearance).

METHODS: The FIELD trial randomized adults to fenofibrate or placebo. Total slope was calculated using a repeated measures 2-slope linear mixed model for the entire intervention period. A three-year sensitivity analysis was performed. Chronic slope was calculated from month four. The composite kidney endpoint was doubling of serum creatinine or 40% decline/eGFR under 15 ml/min/1.73 m2/kidney death/kidney replacement therapy. The total slope from baseline to eight-week washout eGFR was an exploratory subgroup analysis.

RESULTS: 9795 participants were followed for five years. Post-washout eGFR was ascertained in 660 sub-study participants. Fenofibrate produced an acute eGFR decline of -9.05 ml/min/1.73 m2. Fenofibrate improved chronic slope (significant between-group difference 0.61 ml/min/1.73 m2/ annum [95% CI 0.50 to 0.71]) but worsened total slope (significant between group difference -1.54, 95% CI -1.65 to -1.44). Fenofibrate significantly increased the clinical endpoint (hazard ratio 1.48, 95% CI 1.16 to 1.89). Washout analyses demonstrated treatment benefit on total slope, contrary to on-study analyses in the overall cohort.

CONCLUSIONS: Conventional composite endpoints include surrogate components that may not always accord with measured kidney function, though widely accepted in trials. Total slope and the conventional composite yielded concordant treatment effects under an acute eGFR change both larger and mechanistically distinct from those in previous validation work, supporting the conclusion that total slope will produce similar results to conventional endpoints.

articles.title: Dietary sodium restriction enhances the renoprotective efficacy of endothelin-A receptor antagonism in proteinuric chronic kidney disease.
articles.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Endothelin-A receptor antagonists (ERAs) are emerging as an important treatment for proteinuric chronic kidney disease (CKD). As with renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) inhibition, dietary sodium intake may influence their therapeutic efficacy, but this has not been investigated. Here, we examined whether dietary sodium restriction enhances the systemic and kidney effects of acute selective endothelin-A (ETA) receptor antagonism in proteinuric CKD.

METHODS: In a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover study, 12 adults (mean age 46 years) with non-diabetic proteinuric CKD (mean eGFR 55 mL/min/1.73 m2; median proteinuria 1.8 g/day) receiving maximally tolerated RAAS inhibition completed two 14-day dietary interventions (habitual dietary sodium intake [13.3 g salt/day] and dietary sodium restriction [6.3 g salt/day, approximating guideline-recommended levels]) in random order. During each dietary period, participants underwent two study visits and received intravenous infusion of either placebo or the selective ET A receptor antagonist, BQ123. Systemic hemodynamics, arterial stiffness, kidney hemodynamics and proteinuria were assessed following each intervention.

RESULTS: BQ123 produced comparable reductions in systolic blood pressure (about 12-14 mmHg), systemic vascular resistance and arterial stiffness under both dietary conditions and increased kidney blood flow (about 320-335 mL/min) irrespective of dietary sodium intake. In contrast, significant reductions in glomerular filtration rate (peak placebo-adjusted reduction: about 5 mL/min/1.73 m2), effective filtration fraction (peak reduction about 1.5%), and proteinuria (about 300 μg/min) were observed only during dietary sodium restriction and not during habitual sodium intake.

CONCLUSIONS: Dietary sodium restriction enhances the short-term kidney efficacy of selective endothelin-A receptor antagonism in proteinuric CKD while preserving its beneficial systemic hemodynamic effects. As ERAs become established therapies for proteinuric kidney disease, these findings suggest that adherence to dietary sodium restriction may maximize their kidney-protective benefits. Whether the acute changes demonstrated here translate into long-term kidney protection requires prospective evaluation.

articles.title: Alectinib-Induced Tubular Injury Through Lysosomal Phospholipidosis.
Effect of Preoperative Probiotics on Gastric Volume in Diabetic Patients Undergoing Cancer Resection Surgery: An Open-Label Randomised Controlled Trial.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND & AIMS: To evaluate whether a seven-night probiotic regimen reduces fasting gastric residual volume (GRV) in adults with type 2 diabetes undergoing non-gastrointestinal cancer resection surgery.

METHODS: This prospective, open-label, parallel-group randomised trial enrolled 146 adults with type 2 diabetes (HbA1c ≤ 8.0%). Participants were assigned 1:1 to either a seven-night probiotic regimen (150 million spores of Bacillus coagulans SNZ 1969) in 200 mL of water at bedtime, or standard preoperative care. The primary outcome was ultrasound-estimated fasting GRV measured immediately before anaesthesia induction. Secondary outcomes included antral cross-sectional area (CSA), weight-indexed GRV, and qualitative Perlas grading. Analysis followed the intention-to-treat principle.

RESULTS: The mean (SD) fasting GRV was significantly lower in the probiotic group compared with the control group: 43.55 (12.15) versus 60.78 (14.45) mL, respectively; mean difference (MD), -17.23 mL; 95% CI, -21.60 to -12.86; P < 0.001. The treatment effect remained robust after adjusting for baseline cancer-site imbalances, while exploratory analyses across non-randomised adherence subgroups did not show a consistent dose-response relationship. Probiotics also significantly reduced the mean antral CSA to 5.62 (0.99) cm2 versus 6.57 (1.27) cm2, respectively; MD, -0.95 cm2; 95% CI, -1.32 to -0.58; P < 0.001. High-risk Perlas grade 2 findings were present in 19.2% of controls but dropped to 1.4% in the probiotic group, representing an absolute risk reduction of 17.8 percentage points (P < 0.001). No adverse events or volume thresholds > 1.5 mL/kg were observed.

CONCLUSIONS: A short-term, seven-night preoperative probiotic regimen significantly reduced both quantitative gastric ultrasound metrics and high-risk qualitative measures of fasting gastric contents. This represents a simple strategy to optimise preoperative sonographic gastric profiles before surgery.

TRIAL REGISTRATION: Clinical Trials Registry-India, CTRI/2026/03/106336; registered prospectively on 16 March 2026; https://ctri.nic.in/.

articles.title: Optimising Tuberculosis Treatment in Low- and Middle-Income Countries: A Narrative Review of the Role, Challenges, and Innovations in Therapeutic Drug Monitoring.
articles.journal: International journal of infectious diseases : IJID : official publication of the International Society for Infectious Diseases
articles.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Therapeutic drug monitoring (TDM) may improve anti-tuberculosis (TB) therapy by optimising dosing based on patient characteristics. This is especially relevant in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) where TB treatment is largely standardized despite frequent treatment failure and drug-related toxicity.

METHODS: This narrative review summarizes current evidence on the role, barriers, and future directions of TDM for TB treatment in LMICs, including emerging point-of-care and artificial intelligence (AI)-supported technologies.

RESULTS: TDM may improve treatment outcomes for key TB drugs like rifampicin, isoniazid, linezolid, and aminoglycosides. However, its implementation in LMICs is hindered by limited laboratory capacity, high assay costs, and lack of standardized protocols. Emerging approaches like dried blood spot sampling, electrochemical biosensors, wearable monitoring devices, and AI-guided dosing models may facilitate implementation and integration of TDM into routine TB care. Most of this evidence is drawn from observational cohorts, non-TB disease areas (e.g., sepsis, HIV, epilepsy), or early-stage device studies rather than TB-specific randomised or implementation trials.

CONCLUSION: TDM has strong biological rationale and promising observational evidence for improving TB treatment outcomes in LMICs, but this remains to be confirmed by TB-specific clinical and cost-effectiveness studies. Realising its potential will require affordable technologies, robust implementation frameworks, and enabling policy support, with validation of low-cost, point-of-care tools essential for scaling deployment in resource-limited settings.

articles.title: Cardiovascular Outcomes of Semaglutide in Adults With Congenital Heart Disease.
articles.abstract: Adults with congenital heart disease (ACHD) increasingly develop type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) and obesity, yet are excluded from cardiovascular outcome trials, and the effects of semaglutide here are unknown. Using the TriNetX Research Network, we conducted a retrospective new-user active-comparator study of adults with ACHD and T2DM initiating semaglutide (n = 2,385) or a dipeptidyl peptidase-4 (DPP-4) inhibitor (n = 2,889) from December 2017 to December 2025. Cohorts were 1:1 propensity score matched, yielding 1,422 pairs followed for 3 years, with a sensitivity analysis matched on 27 lesion categories. Semaglutide was associated with lower all-cause mortality (7% vs 12%; hazard ratio [HR] 0.66, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.51 to 0.85), hospitalization (40% vs 55%; HR 0.68, CI 0.61 to 0.76), and emergency department (ED) visits (35% vs 43%; HR 0.85, CI 0.75 to 0.96). Major adverse cardiovascular events (HR 0.71), heart failure (HR 0.74), and stroke (HR 0.65) were also lower; myocardial infarction and arrhythmia were not. Mortality, hospitalization, and ED visits were significant at 1, 3, and 5 years and in every sensitivity analysis; the cardiovascular associations were not. Congenital aortic valve disease was twice as common among semaglutide initiators before matching (23% vs 12%), and every great-complexity lesion comprised ≤10 patients per arm. A prespecified negative control was elevated in every analysis. In conclusion, semaglutide was associated with lower mortality and acute care utilization in a predominantly simple-to-moderate complexity ACHD population, but an elevated negative control indicates residual differences in healthcare engagement; these findings are hypothesis-generating.

articles.title: Timing of Coronary Angiography After Successful Fibrinolysis and Clinical Outcomes in ST-Segment Elevation Myocardial Infarction Patients.
articles.abstract: For patients with ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) who cannot undergo timely primary percutaneous coronary intervention, fibrinolysis followed by routine angiography is recommended, but the clinical outcomes associated with different angiography intervals within the guideline-recommended window remain uncertain. In this nationwide retrospective cohort of 130,322 patients treated between 2018 and 2023, 74,021 underwent angiography 2-6 hours and 56,301 underwent angiography 6-24 hours after successful fibrinolysis. The 2-6-hour group more frequently had TIMI flow grade <3 at initial angiography (35.97% vs 29.86%; adjusted odds ratio [OR], 1.28; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.16-1.39) but had less new-onset heart failure (7.34% vs 8.30%; adjusted OR, 0.89; 95% CI, 0.84-0.95), with no significant differences in in-hospital bleeding or mortality. During available follow-up, angiography within 2-6 hours was associated with lower all-cause mortality (adjusted hazard ratio [HR], 0.87; 95% CI, 0.78-0.98) and cardiac death (adjusted subdistribution HR, 0.85; 95% CI, 0.76-0.95). In conclusion, among patients with STEMI undergoing angiography after successful fibrinolysis, a T2C interval of 2-6 hours was associated with lower long-term mortality and less new-onset heart failure without increased in-hospital bleeding or mortality, providing large-scale real-world evidence supporting further prospective evaluation of angiography timing within the recommended 2-24-hour window.

articles.title: Longitudinal NT-proBNP Target Attainment and Clinical Outcomes in Heart Failure With Reduced Ejection Fraction: A Landmark Analysis of the GUIDE-IT Trial.
articles.abstract: Serial N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP) measurements are prognostic in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF), but the prognostic significance of longitudinal target attainment remains uncertain. We performed a secondary 180-day landmark analysis of the GUIDE-IT trial among participants with at least two NT-proBNP measurements through day 180 and follow-up beyond the landmark. The analytic cohort was restricted to participants who remained event-free according to the broad raw-record endpoint and under observation at the 180-day landmark. The exposure was the proportion of pre-landmark visits with NT-proBNP ≤1000 pg/mL, modeled per 10% increase and as ≥50% versus <50% attainment. The outcome was time to first recorded all-cause hospitalization or death. Cox models adjusted for age, sex, treatment arm, log2-transformed baseline NT-proBNP, New York Heart Association class, atrial fibrillation, and kidney disease. Among 324 participants, 155 experienced hospitalization or death; complete-case models included 319 participants and 154 events. Each 10% increase in target attainment was associated with lower risk (hazard ratio [HR] 0.89, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.84-0.96; P=0.001), as was ≥50% versus <50% attainment (HR 0.44, 95% CI 0.27-0.71; P<0.001). Target attainment improved model fit beyond clinical characteristics and baseline NT-proBNP (likelihood-ratio P<0.001), but not after inclusion of the most recent pre-landmark NT-proBNP measurement (HR 0.97 per 10% increase, 95% CI 0.90-1.06; P=0.51). Greater longitudinal target attainment was associated with lower subsequent risk, although its prognostic information substantially overlapped with the most recent NT-proBNP measurement.

articles.title: Oxidative stress biomarkers and residual cardiovascular risk in atherosclerosis: A narrative review of mechanistic rationale, prognostic associations, and translational barriers.
articles.abstract: Despite major advances in lipid-lowering therapy, residual cardiovascular risk persists in patients with atherosclerotic disease, highlighting limitations of conventional risk factors in capturing biological processes involved in disease progression. This review examines the potential relevance of three interconnected oxidative stress-related biomarkers-oxidized low-density lipoprotein (oxLDL), myeloperoxidase (MPO), and soluble lectin-like oxidized low-density lipoprotein receptor-1 (sLOX-1)-with a primary focus on their potential complementary role in cardiovascular risk assessment in coronary artery disease (CAD). MPO can promote LDL oxidation and oxLDL formation, while oxLDL activates LOX-1-related pathways involved in oxidative stress, inflammation, endothelial dysfunction, and vascular injury; proteolytic cleavage of LOX-1 generates circulating sLOX-1. We synthesize evidence regarding associations of these biomarkers with CAD and cardiovascular outcomes and consider whether their combination with established clinical risk factors and risk scores could provide additional information on residual cardiovascular risk. Evidence from carotid and peripheral atherosclerotic disease and from chronic comorbid conditions is considered mainly as supportive biological and clinical context. However, substantial heterogeneity in study populations, clinical endpoints, analytical methods, and reported biomarker thresholds limits direct comparison and prevents conclusions regarding a validated role in clinical risk re-stratification. We therefore propose the combined assessment of oxLDL, MPO, and sLOX-1 as a hypothesis-generating multimarker strategy for evaluation in prospective studies, rather than an established approach for risk classification or treatment guidance.

articles.title: Knowledge graphs for polypharmacy: A systematic review and critical appraisal of reporting quality.
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Ensuring medication safety for patients with multi-morbidity, who are often prescribed multiple drugs concomitantly (i.e., polypharmacy), is challenging due to the high risk of drug-drug interactions (DDIs) and accumulation of side-effects. Leveraging large datasets in the form of Knowledge Graphs (KGs) can improve knowledge on drug safety by modeling complex relationships among biomedical entities such as drugs, diseases, proteins and side effects, allowing for the prediction of novel relations. However, it remains unclear to what extent existing KGs adequately capture the polypharmacy context. Therefore, this systematic review identifies KGs constructed and/or utilized for predicting side effects and DDIs in the polypharmacy context, and evaluates their reporting quality.

METHODS: Publications were identified through a structured search through DBLP, MEDLINE, and the ACM Guide to Computing Literature up to January 2026, and supplemented by snowballing. We included peer-reviewed papers presenting KGs developed for and/or used in the context of polypharmacy-related predictions and containing polypharmacy knowledge. We excluded KGs missing both data and code. We adapted and extended a KG evaluation framework to objectively assess the reporting quality of KGs through a review of their documentation from both a technical and a medical domain-specific perspective.

RESULTS: Ten studies were included following full-text screening. We provide an overview of relevant statistics, contents, and limitations using our KG evaluation framework. Our study revealed inconsistent technical documentation on KG construction and KG metadata, as well as a lack of knowledge on granular pharmacogenetics and (patho)physiological pathways within the included KGs.

CONCLUSION: Our results show a need for improved quality of reporting, and the incorporation of fine-grained knowledge on pharmacogenetics and (patho)physiological pathways to ensure the long-term re-usability and relevance of KGs in the context of polypharmacy-related predictions. We also recommend to involve medical experts in KG development in this domain.

articles.title: DESCRIPTION OF TREATMENT PATTERNS AND POPULATION CHARACTERISTICS OF PRE-DIALYSIS CKD PATIENTS IN THE NEPHROSCREEN SURVEY.
articles.journal: Journal of renal nutrition : the official journal of the Council on Renal Nutrition of the National Kidney Foundation
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To characterize real-world clinical practice, patient profiles, and the use of ketoanalogue (KA)-supplemented low-protein diets (LPD) (KA+LPD) in dialysis-naïve patients with advanced chronic kidney disease (CKD) in the Czech Republic.

METHODS: This multicenter cross-sectional observational survey included adult patients with CKD stages 4-5 not yet on dialysis, recruited from 18 nephrology outpatient clinics and dialysis centers between April and November 2022. Clinical, laboratory, anthropometric, and nutritional data were collected from medical records and patient questionnaires. Descriptive statistics were used to summarize data, and multivariable logistic regression was performed to identify factors associated with prescription of KA therapy. A sensitivity analysis accounted for physician-level clustering.

RESULTS: A total of 792 patients were included (mean age 72.7±12.3 years; 54.9% male). Most patients had CKD stage 4 (76.4%), with a mean eGFR of 18.0 ± 6.0 ml/min/1.73 m2. KA were prescribed in 38.1% of patients. In multivariable logistic regression, KA prescription was associated with CKD stage 5 (OR 3.30, p <0.001), lower serum albumin, hypertension as CKD etiology, and lower medication burden, while older age was generally associated with a lower likelihood of prescription. Patients receiving KA had lower eGFR and higher urea and creatinine levels but showed no evidence of worse nutritional or metabolic status compared with non-users.

CONCLUSION: KA use in advanced CKD is common but varies substantially and appears influenced by both patient characteristics and physician-level practice patterns. In this cross-sectional cohort, KA-treated patients showed no evidence of worse nutritional or metabolic status compared with non-users; however, prospective studies are needed to evaluate longitudinal clinical outcomes.

articles.title: Dose-adjustable amlodipine tablets engineered by semi-solid extrusion 3D printing at room temperature for point-of-care applications.
articles.abstract: Conventional technologies make it difficult to manufacture personalised oral dosage forms for thermosensitive active pharmaceutical ingredients. In addition, there are several drawbacks to the one-size-fits-all approach for hypertension management. For instance, commercial amlodipine products are available as amlodipine salts in limited fixed-dose strengths, which do not accommodate personalised dosing. This proof-of-concept study investigates the feasibility of using semi-solid extrusion (SSE) 3D printing at room temperature to fabricate dose-adjustable, antihypertensive drug susceptible to thermal degradation as oral solid dosage forms, with amlodipine free base as a model drug for point-of-care applications. A single amlodipine-loaded pharma-ink (2.5%w/w) was used to manufacture 3D printed tablets (printlets) containing 5, 7.5 and 15 mg of amlodipine free base by varying printlet dimensions. The printlets were characterised for physical properties, drug content, dissolution, solid-state properties and morphology using HPLC, SEM-EDX, DSC, PXRD, FTIR, Raman spectroscopy and solid-state NMR. Dose-adjustable printlets were successfully 3D printed at room temperature with acceptable drug content (96.8-104.9%), rapid disintegration (<5 min) and immediate drug release (t80% 9-22 min). Solid-state characterisation supports the physicochemical integrity of amlodipine following printing and drying, while HPLC showed no evidence of degradation products. The same pharma-ink enabled accurate fabrication of multiple dose strengths without reformulation. SSE 3D printing provides a simple approach for compounding personalised, dose-adjustable amlodipine free base tablets under mild processing conditions, avoiding its degradation. In addition, this approach could address the conventional manufacturing challenges associated with poor flowability of amlodipine base. The technology offers considerable potential for decentralised point-of-care manufacture of thermosensitive medicines and supports future implementation of personalised cardiovascular therapies.

articles.title: Systematic excipient selection as a tool to optimize solid state properties and aerosol performance of spray dried RNA loaded lipid nanoparticles.
articles.abstract: The advancement of RNA therapeutics, particularly small interfering RNA (siRNA), offers promising new approaches for the treatment of pulmonary diseases driven by aberrant gene expression and chronic inflammation like asthma and COPD. In this study, we systematically engineered dry powder inhaler (DPI) formulations containing low (0.8%) and high (2%) siRNA-loaded lipid nanoparticle (LNP) concentrations using spray drying. The matrix-forming excipients, lactose, mannitol and trehalose were combined with varying concentrations of L-leucine (3% to 30% relative to the sugar or sugar alcohol) and trileucine (3%) as dispersion enhancers. The goal was to address key formulation hurdles: maintaining siRNA gene-silencing efficiency, optimizing solid-state properties, and achieving efficient aerosolization for pulmonary delivery. Lactose and trehalose-based spray-dried powders exhibited yields over 70% and preserved siRNA bioactivity, with gene silencing efficiencies exceeding 95% in vitro. Physicochemical characterization revealed that these formulations containing low to moderate leucine or trileucine content solidified in the glassy state, displaying glass transition temperatures over 76 °C and residual moisture levels below 7%, favorable for long-term stability and pulmonary delivery. In contrast, mannitol-based formulations were highly crystalline and less compatible with LNPs, resulting in low yields, larger, irregular shaped particles and poor aerosolization efficiency. In vitro aerosol performance was assessed using two breath-actuated DPIs in a laser diffraction inhalation setup. Our findings highlight that successful pulmonary delivery of siRNA-LNP powders not only depend on powder attributes but also on the interplay between formulation and DPI device. Optimizing excipient selection with regard to a device's powder dispersion principle is essential to achieve robust aerosol performance, efficient lung deposition, and preservation of therapeutic activity in solid-state siRNA-LNP dry powder formulations.

articles.title: Revisiting the role of fluorescent dyes in the detection of amorphous and amyloid aggregates: The quest continues.
articles.abstract: Protein aggregation is a hallmark of various neurodegenerative and systemic disorders, including Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, and type 2 diabetes. The ability to detect and characterize aggregates in both in vitro and in vivo systems is crucial for understanding disease mechanisms and developing diagnostic strategies. Fluorescent dyes have emerged as powerful tools for probing protein aggregates, offering insights into their structural variations and formation pathways. This review provides a comprehensive comparison of classical and emerging fluorescent dyes. It correlates their binding specificity and performance metrics, including quantum yield, fluorescence enhancement, and binding affinity, with molecular recognition mechanisms such as TICT restriction, π-π stacking, hydrophobic interactions, and electrostatic interactions. We categorize the dyes based on their blood-brain barrier (BBB) crossing ability, positron emission tomography (PET) imaging suitability, environmental sensitivity, nucleic acid binding affinity, luminescent conjugated oligothiophenes (LCOs), and nanoparticle-conjugation. We also consider their applicability to in vitro, in vivo and ex vivo settings, highlighting their use in detecting different aggregate species. We further assess dye suitability for amyloid versus amorphous aggregates and for different experimental contexts, considering critical parameters. By bridging structural features with functional outcomes, this review offers guidance for probe selection and highlights future directions for rational dye design to enhance sensitivity and selectivity in aggregate detection.

articles.title: Activated CD3 + CD25 + CD69 + HIF-1α + T cells and HIF-1α mRNA expression as immunometabolic biomarkers in sensitized chronic kidney disease patients.
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: The immunometabolic foundations of allo-sensitization, characterized by anti-HLA antibody development in chronic kidney disease (CKD) patients awaiting transplantation, remain to be fully elucidated. This study aimed to characterize the activated CD3 + CD25 + CD69 + HIF-1α + T-cell population and evaluate HIF-1α mRNA expression levels as potential immunometabolic biomarkers in sensitized candidates.

METHODS: A total of 36 CKD patients [PRA-positive (n = 20), PRA-negative (n = 16)] and 20 healthy controls were enrolled. We quantified the transcriptional expression of HIF-1α through quantitative real-time PCR (qRT-PCR), while CD3+CD25+CD69+HIF-1α+ T-cell frequencies were evaluated by flow cytometry. Data processing and statistical evaluations were executed via the IBM SPSS Statistics v25.0 software package.

RESULTS: The frequency of CD3+CD25+CD69+HIF-1α+ T cells was significantly higher in the PRA-positive group compared to healthy controls (median [IQR]: 0.90% [0.15-1.68] vs. 0.00% [0.00-0.23], p = 0.003). Notably, patients with 'dual-sensitization' (Class I + II) exhibited the most prominent accumulation of this subset (median [IQR]: 1.75% [1.23-2.42]), suggesting that higher allo-sensitization levels correlate with a more pronounced immunometabolic activation.

CONCLUSION: Our findings demonstrate a robust association between PRA positivity and distinct cellular immunometabolic activation in CKD. The expansion of the CD3+CD25+CD69+HIF-1α+ phenotype may serve as a novel "metabolic signature" for pre-transplant immunological risk stratification. The discordance between cellular percentages and mRNA levels suggests potential post-transcriptional regulation or protein stabilization of HIF-1α. Targeting immunometabolic pathways offers a promising strategy for modulating allo-sensitization.

articles.title: A standardised ultrasound strategy safely excludes recurrent deep-vein thrombosis without prior imaging.
articles.journal: Journal of thrombosis and haemostasis : JTH
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Diagnosing recurrent ipsilateral deep-vein thrombosis (DVT) is challenging because current diagnostic strategies often require comparison with prior imaging, which is frequently unavailable in clinical practice.

OBJECTIVE: To assess whether a sequential diagnostic strategy using colour duplex ultrasound with newly developed standardised criteria, and D-dimer testing could safely exclude recurrent DVT without previous imaging.

METHODS: In this multicentre diagnostic outcome study, we enrolled 466 consecutive outpatients with suspected recurrent ipsilateral lower-limb DVT at 27 centres in France. Ultrasound classified findings as acute occlusive/sub-occlusive thrombosis (absence of vein compressibility and flow, or flow outlining the thrombus, no reflux), chronic post-thrombotic changes (partial obstruction, partial compressibility and filling, reflux), or normal. Patients with non-diagnostic (i.e., inconclusive) ultrasound underwent D-dimer testing and, if positive (≥500 ng/mL FEU), repeat ultrasound at day 7±2. Anticoagulation was withheld after a negative strategy result. The primary outcome was the 3-month cumulative incidence of adjudicated symptomatic venous thromboembolism in untreated patients.

RESULTS: Baseline ultrasound was negative in 280 (60.1%), positive in 176 (37.8%), and non-diagnostic in 10 (2.1%). Five patients with non-diagnostic ultrasound had a negative D-dimer and five had a positive D-dimer but unchanged repeat ultrasound. Two patients (0.4%) were lost to follow-up. Among untreated patients with a negative strategy result, symptomatic venous thromboembolism occurred in three patients (1.1%; 95% CI 0.0-2.2).

CONCLUSIONS: The absence of venous occlusion or sub-occlusion on ultrasound safely excluded recurrent ipsilateral DVT without requiring comparison with prior imaging. This approach could simplify diagnostic pathways and overcome a major limitation of current strategies.

articles.title: Bedside ECMO Cannulation by Intensivists and Emergency Physicians.
articles.abstract: The number of centers capable of initiating extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) for critically ill patients with refractory cardiac or respiratory failure is expanding. Historically, patients were taken to the operating room or catheterization laboratory for ECMO cannulation by cardiothoracic surgeons and perfusionists. More recently, non-surgeons who have undergone specialized training are performing percutaneous ECMO cannulation and initiation of support at the bedside at some centers. This approach is attractive, in part, because of the timely initiation of ECMO and avoidance of the risk of patient deterioration during transport to a procedural area. The purpose of this article is to provide a roadmap for intensivists and emergency physicians to lead ECMO bedside procedures including veno-venous (VV), veno-arterial (VA), and hybrid veno-arteriovenous (V-AV) cannulation at ECMO-capable centers. These procedures demand cognitive and technical skills that are already foundational to critical care practice, including vascular access guided by point-of-care ultrasound and leadership during a dynamic resuscitation. A team-based approach to bedside ECMO cannulation is presented and illustrated with figures and video, including preparation, procedural execution, subsequent patient management, and programmatic considerations such as training and credentialing requirements.

articles.title: Liberation from Veno-venous Extracorporeal Life Support (VV-ECLS) for Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS): the Liberate VV-ECLS study: an international survey.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: The use of veno-venous extracorporeal life support (VV-ECLS) for severe acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) has increased substantially worldwide. However, approaches to liberation from extracorporeal support remain poorly defined, with no standardized protocols or validated readiness criteria.

RESEARCH QUESTION: What are the global practices for VV-ECLS liberation among Extracorporeal Life Support Organization (ELSO) centers? Where is there variability in readiness assessment, liberation strategies, and use of standardized protocols?

STUDY DESIGN AND METHODS: We formulated a cross-sectional survey of 25 questions regarding liberation practices among ECLS providers. Questions focused on assessed parameters for readiness to liberate, determination of liberation success, and strategies to optimize it. Surveys were distributed electronically to 765 institutions globally registered with ELSO between July 1st and Aug 15th, 2022. Descriptive statistics were used to summarize responses.

RESULTS: Of 765 centers contacted, 340 (44%) responded, with 209 (61%) reporting use of VV-ECLS. Most centers were adult-focused, intensivist-led programs with moderate annual volumes. Most respondents (58%) prioritized VV-ECLS liberation before liberation from mechanical ventilation. Readiness for liberation was most determined by improvement in oxygenation under lung-protective ventilation (92%) and respiratory system compliance (90%), while fewer centers used inspiratory effort indices (34%). Liberation strategies were heterogeneous, with progressive reduction of sweep gas flow being most common (40%). Liberation trial duration varied widely (median 120 minutes; mean 497 ± 635 minutes), and most centers performed one trial per day. Arterial blood gas abnormalities (90%) and clinical signs of respiratory distress were the primary indicators of liberation failure. Only 42% of centers reported using a formal liberation protocol.

INTERPRETATION: VV-ECLS liberation practices vary substantially across centers and are largely guided by institutional experience rather than standardized evidence. These findings highlight the need for validated physiologic predictors and protocolized strategies to optimize safe and timely liberation from VV-ECLS.

articles.title: Trends in cirrhosis-related mortality stratified by sex and race/ethnicity in the United States, 2018-2024.
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: A better understanding of the recent cirrhosis burden in the US is needed.

METHODS: A population-based study of US adults aged ≥25 used the National Mortality Database (2018-2024) to determine temporal mortality patterns.

RESULTS: Quarterly age-standardized cirrhosis-related mortality remained stable before the pandemic, then peaked in Q4 2020. Cirrhosis-related mortality varied substantially by race and ethnicity. The highest mortality was observed among non-Hispanic American Indian or Alaska Native (AIAN) individuals, followed by Hispanic individuals and non-Hispanic White individuals; mortality was lower among non-Hispanic Black and non-Hispanic Asian individuals. Cirrhosis-related mortality was consistently higher in males than females, while sex-specific temporal patterns differed, with a steeper overall increase and slower later decline among females.

CONCLUSIONS: Cirrhosis-related mortality increased in the early COVID-19 pandemic and remained disproportionately high among racial and ethnic minority populations, particularly non-Hispanic AIAN individuals.

articles.title: The Comparative Safety of Tramadol versus Oxycodone after Major Procedures, in Patients with Cirrhosis.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: In patients with cirrhosis undergoing surgical procedures, the optimal post-operative pain management strategy is unclear. While oxycodone and tramadol are frequently prescribed, some guidelines caution against tramadol use in cirrhosis, given variable hepatic metabolism and anticholinergic effects.

DESIGN: Within two U.S. datasets (MarketScan [2012-2023]; Optum's de-identified Clinformatics® Data Mart Database [2004-2025]), we constructed a 1:1 propensity score (PS)-matched cohort with cirrhosis initiating either short-acting tramadol or oxycodone within 30 days of a major operative procedure. Patients were followed for 90-days in an intention-to-treat approach for the primary outcome of liver decompensation (i.e., hospitalization for hepatic encephalopathy [HE], ascites, spontaneous bacterial peritonitis [SBP], variceal hemorrhage or hepatorenal syndrome [HRS]); secondary outcomes included all-cause hospitalizations, fractures, hyponatremia, hypoglycemia, seizures, and mortality. We estimated pooled PS-matched hazard ratios (HRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs), controlling for 141 pre-treatment characteristics.

RESULTS: After PS matching, initiators of tramadol versus oxycodone demonstrated no significant differences in rates of liver decompensation (303.9 per 1000 person-years [PY] vs. 288.0/1000PY; HR=1.06 [95%CI=0.93-1.21]; n=6,818 matched pairs). This included non-significant differences in rates of hospitalization for HE (HR=1.07, 95%CI=0.92-1.04), or for ascites, SBP or HRS (HR=1.02, 95%CI=0.87-1.19). We also found no significant differences for the secondary outcomes, between groups. Findings persisted across all subgroup and sensitivity analyses.

CONCLUSION: Among patients with cirrhosis initiating post-procedure tramadol or oxycodone, no significant differences were observed in rates of liver decompensation. Given the caution necessary when prescribing opioids in cirrhosis, future studies will need to assess safety across opioid formulations and dosing ranges.

articles.title: Photobiomodulation for Oral Mucositis Prevention in Hematopoietic Stem Cell Transplantation: Evidence and Unresolved Supportive-Care Outcomes.
articles.abstract:
PURPOSE: To evaluate whether protocol-defined photobiomodulation therapy (PBMT) for prevention of oral mucositis (OM) in hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) has demonstrable benefits beyond mucosal endpoints.

METHODS: A critical narrative synthesis prioritizes HSCT trials, guidelines and recent evidence; source identification and unrecorded systematic-search elements are explicitly distinguished.

RESULTS: Mucositis prevention has the strongest direct support. In POMFITT (n = 30), severe OM occurred in 0/15 PBMT-treated and 4/15 control patients (absolute difference -26.7 percentage points), but this sparse comparison is sensitive to the statistical test used. Hospitalization, physical function and quality of life did not differ significantly at discharge. Pediatric controlled and abstract-only findings are indirect or preliminary for several supportive-care endpoints. Associations between OM and infection, opioid use or nutrition cannot establish causal PBMT effects.

CONCLUSION: PBMT should be positioned as a preventive OM intervention in defined HSCT settings, not an established multidimensional supportive-care treatment. Adequately powered endpoint-specific studies with reproducible optical dosimetry are needed.

articles.title: Changes in Retinal and Choroidal Thickness and OCTA-Derived Vessel Density after Anti-VEGF Therapy for Diabetic Macular Edema.
articles.abstract:
PURPOSE: To evaluate the effects of anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (anti-VEGF) therapy on retinal and choroidal thickness and optical coherence tomography angiography (OCTA)-derived retinal vessel density in patients with diabetic macular edema (DME), with prespecified primary outcomes and exploratory OCTA outcomes controlled for multiplicity.

METHODS: This retrospective clinical study included 45 patients (45 eyes) with DME treated at the Affiliated Eye Hospital of Chengdu University of Traditional Chinese Medicine between January 2023 and January 2026. All patients received three consecutive monthly intravitreal injections of conbercept (0.5 mg/0.05 mL). OCTA examinations were performed at baseline, 1 month, and 3 months after the first injection to measure central macular thickness (CMT), subfoveal choroidal thickness (SFCT), vessel density of the superficial capillary plexus (SCP) and deep capillary plexus (DCP), foveal avascular zone (FAZ) area, and parafoveal vessel density at 300 μm (FD-300). Best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) was also recorded. BCVA, CMT, and SFCT were prespecified as primary outcomes. All OCTA-derived parameters were exploratory and were corrected using the Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) procedure across 12 comparisons.

RESULTS: The study included 45 patients (45 eyes), comprising 21 male patients (21 eyes) and 24 female patients (24 eyes), with a mean age of 54.44 ± 12.09 years. The mean duration of diabetes was 13.33 ± 4.36 years, and the baseline HbA1c level was 7.36% ± 1.73%. At 3 months, BCVA significantly improved from 0.65 ± 0.45 to 0.33 ± 0.27 logMAR (P < 0.001). CMT significantly decreased from 392.02 ± 139.90 μm at baseline to 322.26 ± 85.60 μm at 3 months (P = 0.002 vs baseline; overall P = 0.006). SFCT significantly decreased from 260.51 ± 106.16 μm at baseline to 243.80 ± 91.15 μm at 3 months (P = 0.020 vs baseline; overall P = 0.037). In exploratory OCTA analyses, foveal SCP and DCP vessel density showed numerical increases at 3 months (SCP: 26.88 ± 6.71% to 29.94 ± 7.32%; DCP: 30.02 ± 6.46% to 33.54 ± 6.74%), with uncorrected main-effect P values of 0.041 and 0.043, respectively. However, neither remained statistically significant after FDR correction (adjusted P = 0.224 and 0.256, respectively). No significant changes were observed in parafoveal SCP or DCP vessel density, FAZ area, or FD-300 (all FDR-adjusted P > 0.05). No serious adverse events occurred.

CONCLUSION: Anti-VEGF therapy significantly improved BCVA and reduced CMT and SFCT over 3 months. Foveal SCP and DCP vessel density increased numerically, but these exploratory OCTA changes did not survive FDR correction and may reflect edema-resolution-related segmentation effects; they are hypothesis-generating only. Longer prospective studies with standardized OCTA metrics are needed.

articles.title: Real-world outcomes after ensifentrine initiation in patients receiving single-inhaler triple therapy for COPD: a propensity-matched multicenter study.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Ensifentrine improves lung function, dyspnea, and exacerbation outcomes in phase III COPD studies, but patients receiving background LAMA/LABA or LABA/LAMA/ICS therapy were excluded. Comparative effectiveness after addition to established single-inhaler triple therapy is uncertain.

RESEARCH QUESTION: Among adults with COPD already receiving F/UMEC/VI or BGF, is ensifentrine initiation associated with lower 180-day exacerbation risk and improved clinical outcomes compared with continuation of the same triple inhaler?

STUDY DESIGN AND METHODS: We conducted parallel retrospective propensity-matched cohort studies using the TriNetX US Collaborative Network. Adults aged ≥40 years with established COPD receiving F/UMEC/VI or BGF were classified as ensifentrine initiators or same-inhaler comparators. Baseline covariates were measured during days -365 to -1 and matched 1:1 across 45 prespecified characteristics. The primary outcome was coded COPD exacerbation (ICD-10-CM J44.1) during days 1-180. Sensitivity analyses evaluated days 31-180 and a January 2025-March 2026 calendar-restricted cohort with de novo matching.

RESULTS: For F/UMEC/VI, 313 ensifentrine initiators and 4015 comparators entered matching, yielding 304 patients per cohort. Exacerbations occurred in 39.8% versus 33.6% (RR, 1.186; 95% CI, 0.961-1.464). For BGF, 182 initiators and 851 comparators yielded 172 patients per cohort; exacerbations occurred in 40.1% versus 39.0% (RR, 1.030; 95% CI, 0.793-1.338). Hospitalization, ED utilization, and systemic glucocorticoid exposure were not significantly different in either primary analysis. Exacerbation estimates remained close to the null in lagged and calendar-restricted analyses.

CONCLUSIONS: Among adults already receiving F/UMEC/VI or BGF, ensifentrine initiation was not associated with lower 180-day coded exacerbation risk or a consistent improvement in major healthcare-utilization outcomes. The concordant primary and sensitivity analyses provide early comparative-effectiveness evidence in a triple-therapy population underrepresented in pivotal ensifentrine trials.

articles.title: Demoralization syndrome in hemodialysis patients: Development and validation of an interpretable machine learning prediction model.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Demoralization syndrome (DS)-an existential distress state marked by hopelessness, helplessness, and loss of meaning-is a prevalent yet underrecognized affective comorbidity among maintenance hemodialysis (MHD) patients. Unlike depression, it stems from impaired coping capacity and carries distinct suicidal ideation risk, yet no practical prediction tool exists for early identification in routine care.

OBJECTIVE: To develop and externally validate a parsimonious, interpretable machine learning model for predicting early DS risk in MHD patients without baseline demoralization.

METHODS: This prospective multicenter cohort enrolled 592 participants. Incident DS symptoms were evaluated at a 5-month follow-up using the Demoralization Scale-II (cutoff ≥20). Twelve core predictors were screened from 87 clinical, laboratory and psychological indicators via a funnel-like feature selection workflow. A Stacking ensemble model with Bayesian-optimized base learners was built, interpreted using SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP), and assessed through sensitivity and ablation analyses to evaluate predictor stability and variable incremental value.

RESULTS: In external validation (N = 245), the 12-variable Stacking-Ridge model achieved an AUC of 0.922 (95% CI: 0.883-0.955), with accuracy 0.886, recall 0.652, precision 0.714, and F1-score 0.682-comparable to the 28-variable model while lowering clinical data-collection burden. SHAP analysis identified urinary microalbumin (U-MALB), PHQ-9 score, and HALP score as top contributors. Decision curve analysis indicated favorable clinical net benefit across broad threshold.

CONCLUSIONS: The model provides an accurate, interpretable tool for DS prediction in MHD patients. By integrating predictive analytics with clinical feasibility, it supports early identification of affective distress in nephrology practice and lays the groundwork for targeted psychosocial intervention.

articles.title: Right-to-left shunt burden and altered white matter functional networks in stroke-free patients with patent foramen ovale.
articles.abstract: Resting-state functional MRI (rsfMRI) is a useful technique for investigating the functional organization of human brain networks. Nevertheless, most rsfMRI studies in patent foramen ovale (PFO) have focused on gray-matter connectivity or structural imaging, whereas white-matter functional networks remain poorly characterized. PFO has been hypothesized to expose the brain to recurrent right-to-left shunt (RLS)-related microembolic, vasoactive and hemodynamic stressors, but whether these stressors are associated with altered white-matter functional organization in patients without overt stroke is unclear. The current study used rsfMRI to evaluate white-matter functional networks in stroke-free PFO patients and healthy controls. In the PFO group, RLS severity and anatomical features were characterized using contrast-enhanced transcranial Doppler and transesophageal echocardiography. Nine large-scale white-matter networks were identified by K-means clustering of voxel-wise white-matter functional connectivity. Evaluation of spontaneous oscillations and inter-network functional connectivity showed that PFO patients had widespread reductions in fast Fourier transform-derived band-averaged amplitude, mainly involving motor, occipital, cerebellar, deep and cingulum networks, and consistently reduced inferior frontal-to-fronto-temporal connectivity across frequency bands. Higher RLS grade was associated with lower white-matter amplitude in several networks, whereas PFO anatomical measurements showed no independent associations after multiple-comparison correction. Exploratory mediation analyses showed no significant indirect pathways after FDR correction. In this cross-sectional study, these findings suggest that RLS burden may be relevant to subclinical white-matter functional vulnerability in stroke-free PFO.

articles.title: Elevated serum levels of interferon-stimulated gene 15 are associated with the prevalence of hypertriglyceridemia.
