Respondents identified key lessons to guide future pandemic response. Two investigators conducted qualitative content analysis using an inductive-deductive approach to identify themes and subthemes. Themes were mapped to the Resilience Engineering framework and CDC Public Health Emergency Preparedness and Response Capabilities to assess alignment with preparedness domains.

RESULTS: Among 514 responses, eight themes emerged: Transparent and Multi-Directional Communication (n=152); Implementation of Federal Guidelines (n=137); Collaborative & Inclusive Teamwork (n=128); Agile Hospital Policies & Procedures (n=125); Sustainable & Flexible Workforce Capacity (n=123); Comprehensive Preparedness & Response Infrastructure (n=113); Professional Mindset & Coping Strategies (n=100); and Reliable and Resilient Resources (n=99).

CONCLUSION: IPs identified a broad and sometimes divergent range of lessons, reflecting the complexity of pandemic response. The findings suggest that preparedness requires flexible strategies addressing organizational infrastructure, workforce needs, and changing circumstances rather than a single, uniform approach.

articles.title: Predictive Factors for Outcomes After Maxillofacial Reconstruction With Fibula Osteocutaneous Flaps: An 11-Year Institutional Experience.
articles.journal: Journal of stomatology, oral and maxillofacial surgery
articles.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Fibula osteocutaneous flaps are a primary option for maxillomandibular reconstruction. This study aimed to evaluate the outcomes of delayed maxillofacial reconstruction using fibula osteocutaneous flaps and to identify clinical and reconstructive factors associated with flap survival and postoperative complications.

MATERIALS AND METHODS: This retrospective cohort study included 135 patients who underwent delayed maxillofacial reconstruction with fibula osteocutaneous flaps. Reconstructive history was categorized as first-time delayed or salvage delayed reconstruction. The primary outcome was complete flap survival; the secondary outcomes were urgent vascular re-exploration, postoperative infection, and wound dehiscence. Because only 24 complete flap failures occurred and complete separation was present for radiotherapy, an exploratory parsimonious Firth penalized logistic regression model including reconstructive history and previous radiotherapy was used for the primary outcome. Firth penalized regression was also used for exploratory analyses of the secondary outcomes.

RESULTS: Complete flap survival was observed in 111 of 135 subjects (82.2%). All 24 flap failures occurred among 36 subjects with previous radiotherapy, whereas no flap failures occurred among 99 subjects without previous radiotherapy. In the exploratory adjusted primary model, first-time delayed reconstruction was associated with higher odds of flap survival compared with salvage delayed reconstruction (OR = 11.93; 95% profile-likelihood CI, 2.62-75.53; P < 0.001), whereas previous radiotherapy was associated with markedly lower odds of flap survival (OR = 0.0039; 95% profile-likelihood CI, 0.00003-0.0336; P < 0.001). In exploratory secondary-outcome models, previous radiotherapy was associated with increased odds of postoperative infection, and two fibular osteotomies were associated with increased odds of wound dehiscence.Urgent vascular re-exploration was performed in 14 subjects (10.4%), with successful flap salvage in 2 of 14 cases (14.3%) CONCLUSION: First-time delayed reconstruction was associated with higher flap survival, whereas previous radiotherapy was strongly associated with reduced flap survival. However, the complete separation observed for radiotherapy, limited number of flap failures, and wide confidence intervals indicate substantial statistical uncertainty; therefore, the magnitude of these associations should be interpreted with caution. Findings for less frequent postoperative complications should also be considered exploratory and require confirmation in larger multicenter cohorts.

articles.title: Association between youth sexuality and gender identity and outcomes after hospitalization for suicide attempt.
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVES: To determine the prevalence of sexual minority (SM) and gender minority (GM) identities among youth hospitalized for suicide attempt (SA) relative to the state youth population (27.8% sexual and gender minority [SGM] in 2021), and to characterize differences in SA outcomes among SGM vs non-SGM youth.

STUDY DESIGN: We conducted a retrospective cohort study of youth 9-24 years medically hospitalized for SA between 2010-2022 at 2 tertiary pediatric centers. Encounters were manually reviewed to extract outcomes and SGM identities. We performed Poisson regression adjusted for age, race and ethnicity, and area deprivation index to evaluate associations between SGM identity with intensive care unit (ICU) admission, in-hospital mortality, and SA readmission.

RESULTS: Of 1,537 included youth, 21.2% (n=326) identified as SM and 11.7% (n=180) as GM. SGM identity rose from 5.0% in 2010 to 47.1% in 2022. Readmission for subsequent SA was higher among both SM (15.6% vs 7.9%; aRR 1.99 [1.30-3.06]) and GM youth (20.0% vs 5.3%; aRR 2.71 [1.76-4.17]). SGM identities were not associated with a difference in ICU admission for SA and were associated with lower in-hospital mortality. However, GM identity was associated with higher risk of mortality following intentional ingestion relative to non-GM youth (1.2% vs 0.4%; RR 3.06 [1.99-4.70]).

CONCLUSIONS: A higher proportion of youth hospitalized for SA identified as SGM compared with the general youth population, and this proportion rose between 2010-2022. SGM youth are particularly vulnerable to suicide by ingestion and to readmission for SA, warranting targeted prevention efforts.

articles.title: LARGE DIAPHRAGMATIC HERNIA: PARTICULAR RELEVANCE IN GASTROENTEROLOGY.
In vitro anthelmintic activity and safety profile of leaf and root extracts of Vernonia amygdalina against adult Onchocercaochengi.
articles.abstract:
ETHNOPHARMACOLOGICAL RELEVANCE: Vernonia amygdalina is widely used in Cameroon folk medicine for intestinal worms, schistosomiasis and filarial-related conditions. Ethnobotanical surveys in Adamawa, including Ngaoundere, report its antifilarial use with high frequency indices among traditional healers.

AIM OF THE STUDY: To evaluate the in vitro anthelmintic activity and safety profile of leaf and root extracts of V. amygdalina against adult male Onchocerca ochengi.

MATERIAL AND METHODS: Aqueous and ethanolic extracts were prepared by maceration. In vitro anthelmintic activity was tested against Onchocerca ochengi males at different concentrations (1 worm/well and 6 worm/concentration). Acute toxicity was evaluated in mice at 2000 mg/kg (OECD 423, 14 days). For sub-acute toxicity, 40 mice (5 males and 5 females/group, n ⹀ 10) received 0, 250, 500 and 1000 mg/kg b. w. of root aqueous extract orally (OECD 407). Organ weights, hematology, AST/ALT, lipid profile, creatinine and total protein were evaluated (ANOVA + Dunnett).

RESULTS: Phytochemical screening revealed saponins, flavonoids, tannins, and alkaloids. All extracts showed concentration-and time-dependent activity. Aqueous root extract was the most potent with LC50 40.24 ± 1.15 μg/mL at 48 h and 100% mortality at 100 μg/mL (ivermectin LC50 of 17.78 ± 2.01 μg/mL). LD50 > 2000 mg/kg. All hematological parameters showed significant variations (p ⹀ 0.019 to < 0.0001) except MCV (p ⹀ 0.064) and MPV (p ⹀ 0.34). Liver (p ⹀ 0.321) and heart weights (p ⹀ 0.052) were unchanged. Despite increased kidney (p ⹀ 0.009) and spleen (p < 0.0001) weights (marked splenomegaly), histology remained normal. Total cholesterol (p < 0.0001), triglycerides (p < 0.0001), HDL (p ⹀ 0.017), LDL (p ⹀ 0.0002) and total protein (p < 0.0001) were decreased in all treated groups, indicating hypolipidemic activity. Creatinine remained unchanged (p ⹀ 0.627). No AST/ALT co-elevation.

CONCLUSIONS: Root aqueous extract showed potent anthelmintic activity supporting traditional use with hypolipidemic effect. No hepato, cardio or nephrotoxicity was observed. The NOAEL was considered to be 500 mg/kg b. w., with mild and reversible high-dose splenomegaly and hypoproteinemia without histological lesions at 1000 mg/kg, indicating a wide safety margin.

articles.title: Huanglian Jiedu Decoction: An Ethnopharmacological Perspective on Molecular Mechanisms and Clinical Applications in Inflammatory Diseases.
articles.abstract:
ETHNOPHARMACOLOGICAL RELEVANCE: Huanglian Jiedu Decoction (HLJDD) is a classic traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) renowned for its heat-clearing and detoxifying effects. For centuries, this formula has been widely used under the guidance of TCM theory to treat various inflammatory disorders characterized as "heat toxin" or "excess fire in the three burners." TCM considers "heat toxin" to be a common pathological mechanism underlying many inflammatory diseases, with clinical manifestations functionally analogous and corresponding to the infectious and non-infectious inflammation defined by modern Western medicine, rather than being strictly equivalent. Therefore, the traditional effects of HLJDD in clearing heat, purging fire, detoxifying, and cooling the blood provide a unique TCM theoretical foundation and alternative intervention strategy for the treatment of modern inflammatory diseases.

AIM OF THE REVIEW: This review aims to systematically summarize the components, traditional efficacy, main active ingredients of HLJDD in inflammatory diseases, as well as its modern pharmacological effects and molecular mechanisms. By integrating traditional experience with modern scientific evidence, we strive to provide a solid scientific basis and translational strategies for the ethnomedicinal applications of this herbal medicine and its modern use in the prevention and treatment of inflammatory diseases.

MATERIALS AND METHODS: A narrative literature search was performed in PubMed and CNKI from database inception to December 31, 2025, using "Huanglian Jiedu Decoction", "HLJDD", "anti-inflammatory", "inflammation" and their synonyms. Original research articles on the phytochemistry, network pharmacology, mechanisms, or clinical applications of HLJDD or its constituent herbs in inflammatory diseases were included; reviews, case reports, non-English/Chinese publications, and duplicates were excluded. Two reviewers independently screened titles/abstracts and full texts, with disagreements resolved by consensus. A three-tier evidence classification (whole formula / single herb / pure compound) was applied to mechanistic studies, and findings were synthesized narratively given substantial heterogeneity. Only PubMed and CNKI were searched, which may limit comprehensiveness.

RESULTS: The anti-inflammatory activity of HLJDD is mainly attributed to its various alkaloids and flavonoid compounds. These components exert synergistic effects through multi-target and multi-pathway mechanisms, significantly inhibiting the release of pro-inflammatory cytokines (such as TNF-α, IL-1β, and IL-6) and effectively regulating the activation of key inflammatory signaling pathways (such as NF-κB, MAPK, JAK-STAT, and the NLRP3 inflammasome). Both in vivo and in vitro experiments have confirmed that HLJDD exhibits significant anti-inflammatory and tissue-protective effects in various inflammatory disease models, including sepsis, acute lung injury, colitis, and skin inflammation. Its mechanism of action is characterized by a typical "multi-component, multi-target, multi-pathway" network regulation feature.

CONCLUSIONS: What is established is that HLJDD and its constituent compounds modulate the NF-κB, MAPK, JAK-STAT, and NLRP3 pathways in cellular and animal systems, although most mechanistic evidence derives from isolated compounds rather than the whole formula. What is suggestive is that HLJDD-containing interventions may confer clinical benefit in selected inflammatory conditions; however, current clinical evidence remains of very low certainty, as most reported studies are small-sample, non-blinded trials using modified formulas or combination therapies rather than the classic HLJDD formula alone. What remains hypothetical is whether these preclinical mechanisms translate into clinically meaningful efficacy in humans. Future research should therefore prioritize: in-depth mechanistic studies that rigorously distinguish whole-formula from compound-level evidence; standardized extraction and quality-control systems; delivery systems to improve bioavailability; and large-scale, rigorously designed randomized controlled trials-so that HLJDD may progressively advance from empirical use toward a safe and effective evidence-based anti-inflammatory therapy..

articles.title: Monitoring the Metabolic Microenvironment of Insulin-Secreting and Insulin-Responsive Cells: Sensing Technologies, Byproduct Dynamics, and Culture-Health Prediction.
articles.abstract: Insulin-secreting and insulin-responsive cells are central in vitro models for metabolic disease. Yet, the phenotypes they report, glucose-stimulated insulin secretion, insulin sensitivity, and downstream signalling, are sensitive to the chemical state of the surrounding culture medium. Cellular metabolism continuously alters oxygen tension, pH, substrate availability, and the accumulation of byproducts such as lactate, ammonia, and reactive species, and endpoint assays cannot resolve these dynamics. This narrative review maps the real-time sensing of the metabolic microenvironment for insulin-secreting and insulin-responsive cell models, with the aim of distinguishing genuine metabolic dysfunction from artefacts of the culture system. The cell-type scope, basal media composition, and the distinction between two-dimensional and three-dimensional culture are defined as determinants of byproduct accumulation and sensor interpretation. The principal metabolic byproducts and their concentration windows are described, followed by the four recognition paradigms that dominate real-time measurement: electrochemical enzymatic biosensors, optical and luminescence-based sensors, and vibrational spectroscopy with chemometric modelling, with electrochemical aptamer-based sensing extending coverage to enzyme-inaccessible analytes. Commercial monitoring systems and multi-analyte signal-integration strategies are then surveyed. Throughout the culture matrix, in particular serum-borne growth factors and diffusion-limited gradients, emerge as the dominant constraint. No current approach provides continuous, in situ, multi-analyte inference of culture health for insulin-secreting and insulin-responsive models, which remains an open challenge.

articles.title: Validation of Primary and Hospital Care Resource Use and Cost Estimates in OMOP-mapped vs Source Healthcare Administrative Datasets.
articles.journal: Value in health : the journal of the International Society for Pharmacoeconomics and Outcomes Research
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVES: To assess whether estimates of primary and hospital care resource use and costs from Observational Medical Outcomes Partnership (OMOP) Common Data Model (CDM) mapped data are consistent with source healthcare administrative datasets and to discuss implications for OMOP-based health economic analyses.

METHODS: We conducted a retrospective cohort study (2010-2018) of women aged >50 years with a fragility fracture. Analyses were performed in parallel using source Clinical Practice Research Datalink Aurum linked to Hospital Episode Statistics data and two OMOP-based strategies: OMOP-standard (standardised concepts only) and OMOP-source (also including source variables). Primary and hospital care utilisation and costs were estimated over two years. Mean differences were summarised with bootstrapped 95% confidence intervals.

RESULTS: Cohorts were comparable (23,106 source; 22,900 OMOP), with similar characteristics and follow-up. Resource utilisation was consistent across databases (<1% difference). Total cost differences were 2.2% (OMOP-standard) and 1.7% (OMOP-source, not statistically significant). Primary care, inpatient and outpatient cost differences were ≤3% among costed records. Emergency care costs were ∼21% lower in both OMOP strategies, reflecting a different costing method rather than mapping fidelity (0.1% when the same method was applied to source data). Discrepancies were mainly due to costing assumptions, and less so to incomplete vocabularies and structural constraints.

CONCLUSIONS: OMOP-mapped data produced resource use estimates highly consistent and aggregate cost estimates concordant with source data. Remaining cost discrepancies were concentrated in specific settings and reduced when source variables were used. Refining mapping and costing approaches will improve accuracy and support federated economic research using OMOP-CDM.

articles.title: Automated insulin delivery and lower burden of hypoglycemia in type 1 diabetes: a prospective analysis of the BETTER registry.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Automated insulin delivery (AID) systems are expected to reduce the burden of hypoglycemia, including fear of hypoglycemia (FOH), but evidence on how they might shape management behaviors in type 1 diabetes (T1D) is not well defined. This study evaluates changes in Hypoglycemia Fear Survey-II (HFS-II) scores and FOH related worries and behaviors after AID initiation compared with non-AID use.

METHODS: In this prospective analysis, participants from the BETTER registry were categorized into three groups: multiple daily injections (MDI) users at baseline and follow-up, continuous subcutaneous insulin infusion (CSII) users at baseline and follow-up, and AID group (MDI or CSII at baseline, started AID during follow-up). Pairwise comparisons were conducted using propensity score-weighted generalized linear regression models.

RESULTS: Among 466 participants, 66% were women, mean age and diabetes duration were 46.6 ± 14.8 and 26.0 ± 15.8 years, respectively. HFS-II total and subscale scores were not statistically different at baseline between the three groups (all P> 0.05). At follow-up, AID initiation was associated with lower HFS-II total (-4.05 [-7.04, -1.06], worry (-2.27 [-4.34, -0.20]), and behavior scores (-1.78 [-3.22, -0.33]) compared to baseline. In contrast, MDI users reported less favorable changes in HFS-II total (3.86 [0.21, 7.52]) and behavior scores (2.06 [0.33, 3.80]) compared to AID. Overall, the results remained consistent after adjustment for baseline HFS-II score and change in hypoglycemia frequency. AID users were more likely to meet target hemoglobin A1c ≤7% at follow-up.

CONCLUSION: Findings suggest AID use may influence FOH-related behaviors without compromising overall glycemic outcomes.

articles.title: Acupuncture alleviates post-stroke depression by inhibiting proline-driven ferroptosis in hippocampal neurons.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Post-stroke depression (PSD) represents a prevalent stroke complication with scarce therapeutic interventions. Acupuncture has shown clinical efficacy in PSD, but the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. This study investigates whether acupuncture alleviates PSD by regulating proline metabolism-mediated ferroptosis.

METHODS: We generated a rat PSD model via common carotid artery ligation coupled with chronic unpredictable mild stress (CUMS). Acupuncture at GV20, GV26, GV24, and GV14 was administered for four weeks. Behavioral tests, TTC and Nissl staining, ELISA, qPCR, western blot, amino acid metabolomics, and hippocampal neuron cultures with proline intervention were performed.

RESULTS: Acupuncture robustly rescued depression-like phenotypes and mitigated hippocampal neuronal injury in PSD rats. Acupuncture decreased serum levels of iron ions, malondialdehyde (MDA) and reactive oxygen species (ROS), increased glutathione (GSH), and reversed the aberrant expression of ferroptosis-related proteins (GPX4, SLC7A11, ACSL4, TFR1) in the hippocampus. Amino acid metabolomics revealed elevated serum proline in PSD rats, which was normalized by acupuncture. Exogenous proline administration aggravated depressive behaviors and hippocampal ferroptosis. In cultured hippocampal neurons, high-dose proline directly induced ferroptosis and reduced cell viability.

CONCLUSION: Acupuncture ameliorates PSD by inhibiting hippocampal neuronal ferroptosis through regulation of proline metabolism, revealing a novel mechanism for acupuncture treatment.

articles.title: Integrating Mouse Transcriptomics and Human Multi-Cohort Data Reveals an Inflammatory Gene Signature Mediating Jaceosidin's Therapeutic Effect in Ulcerative Colitis.
articles.abstract: Jaceosidin exerts protective effects against ulcerative colitis (UC), but its molecular mechanisms remain poorly understood. This study integrates transcriptomics, machine learning, and co-expression network analysis to elucidate Jaceosidin's targets in UC. A dextran sulfate sodium (DSS)-induced mouse colitis model with transcriptome sequencing was established. Core genes were identified by WGCNA and cross-dataset analysis of public UC datasets. Three machine learning algorithms constructed a risk prediction model. GO/KEGG, GSEA, immune infiltration, and single-cell analyses were performed. In vivo validation included enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) for cytokines (TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-6, IL-10) and Western blot for core proteins and NF-κB. Two-sample Mendelian randomization (MR) explored causality. Forty-one core genes were narrowed to four (CXCL3, LCN2, LMCD1, S100A9) by machine learning. The model achieved AUC > 0.9. GSEA linked the four genes to NF-κB signaling and immune infiltration. ELISA confirmed Jaceosidin reduced TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-6 and elevated IL-10. Western blot confirmed NF-κB suppression. MR for LCN2 showed no causal effect on UC risk (p = 0.682), supporting these genes as downstream effectors. Jaceosidin alleviated colitis and downregulated the four genes. Jaceosidin ameliorates UC by modulating a four-gene module and inhibiting NF-κB-mediated inflammation. The model provides new targets for UC treatment monitoring.

articles.title: Carboxymethyl cellulose/polyvinyl alcohol films based on ethanol-based carbon dots with pH-responsive indication and photothermal-chemical synergistic antimicrobial activity for blueberry preservation.
articles.abstract: To mitigate the postharvest challenges of blueberries, such as intense respiration and microbial spoilage, this study developed a multifunctional biodegradable film capable of real-time freshness monitoring and synergistic antimicrobial activity. Ethanol-based carbon dots (EN-CDs) were synthesized via a hydrothermal method using citric acid (CA) and urea, followed by ethanol precipitation. The EN-CDs exhibited an average particle size of 1.98 nm and a lattice spacing of 0.21 nm. These EN-CDs were incorporated into a polyvinyl alcohol/carboxymethyl cellulose (PVA/CMC) matrix alongside carvacrol (CAR) and cyclodextrins (β-CD or γ-CD) to construct a multifunctional packaging system. The resulting composite film displayed sensitive pH-responsivity, exhibiting a distinct transition at pH 5.6 to monitor CO2-induced acidity changes within the packaging. After 808 nm near-infrared (NIR) irradiation, the PVA/CMC/0.3EN-CDs/CAR/γ film demonstrated excellent photothermal performance. The instantaneous photothermal effect of EN-CDs and the sustained release of CAR established a synergistic antimicrobial effect, which achieved inhibition rates of 97.03% and 95.79% against Escherichia coli (E. coli) and Staphylococcus aureus (S. aureus), respectively. Blueberry preservation experiments demonstrated that the composite film significantly delayed fruit softening and inhibited microbial infection, thereby extending the shelf life to 16 days. This study provides a theoretical basis and practical support for the advancement of smart and antimicrobial packaging technologies in postharvest science.

articles.title: Soft-sprayed sodium alginate/cellulose nanofibril hydrogel membrane for temporally differentiated curcumin/ibuprofen release and enhanced infected wound healing.
articles.abstract: Infected wound healing requires both effective early infection control and sustained regulation of the inflammatory microenvironment, while conventional prefabricated dressings often provide limited adaptability to irregular wound surfaces. Here, we developed a soft-sprayed sodium alginate/cellulose nanofibril hydrogel membrane (CUR@IC/SA) integrating conformal in-situ formation with temporally differentiated curcumin (CUR) and ibuprofen (IBU) release. CUR was encapsulated in Pluronic F127 nanomicelles and physically confined within the hydrogel network, enabling rapid release for early antibacterial and antioxidant intervention. In contrast, IBU was covalently grafted onto cellulose nanofibrils through hydrolyzable ester linkages, resulting in prolonged hydrolysis-mediated release. The precursor was deposited by low-impetus ultrasonic spraying and rapidly crosslinked by Cu2+ to form a self-supporting hydrogel membrane, which could also be formed directly on irregular wound surfaces. The optimized CUR@IC/SA membrane exhibited favorable porous structure, mechanical flexibility, fluid-management capability, short-term in vitro cytocompatibility, and wet-tissue interfacial stability. In vitro, CUR@IC/SA showed strong antibacterial activity against Staphylococcus aureus and Escherichia coli, with inhibition rates of approximately 99.8%, together with pronounced radical-scavenging activity. In an S. aureus-infected mouse wound model, CUR@IC/SA significantly reduced the early bacterial burden and achieved approximately 97% wound closure by day 13. Histological and immunohistochemical analyses further indicated improved tissue repair and reduced local inflammatory responses. Transcriptomic analysis revealed broad treatment-associated changes in inflammation- and repair-related transcriptional programs, including NF-κB-associated signaling. Overall, this work demonstrates a soft-spray hydrogel platform that couples conformal wound coverage with temporally differentiated therapeutic release for infected wound management.

articles.title: A Multi-Epitope Peptide Vaccine Confers Protection against Staphylococcus aureus in a Murine Peritonitis Model.
articles.abstract: The development of an effective vaccine against Staphylococcus aureus (S. aureus) remains a critical unmet medical need, particularly given the pathogen's ability to cause life-threatening invasive diseases. The aim of this research is the demonstration of the protective effect of the novel multi-epitope peptide vaccine comprising leukotoxin D (LukD), leukocidin S (LukS), and the previously published Phosphatidylinositol phosphodiesterase (PIc) peptide in a Murine peritonitis model of lethal S. aureus sepsis. Results shown robust humoral immunity correlated with improved survival in all the mice vaccinated groups especially the peptide mixture group. The histopathology results of kidney tissues revealed almost normal histological profile of mice vaccinated with PIc peptides and the peptide mixture group 10 days post challenge with S. aureus pathogenic strain. Histopathology examination of hepatic tissues from mice groups vaccinated with PIc peptides, LukS peptides and the peptide mixture group revealed normal histological profile 10 days post challenge with S. aureus pathogenic strain. This finding aligns with recent advances in peptide-based vaccine that emphasize targeting key virulence factors while leveraging host immune memory for durable protection.

articles.title: Pharmacist-led management of atopic dermatitis: Evaluation of a telephonic patient management program in a specialty pharmacy.
articles.journal: Journal of the American Pharmacists Association : JAPhA
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Atopic dermatitis (AD) is a chronic condition that can significantly affect patients' quality of life. Because of its complex pathophysiology, multidisciplinary care models have been implemented to guide patients in AD disease state management (DSM). Patients receiving therapy through specialty pharmacies often have more severe disease requiring more complex drug therapies, placing pharmacists strategically to deliver DSM services for AD.

OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the effect of a pharmacist-led patient management program (PMP) on disease severity among patients with AD.

METHODS: This retrospective cohort study included adult patients who received treatment for AD at a specialty pharmacy for at least six months. Patients were enrolled in a pharmacist-led PMP, which included monthly assessments using the Patient-Oriented Eczema Measure (POEM) to evaluate AD severity. Changes in POEM scores were analyzed using univariate methods, with a reduction of at least 3.4 points considered the minimal clinically important difference (MCID). Subgroup analyses based on age, sex, diabetes mellitus (DM), and select drug therapies were performed to assess potential associations between these variables and changes in POEM scores. Time-series analyses were conducted to evaluate POEM score change with an MCID equivalent of 17.3%.

RESULTS: Among 263 patient records reviewed, the mean (SD) POEM score at baseline was 3.67 (5.36), compared to 2.68 (4.20) at month six in the program (mean difference -0.98, p = 0.008). In a subgroup analysis that excluded patients with a baseline POEM score of 0, 146/152 (96.1%) achieved a POEM score reduction of at least 17.3% within a median of 84.5 days. No associations were identified between age, sex, diabetes mellitus (DM), or drug therapy and magnitude or timing of POEM score change.

CONCLUSION: Few studies have shown the potential impact of pharmacist interventions on AD DSM. This study suggests that a specialty pharmacist-led PMP may help patients reduce AD severity.

articles.title: Real-life de-escalation practices in the era of high antimicrobial resistance rates: Insights from a prospective observational cohort study.
articles.journal: International journal of infectious diseases : IJID : official publication of the International Society for Infectious Diseases
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVES: Antibiotic de-escalation is a key component of antimicrobial stewardship (AMS); however, its real-life application, associations with clinical outcomes and resistance remain incompletely defined, particularly in high-resistance settings.

METHODS: In this single-centre prospective observational cohort study conducted at Ankara University Hospitals, a tertiary-care centre, between January and July 2024, hospitalized adults receiving empirical intravenous antibiotics for suspected infection were evaluated. Of 1,096 patients screened, 468 were included, each contributing a single empirical antibiotic course. Cumulative Antibiotic Spectrum Index (ASI) scores were used to classify patients into de-escalation (DE), no-change (NC), and escalation (E) groups. Clinical outcomes, adverse events, acute kidney injury (AKI), 90-day mortality, and new resistance development were assessed, using time-dependent Cox and Fine-Gray regression.

RESULTS: De-escalation was implemented in 27.8% of patients. Clinical response was higher in the DE group than in the NC and E groups (99.2% vs 92.9% vs 84.9%; p<0.001). Adverse events (6.2% vs 11.8% vs 30.2%; p<0.001) and AKI (5.4% vs 10.4% vs 25.4%; p<0.001) were least frequent in the DE group. In multivariable analysis, the risk of adverse events was higher in the NC (HR 2.51, 95% CI 1.11-5.67) and E (HR 4.28, 95% CI 1.95-9.36) groups compared with de-escalation. 90-day mortality followed a similar pattern, being higher in the NC (HR 4.10, 95% CI 1.31-12.84) and E (HR 6.70, 95% CI 2.30-19.50) groups. New resistance within 90 days did not differ significantly (11.3% vs 14.4% vs 11.9%; p=0.733). Among the 153 patients for whom de-escalation was microbiologically appropriate, it was withheld in 46.4%.

CONCLUSIONS: In this high-resistance setting, DE was applied to only 27.8% of patients and was withheld in 46.4% of those for whom it was microbiologically appropriate. The main barriers were clinical instability, inadequate source control and an additional infection site. Rather than demonstrating a treatment effect, these observational data reveal a substantial gap between DE eligibility and practice and identify modifiable barriers that antimicrobial stewardship programmes could address.

articles.title: Beyond the Guidelines: Successful CRT-D Rescue in Patients Unable to Tolerate Guideline-Directed Medical Therapy.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Current ACC/AHA/HFSA guidelines endorse cardiac resynchronization therapy with defibrillation (CRT-D) as a Class I recommendation for patients with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF), left bundle branch block (LBBB), and QRS ≥150 ms but only after at least three months of maximally tolerated guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT). A critical and under-addressed clinical scenario exists - patients with electromechanical dyssynchrony who cannot achieve GDMT optimization due to hypotension, renal dysfunction, or inotrope dependence. Current guidelines do not provide a recommendation pathway for this population, leaving clinicians without evidence-based guidance in a high-stakes decision context.

CASE PRESENTATIONS: We present two patients with advanced non-ischemic cardiomyopathy, LBBB with markedly prolonged QRS duration (166-168 ms), and LVEF <20%, both of whom were inotrope-dependent and unable to tolerate GDMT. Neither met traditional prerequisites for CRT-D implantation. Following multidisciplinary evaluation, both patients underwent successful CRT-D implantation, were weaned from intravenous inotropic support, improved from NYHA Class IV to Class II at one year, and had no heart failure hospitalizations during follow-up, with meaningful gains in LVEF in both cases.

CLINICAL IMPLICATIONS: CRT-D may serve as a salvage or enabling therapy in select patients with advanced HFrEF and electrical dyssynchrony who are unable to complete the recommended GDMT optimization period. Prospective studies are needed to refine selection criteria in this high-risk population.

articles.title: Venous thromboembolism in inflammatory bowel disease: a phase-specific framework for risk stratification and anticoagulant management.
articles.abstract: Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), encompassing ulcerative colitis and Crohn's disease, is a chronic inflammatory disorder associated with an increased risk of venous thromboembolism (VTE), particularly during active disease, hospitalization or after surgery. The risk of VTE is approximately two to three times higher in patients with IBD than in the general population. The underlying mechanisms are multifactorial and include systemic inflammation, platelet activation, endothelial dysfunction, and alterations in the intestinal microbiota. Diagnosis requires a high index of clinical suspicion. D-dimer may help exclude VTE in patients with low pretest probability but is frequently elevated during active inflammation and therefore lacks specificity. Pharmacological thromboprophylaxis, preferably with low-molecular-weight heparin, is recommended for hospitalized patients with IBD, whereas the choice and duration of therapeutic anticoagulation should be individualized according to thrombotic and bleeding risk. This review summarizes current evidence on the epidemiology, pathophysiology, diagnosis, prevention and management of VTE in IBD, with particular focus on recent population-based incidence data, phase-dependent thrombotic risk post-discharge prophylaxis and individualized anticoagulant selection.

articles.title: Convergent mechanisms between GLP-1 and adenosine in epilepsy: opportunities for therapeutic exploitation?
articles.abstract: Epilepsy is a serious neurological condition characterized by spontaneous recurrent seizures affecting approximately 83 million people worldwide. Type 2 diabetes (T2D) and obesity are highly prevalent in persons with epilepsy, significantly influencing long-term outcomes, quality of life, and mortality. Traditionally, glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) are used to treat T2D and obesity, and they have recently been highlighted as a therapeutic intervention for neurological disorders, including epilepsy. In epilepsy, adenosine signaling plays a crucial role, as it not only controls seizures but also affects epileptogenesis. As a metabolite and metabolic regulator adenosine is also implicated in the pathophysiology of T2D and obesity. The involvement of adenosine in both conditions raises the possibility of convergent mechanisms implicated in the antiepileptic effects of GLP-1 RAs. This review provides a comprehensive overview of the effects of GLP-1 RAs and adenosine in epilepsy and their convergent mechanisms, which could serve as a basis for synergistic therapeutic applications and insight into their underlying mechanisms. GLP-1 RAs affect several mechanisms shared with adenosine signaling. These include reduction of astrogliosis, neuroinflammation, and mTOR activity, and restoration of the excitation and inhibition balance by suppressing the glutamatergic pathway and upregulating the GABAergic pathway. In peripheral organs, direct convergent mechanisms between adenosine signaling and GLP-1 RAs include interactions between adenosine deaminase and dipeptidylpeptidase-4, lipid metabolism, and pancreatic β-cell homeostasis. These convergent mechanisms highlight the need to further investigate possible bidirectional relationships with the involvement of adenosine in both conditions.

articles.title: Construction of minigenomic replicon and infectious virus-like particle systems for Ebola virus with epitope-tagged L polymerase.
articles.abstract: Ebola virus (EBOV) L protein is the viral RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp) and a key antiviral target. Functional dissection of L during infection is hampered by scarce specific anti-L antibodies and mandatory BSL-4 containment for live EBOV. Here, we established two BSL-2 reverse genetic systems harboring tagged L protein to address these obstacles. First, we generated stable EBOV minigenomic replicon cells constitutively expressing NP, VP30, VP35 and TagL, supporting sustained viral minigenome replication. Second, we developed an infectious virus-like particle (iVLP) system in which an EBOV subgenome encoding GP, VP40 and VP24 replicates robustly in optimized TagL-expressing helper cells to generate fully infectious iVLPs, recapitulating the entire EBOV life cycle. Proteomic analysis of intact iVLPs and delipidated ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complexes uncovered a previously unrecognized association between EBOV RNP and cytoskeletal proteins. Pharmacological disruption of microtubules enhanced EBOV replication/transcription and virion production, providing new insights into virus-host interactions during EBOV infection. Collectively, these optimized TagL-integrated reverse genetics tools provide tractable BSL-2 tools to study EBOV L-RNP biology during the full viral life cycle.

articles.title: Regionalization of Pancreatectomy Within a Health System: Impact on Travel Burden and Surgical Outcomes.
articles.journal: Journal of gastrointestinal surgery : official journal of the Society for Surgery of the Alimentary Tract
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Centralizing pancreatic surgery at high-volume centers improves outcomes but may limit access. Regionalizing pancreatectomies within a large health system where the same surgical faculty operate across multiple sites could reconcile quality and access. This study evaluates the impact of a shared-faculty regionalization initiative on patient travel burden and surgical outcomes.

METHODS: A retrospective cohort study was performed on patients undergoing elective pancreatectomy between January 2021 and September 2025 at a main cancer center and two regional facilities within a single health system in the Phoenix metropolitan area. Travel distance and duration were calculated and outcome were compared between sites using univariate and multivariable analyses adjusting for procedure type, surgical approach, age, sex, and pathology.

RESULTS: A total of 364 patients underwent pancreatectomy (main: 246; regional: 118). The proportion of pancreatectomies at regional sites increased from 1.7% (2021) to 32.4% (2025). Mean travel distance and duration were higher at the main site compared to regional sites (98.1 vs. 69.2 miles and 100.6 vs. 74.9minutes, p<0.05). On multivariable analysis, there were no differences in 30-day readmission, length of stay, or mortality between sites. Organ-space surgical site infection (OR 1.9, p<0.05) and acute kidney injury (OR 2.7, p<0.05) were higher at the main site. Patients traveling 60-120minutes had increased 30-day readmission compared to all other travel-time groups (OR 2.2-3.9, p<0.05).

CONCLUSIONS: Regionalization of pancreatectomy using a shared-faculty model reduces patient travel burden while maintaining comparable surgical outcomes. Patients traveling 60-120minutes may benefit from targeted follow-up interventions.

articles.title: Tubular EZH2-HIF1α axis promotes mouse renal fibrosis after ischemia-reperfusion-induced acute kidney injury by accelerating cellular senescence.
articles.abstract: Maladaptive tubular repair and cellular senescence contribute to the transition from acute kidney injury (AKI) to chronic kidney disease (CKD), but the associated regulatory mechanisms remain incompletely understood. This study investigated the involvement of EZH2- and HIF-1α-associated signaling in tubular senescence and renal fibrosis. A murine unilateral ischemia-reperfusion injury model combined with contralateral nephrectomy was used to examine AKI-to-CKD progression, and DZNep was administered to evaluate its pharmacological effects. Hypoxia/reoxygenation- and TGF-β1-stimulated tubular epithelial cells were used for complementary in vitro analyses. EZH2 and HIF-1α remained elevated during post-ischemic kidney injury, whereas DZNep treatment improved renal function and attenuated tubular damage, fibrosis, and senescence-associated changes. In HK-2 cells, DZNep and 2-MeOE2 reduced injury-, fibrosis-, and senescence-related responses. To strengthen target-specific evidence, EZH2 knockdown attenuated H/R-induced HIF-1α expression, SASP production, and α-SMA and FN accumulation. Similarly, HIF1A knockdown reduced EZH2 expression and the induction of SASP and profibrotic proteins following H/R. These genetic findings support the involvement of both EZH2 and HIF-1α in the cellular response to ischemic stress, although they do not establish direct regulation or a feedback loop. Collectively, EZH2- and HIF-1α-associated signaling may contribute to maladaptive tubular senescence and fibrotic remodeling after AKI and warrants further mechanistic evaluation.

articles.title: Axon-guidance factors and their receptors could be potential targets to promote functional recovery via stimulating angiogenesis and blood-brain barrier repair after ischemic stroke.
articles.abstract: Angiogenesis and blood-brain barrier (BBB) repair play important roles in neural functional recovery after ischemic stroke. The formation of new blood vessels improves the local blood supply, enhancing the oxygen and nutrient supply of newly formed neurons. Despite advances in the mechanistic understanding of vascular growth and repair, there are no safe and effective angiogenic treatments that currently exist because of the immature vessel-induced BBB leakage. In addition to the most studied angiogenic growth factors, the process of vascular budding and migration requires the involvement of guiding factors, many of which were initially identified as regulators of axon growth. In this review, the inhibitory and promoting effects of axon-guiding factors on the vascular system are summarized, and their roles in angiogenesis, BBB repair and neural functional recovery after ischemic stroke are discussed.

articles.title: Associations of Gestational Diabetes Mellitus with PFAS Distribution and Partitioning across the Maternal-Placental-Fetal Continuum.
articles.abstract: Previous studies have indicated that maternal exposure to per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) is associated with gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM), although the causality of this association remains uncertain. Given the metabolic disturbances, altered serum protein binding, and placental dysfunction associated with GDM, we hypothesized that PFAS concentrations and their concentration ratios across the maternal-placental-fetal continuum might differ by GDM status. In this study, we simultaneously quantified PFAS concentrations in four matched biological matrices, including maternal serum, placenta, cord serum, and umbilical cord tissue, from 156 mother-infant pairs; 30 mothers were diagnosed with GDM. We evaluated the distribution and partitioning patterns of PFAS across the four matrices and assessed the potential modifying role of GDM. PFAS concentrations showed matrix-specific distribution patterns, with higher concentrations in maternal serum than cord serum and higher in placental than umbilical cord tissue. Perfluorohexane sulfonic acid (PFHxS) concentrations in umbilical cord tissue were higher in the GDM group, whereas no significant differences were observed for other PFAS or total PFAS across matrices. Compared with controls, the GDM group exhibited higher cord serum/placenta-to-maternal serum ratios for perfluorobutane sulfonic acid (PFBS) and higher umbilical cord-to-cord serum ratios for PFHxS and perfluorooctanoic acid. GDM showed nominal positive associations with the placenta-to-maternal serum ratio of PFBS and the umbilical cord tissue-to-cord serum ratios of perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA), perfluorooctane sulfonate (PFOS), and PFHxS, although none remained significant after correction for multiple comparisons. Interaction analyses further indicated that GDM modified the associations between maternal serum and placental PFAS concentrations for perfluoroheptane sulfonate (PFHpS), PFOA, and 6:2 chlorinated polyfluoroalkyl ether sulfonic acid (6:2 Cl-PFESA).

articles.title: Corticospinal tract remodeling after stroke: Experimental mechanisms and implications for functional recovery.
articles.abstract: Recovery of voluntary motor function after stroke is strongly constrained by the integrity of the corticospinal tract (CST), a principal descending pathway controlling skilled and fractionated movements. Although ischemic or hemorrhagic stroke frequently disrupts CST projections, surviving corticospinal neurons retain a significant capacity for structural and functional remodeling. Understanding how this residual capacity contributes to recovery is therefore central to neurorestorative research. This narrative review synthesizes experimental and clinical findings to define the structural, cellular, molecular, and activity-dependent mechanisms underlying CST remodeling after stroke. Clinical studies using diffusion tensor imaging and transcranial magnetic stimulation demonstrate that CST integrity is a major determinant of recovery potential, forming the basis of widely used prognostic models. Experimental work, particularly in rodent stroke models, indicates that post-stroke CST remodeling commonly involves short-range axonal sprouting of spared corticospinal neurons within spinal gray matter, rather than long-distance regeneration across damaged white matter pathways. These structural changes are regulated by a complex interplay of intrinsic neuronal growth programs, myelin-associated inhibitory signaling, extracellular matrix remodeling, glial responses, and activity-dependent circuit selection. Importantly, CST remodeling occurs within a broader network of cortical, brainstem, and spinal adaptations and may contribute to restitution, compensation, or both depending on lesion severity and residual structural capacity. We further examine emerging pharmacological, gene-based, cell-based, neuromodulatory, environmental, and rehabilitation strategies designed to enhance or guide CST plasticity. Finally, we discuss biological heterogeneity, spontaneous recovery, experimental model limitations, and the challenges of translating preclinical CST remodeling into clinically meaningful restoration of dexterous motor function. Together, these findings support a framework in which structural reserve, the post-injury biological environment, and patterned activity interact to determine the functional value of CST remodeling and inform biologically stratified therapeutic approaches.

articles.title: Rhinovirus Infection of Human Airway Epithelial Cells Stimulates Neutrophil Superoxide.
articles.journal: The Journal of allergy and clinical immunology
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Neutrophils migrate to the respiratory epithelium during rhinovirus (RV) infection, but whether RV directly activates neutrophils or whether activation arises from epithelial responses remains unclear.

OBJECTIVE: To determine whether RV directly activates human neutrophils or indirectly activates them through RV-infected airway epithelial cells.

METHODS: Human neutrophils were exposed to purified RV, and activation was assessed by myeloperoxidase activity, CD11b/CD66b expression, and reactive oxygen species (ROS) production. Neutrophils were co-cultured with RV-infected air-liquid interface (ALI) bronchial epithelium evaluated for effects on epithelial integrity. At 48-72 hours post-infection, we used live-cell imaging to measure ROS responses and neutrophil-tracking assays to measure migration velocity and ROS responses to basolateral supernatants, clarified apical washes, and apical debris from RV-infected epithelial cells. Plaque assays were used to assess for RV infectivity after incubation with apical neutrophils.

RESULTS: RV did not directly activate neutrophils. Adding neutrophils to the apical surface of airway epithelial cells increased neutrophil ROS production at 48-72 hrs post-infection but did not alter epithelial cytotoxicity. Conversely, basolateral supernatants from infected cells enhanced neutrophil migration but not ROS, consistent with cytokine-mediated priming. Clarified apical washes had no effect on migration or ROS. By contrast, apical debris from infected cultures triggered a robust ROS response. Basolateral fractions from medium control- or RV-infected cultures did not induce ROS. Infectivity is not impacted by apical neutrophil presence.

CONCLUSION: RV does not directly activate neutrophils. Instead, RV-infected epithelial cells release basolateral factors that enhance neutrophil migration, while apical debris from infected cells drives ROS activation. These findings indicate that epithelial injury, not RV itself, is the dominant trigger of neutrophil activation during infection.

articles.title: Clinical and proteomic features of children with Type 2-low asthma.
articles.journal: The Journal of allergy and clinical immunology
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Biologics for Type 2 (T2) inflammation have advanced asthma care, but T2-low asthma is relatively common in children and remains poorly understood.

OBJECTIVE: This study compared clinical and proteomic features of T2-low and T2-high asthma in difficult-to-treat children age 6-18 years.

METHODS: T2 subgroups were defined with k-means cluster analysis of blood eosinophils, total IgE, and positive aeroallergens. Clinical features were assessed at baseline, after systemic corticosteroids, and at 12 months. Exploratory proteomics analyses for ∼4,000 plasma proteins were performed in a subset and analyzed with CytoMod to identify modules of co-signaling proteins. Pathway analyses were performed with Reactome.

RESULTS: 361 children were enrolled (T2-low, N=65; T2-intermediate, N=141; T2-high, N=155). T2 groupings were biologically and temporally stable. Although all groups had a clinically significant symptom and exacerbation burden, children with T2-low asthma had more infectious comorbidity, lesser exacerbation severity, and higher lung function. CytoMod analyses identified three protein modules. Module 1 was strongly associated with T2-low asthma and contained 80 proteins encompassing 18 biological pathways. Notable proteins in Module 1 included signal transducer and activator of transcription 5A, collagens, and extracellular matrix proteins.

CONCLUSION: Children with T2-low asthma have a different clinical phenotype with more preserved lung function despite symptoms and exacerbations. Exploratory analyses suggest the proteome of children with T2-low asthma also differs, with co-signaling modular analyses implicating extracellular matrix and signaling pathways for future study.

articles.title: The biological basis underlying the local brain functional changes of taVNS in treating major depressive disorder: An imaging transcriptomics study.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Transcutaneous auricular vagus nerve stimulation (taVNS) is a promising non-invasive intervention for major depressive disorder (MDD). However, the molecular basis underlying functional brain changes associated with taVNS treatment remains poorly understood.

METHODS: In this prospective longitudinal cohort study, 122 patients with MDD were included in the final analysis from an initial sample of 172 enrolled participants, with 50 excluded owing to dropout or incomplete data. These participants underwent resting-state fMRI before and after 8 weeks of taVNS treatment. For each of the 246 Brainnetome Atlas regions, we calculated treatment-related changes in the amplitude of low-frequency fluctuations (ALFF) and regional homogeneity (ReHo). These changes were correlated with symptom improvement (HAMD-17) to generate specific ALFF and ReHo response maps. To explore candidate spatial molecular associations, we linked these response maps to whole-brain gene expression profiles from the Allen Human Brain Atlas (15,633 genes) via LASSO regression with cross-validation, followed by gene-set enrichment analysis and spatial correlation with 32 PET-based neurotransmitter receptor/transporter maps.

RESULTS: In this single-arm study, 86 participants (70.5%) met the response criterion. Given the absence of a control group, this reflects treatment-related improvement rather than direct evidence of taVNS efficacy. Imaging transcriptomics revealed that gene expression was spatially associated with both response maps, with higher cross-validated regional prediction performance for ReHo (R2 = 0.309, r = 0.558) than for ALFF (R2 = 0.174, r = 0.418). ALFF responses were spatially enriched for cation channel and NMDA receptor-related pathways, whereas ReHo responses were predominantly enriched for microglial and interferon-related immune signaling. The ReHo response map correlated most strongly with GABA-A receptor density, while ALFF changes showed closer links to κ-opioid and CB1 receptor distributions.

CONCLUSIONS: These results indicate that the functional changes associated with taVNS treatment show spatial transcriptomic enrichment for distinct synaptic and neuroimmune pathways, providing candidate molecular correlates to guide further study of this neuromodulation approach in MDD.

articles.title: Silent brain infarction and clinical outcomes in rheumatic mitral stenosis: A prospective cohort study.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Rheumatic mitral stenosis (MS) affects a relatively young population. Thromboembolic risk in MS is traditionally attributed to atrial fibrillation (AF), although silent brain infarction (SBI) may occur in sinus rhythm. Further, the contribution of underlying atrial disease independent of rhythm remains uncertain.

OBJECTIVES: To determine the prevalence and correlates of SBI and evaluate associations with subsequent cerebrovascular and clinical outcomes.

METHODS: In this prospective cohort, 211 adults with moderate-to-severe rheumatic MS underwent baseline brain MRI, echocardiography, biomarker assessment, and rhythm evaluation. Firth penalized logistic regression was used for SBI and longitudinal outcomes. Clinical follow-up was available in 194 patients.

RESULTS: SBI was present in 44 patients (20.9%). SBI occurred in 25.4% with AF and 18.6% in sinus rhythm (unadjusted OR 1.49, 95% CI 0.70-3.10; p = 0.284); adjusted AF was not significantly associated with SBI (OR 0.82, 95% CI 0.37-1.76; p = 0.605). Each doubling of BNP was associated with SBI overall (OR 1.34, 95% CI 1.01-1.82; p = 0.040) and in sinus rhythm (OR 1.56, 95% CI 1.12-2.27; p = 0.007). During follow-up, 15 patients developed stroke/TIA; baseline SBI was associated with subsequent stroke/TIA (17.1% vs 5.2%; adjusted OR 3.40, 95% CI 1.14-9.96; p = 0.029). BNP was associated with stroke/death (49 events; OR per doubling 1.45, 95% CI 1.09-2.00; p = 0.010) and death (40 events; OR 1.57, 95% CI 1.14-2.25; p = 0.005), but not stroke/TIA.

CONCLUSIONS: SBI is common in rheumatic MS and identifies patients at higher subsequent cerebrovascular risk. BNP is associated with SBI and broader adverse prognosis, particularly mortality. These findings are hypothesis-generating and require further validation.

articles.title: Perioperative medication optimisation: what to continue, what to stop and what to deprescribe.
articles.abstract: Polypharmacy is common in patients undergoing surgery. This reflects an increasingly older, frail surgical population prescribed medications for multiple long term conditions. Inappropriate management of pre-admission medications has patient safety implications; inappropriate continuation risks cancellations, whereas inappropriate cessation risks postoperative complications or withdrawal. Medications should be continued preoperatively unless the risk of bleeding, thrombosis, infection, anaesthetic interactions or impact of fasting outweighs the benefits of continuation. The evidence base underpinning this is continually evolving, with recent publications suggesting continuation of medications that would historically have been stopped. Perioperative medication optimisation, however, should go beyond simple continuation or cessation of medications. Polypharmacy is independently associated with postoperative complications, longer length of hospital stay and increased readmission. The preoperative period represents an opportunity to reduce these risks by utilising comprehensive geriatric assessment to holistically review patients, optimise long term conditions and deprescribe medications associated with an increased risk of postoperative harm.

articles.title: Tailored Dosing Recommendations for Amikacin in Severely Ill Children: A Population Pharmacokinetic-Pharmacodynamic Evaluation using Cmax/MIC and AUC/MIC-based Indices.
articles.journal: Clinical microbiology and infection : the official publication of the European Society of Clinical Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVES: Optimal amikacin dosing in severely ill patients remains challenging due to maturational and pathophysiological alterations affecting the pharmacokinetics (PK). This study aimed to develop a population PK model for amikacin, evaluate pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic (PK/PD) indices, and propose personalised dosing recommendations for this patient population.

METHODS: A prospective PK study was conducted in 38 severely ill children receiving intravenous 20 mg/kg amikacin every 24h. PK parameters were determined using nonlinear mixed-effects modelling (Monolix 2024R1). Probability of target attainment (PTA) was simulated for the minimal inhibitory concentration (MIC) of 2 mg/L and 8 mg/L for Enterobacterales. Evaluated PK/PD targets were a peak concentration (Cmax)/MIC ≥ 8 and a 24h area under the concentration-time curve (AUC0-24h)/MIC ≥ 62.5h, in combination with a trough concentration (Ctrough) ≤ 5 mg/L toxicity threshold.

RESULTS: A two-compartment model with a priori allometric weight scaling on the PK parameters best described the data. Clearance was predicted using the Bouvet estimated glomerular filtration (eGFR) formula, combining creatinine and cystatin C. The central volume of distribution was 41% lower in oncology patients compared with intensive care patients. The population parameters for clearance and the total volume of distribution were 7.4 L/h/70 kg and 39.0 L/70 kg, respectively. AUC0-24h/MIC, as PK/PD index, was less frequently attained than the Cmax/MIC index. For a MIC of 2 mg/L, a dose of 20 mg/kg every 18h achieved a 100% PTA for the targets Cmax/MIC ≥ 8, AUC0-24h/MIC ≥ 62.5h, and Ctrough ≤ 5 mg/L in typical patients with a 120-150 mL/min/1.73 m2 eGFR, compared with ≤76% for the current regimen. For a MIC of 8 mg/L, ≥80% PTA could not be achieved.

CONCLUSIONS: Current amikacin dosing regimens may result in subtherapeutic exposure, particularly in intensive care patients with high eGFR or when targeting higher MIC values or AUC/MIC targets. Optimised dosing regimens were proposed.

articles.title: IDEntifying pAtients with suspicion of infection in the ED who have Low disease severity using midregional proadrenomedullin (MR-proADM) - A pragmatic pivotal randomised controlled trial.
articles.journal: Clinical microbiology and infection : the official publication of the European Society of Clinical Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVES: Concentrations of blood biomarker midregional-proadrenomedullin (MR-proADM) can reflect the early microvascular changes and organ dysfunction, which drive the pathophysiology of sepsis. Observational studies and a single-country randomised trial suggested MR-proADM could assist emergency department (ED) clinicians with regards to safer discharges or admission avoidance. The objective of this trial is to evaluate the efficacy/safety of incorporating MR-proADM, into clinical decision-making for hospitalisation or discharge in patients presenting with clinical suspicion of infection to EDs in different countries.

METHODS: An open-label randomised-controlled, interventional trial, conducted across nine European EDs. Patients with suspicion of infection and unclear decision of hospitlisataion in the EDs were randomised 1:1 to either MR-proADM-guided algorithm for admission or discharge from ED or to the standard care (SC) arms. The primary efficacy endpoint was the proportion of patients admitted to hospital targeting a reduction in hospitalisation by the intervention compared to SC. The primary safety objective was to show non-inferiority (against 14% margin) in 5-day all-cause ED re-presentation.

RESULTS: In low severity illness setting, among 460 patients enrolled a similar hospitalisation rate was seen between the MR-proADM (80/230=34.8%) and the SC (78/230=33.9%) arms in the intention to treat (ITT) population, i.e. a rate difference of 0.9% with 95% CI from -7.8% to 9.5% (p=0.922). In the per-protocol (PP) population, there were fewer admissions (43/168=25.6% when MR-proADM guided vs. 77/221=34.8% in SC), but statistically not significant. Re-presentation within 5-days demonstrated non-inferiority for the MR-proADM-guided arm versus the SC in the PP population with a rate reduction estimated at -2.5% (95% CI [-9.5%, 4.6%], p=0.607).

CONCLUSIONS: In this study, the addition of MR-proADM was not associated with statistically different hospitalisation rate. [trial registration: ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT05108883)] Date: November 3rd, 2021.

articles.title: Model-informed dosing strategies for inhaled aminoglycosides in nosocomial pneumonia.
articles.journal: Clinical microbiology and infection : the official publication of the European Society of Clinical Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVES: Nosocomial pneumonia caused by Gram-negative pathogens is a major cause of morbidity and mortality in critically ill patients. Randomised trials adding nebulised aminoglycosides to systemic therapy have not improved outcomes in ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP), possibly because of suboptimal dosing. The efficacious dose remains uncertain. We used translational modelling to inform inhaled aminoglycoside dosing for VAP and hospital-acquired pneumonia (HAP).

METHODS: A translational physiologically based pharmacokinetic (PBPK) model was fitted to rat aminoglycoside pharmacokinetic (PK) data, scaled, and evaluated with observed lung and plasma concentrations from patients with VAP. Model-predicted infection-site concentrations drove pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic (PK/PD) models of bacterial killing under intravenous (IV), nebulised, and combined (IV plus nebulised) regimens, with efficacy defined as bacterial stasis at 24 h. Plasma exposure served as a toxicity surrogate.

RESULTS: The models well captured pulmonary and plasma PK of gentamicin and amikacin in VAP patients. Nebulisation at standard IV doses (gentamicin 7 mg/kg; amikacin 30 mg/kg) achieved less bacterial killing at the alveolar sites than IV monotherapy. To match IV monotherapy, the nebulised doses required were considerably higher (gentamicin 60/20 mg/kg; amikacin 170/70 mg/kg for VAP/HAP), whereas moderate nebulised doses (gentamicin 15/5 mg/kg; amikacin 45/20 mg/kg for VAP/HAP) combined with halved IV dosing matched full-dose IV activity against P. aeruginosa and S. aureus. Plasma troughs remained below toxicity thresholds across all regimens, and combination regimens reduced cumulative systemic exposure relative to standard IV therapy.

CONCLUSIONS: Adjunctive regimens combining moderate nebulised and half IV doses are predicted to match full-dose IV efficacy while limiting systemic exposure; whereas nebulised monotherapy required impractically high doses in VAP and was feasible only under the higher deposition reported for HAP. The simulations indicate that the efficacious doses are dependent on determinants such as pulmonary deposition and pathogen MIC. The proposed model-derived regimens warrant evaluation in future clinical trials.

articles.title: Purkinje-Targeted Catheter Ablation for Refractory Ventricular Fibrillation and Polymorphic Ventricular Tachycardia: A Systematic Review, Network Meta-Analysis, and Meta-Regression.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Ventricular fibrillation (VF) and polymorphic ventricular tachycardia (PVT) are major causes of sudden cardiac death. Although Purkinje-targeted catheter ablation has emerged as a rescue therapy for refractory ventricular arrhythmias, the comparative safety and efficacy of trigger-focused ablation versus Purkinje de-networking (PDN) remain uncertain.

OBJECTIVE: To synthesize clinical outcomes for Purkinje-targeted interventions across diverse arrhythmic phenotypes.

METHODS: We searched PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, Ovid, and CENTRAL for studies enrolling adults with recurrent or refractory ventricular fibrillation (VF) or polymorphic ventricular tachycardia (PVT). We performed pairwise and network meta-analyses using random-effects models. We evaluated the certainty of evidence using GRADE frameworks (PROSPERO: CRD420261423684).

RESULTS: We included 22 studies involving 959 patients. Among PDN cohorts, pooled mortality was 13.5% (n = 435; 16 cohorts; 95% CI: 9.0%-20.1%; I2 = 99.28%), acute success was 83.5% (n = 388; 14 cohorts; 95% CI: 78.9%-88.4%; I2 = 34.33%), and VF/PVT recurrence was 18.9% (n = 412; 15 cohorts; 95% CI: 15.7%-22.6%; I2 = 0%). Compared with standard ablation, PDN showed nonsignificant reductions in mortality (RR 0.672, 95% CI: 0.267-1.69; I2 = 0%) and recurrence (RR 0.820, 95% CI: 0.239-2.807; I2 = 70.33%). In the primary network meta-analysis, PDN ranked highest for acute success (SUCRA 86.27%) and freedom from recurrence (77.05%). However, in a sensitivity analysis of comparative trials (9 trials; n = 457), trigger-focused ablation ranked highest for acute success (SUCRA 88.08% vs. 51.52% for PDN). New-onset LBBB occurred in up to 20.8% after substrate-based PDN.

CONCLUSIONS: In this exploratory network meta-analysis, PDN ranked favorably for acute procedural success and short-term arrhythmia freedom. However, low-certainty evidence, imprecise estimates, and substantial clinical heterogeneity preclude definitive conclusions about its comparative efficacy. Large-scale randomized trials are needed to establish its clinical benefit.

articles.title: Final 5-year results of the Thoracic Branch Endoprosthesis Feasibility Trials for Treatment of Aortic Arch Aneurysms.
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To report final 5-year outcomes from prospective multicenter feasibility studies of the GORE® TAG® Thoracic Branch Endoprosthesis (TBE) for aneurysms involving the proximal descending thoracic aorta and aortic arch (zones 0-2).

METHODS: Forty consecutive patients (23 male; mean age, 74±10 years) were enrolled at six sites in prospective, nonrandomized feasibility trials (2014-2016). Patients underwent TEVAR with proximal TBE in zone 0/1 (n=9; NCT02264977) or zone 2 (n=31; NCT02021812). A clinical events committee adjudicated aneurysm-related and all-cause mortality, major adverse events, and cerebrovascular events. Core laboratory analysis assessed endoleaks (types I-IV), aneurysm sac enlargement, device migration, and side branch patency. Five-year cumulative risk rates (2006 days) were estimated using Kaplan-Meier analysis.

RESULTS: The median follow-up time among survivors was 60.2 months (range, 25.8 to 66.0), with 17 patients completing the required 5-year clinical and imaging follow-up across both studies. Eleven late deaths occurred; KM-estimated cumulative risk of 5-year all-cause mortality was 29% (95% CI: 17%-46%). One zone 2 death was adjudicated as aortic-related (2.5%; 95% CI: 0.4%-16%) due to ascending aortic rupture, with no ruptures occurring within treated aortic segments. Reintervention risk through 5 years was low (KM-estimated cumulative risk, 5.1%; 95% CI: 1.3%-19%), with two events, both in the zone 2 cohort. Five patients experienced stroke events through 5 years, corresponding to a KM cumulative risk of 19.0% ( 95% CI: 7.2%-43%), two in zone 2 and three in zone 0/1. Two patients had target vessel instability (5.0%, 95% CI: 0.6%-16.9%). Two side-branch patency events occurred in zone 2: one complete side-branch occlusion in the LSA associated with transient mild arm claudication and one asymptomatic partial occlusion, primary patency through 5-year follow-up was 94.8% (37/39 evaluable patients). Core laboratory identified endoleaks in 12 patients (30.8%; 95% CI: 15%-45%). Three patients (7.7%) had a type I or III endoleak by 5 years, all in the zone 2 arm; these included type IA in one patient (2.6%) and type III in two patients (5.1%). Additionally indeterminate (n=8, 20.5%) and type II (n=6, 15.4%) endoleaks were observed. Cumulative risk rate of aneurysm sac enlargement through 5-years was 15.0% for all patients (95% CI: 5.6%-30.3%), with events occurring in three zone 2 patients and one zone 0/1 patient.

CONCLUSIONS: At 5 years, the early feasibility studies demonstrated excellent side branch patency, a low incidence of type IA endoleak, low aortic-related mortality, and no rupture within the treated aortic segments. Larger studies are needed to better define zone-specific cerebrovascular risk and long-term durability.

articles.title: Incidence of Aortic Vascular Graft and Endograft Infection in Patients with Bloodstream Infection - A Population-Based Study.
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To assess incidence and predictors of vascular graft and endograft infection in patients with prior aorto-iliac graft surgery and concurrent blood stream infection.

METHODS: A population-based observational study was conducted in Skåne, Sweden, between 2010-2022. Patients with prior aorto-iliac graft or endograft surgery were identified in the Swedish Vascular Registry and linked to local blood culture data. Electronic medical records were reviewed according to a predefined protocol and vascular graft and endograft infection was assessed using MAGIC-criteria. Fine-Gray models were used to evaluate predictors of vascular graft and endograft infection diagnosis within three months of a bloodstream infection episode.

RESULTS: A total of 418 patients were identified with 569 bloodstream infection episodes. Of 569 bloodstream infection episodes, 83% (n=473) occurred in men and mean age was 74.9 ± 9 years. The 3-month incidence of vascular graft and endograft infection diagnosis was 7.5%. Elevated C-reactive protein at bloodstream infection onset (sHR; 1.004, 95% CI 1.002-1.007, p<.001) and prior urgent aorto-iliac index surgery (sHR 2.77, 95% CI 1.31-5.87, p=.007) were positively associated with vascular graft and endograft infection. C. albicans (sHR 3.97, 95% CI 1.3-12.1, p=.02), Actinomycetales (sHR 8.29, 95% CI 2.3-29.84, p=0.001), L. monocytogenes (sHR 18.22, 95% CI 11.21-29.63, p <.001) or S. aureus (sHR 1.98, 95% CI 1.05-3.72, p=.03) bloodstream infections were positively associated with vascular graft and endograft infection.

CONCLUSION: The 3-month incidence of vascular graft and endograft infection diagnosis after bloodstream infection was 7.5%. Clinical suspicion of vascular graft and endograft infection should be higher in patients with prior urgent aorto-iliac surgery, markedly elevated levels of C-reactive protein at index culture, or bloodstream infection with S. aureus, Actinomycetales, L. monocytogenes or C. albicans.

articles.title: How Allergists Choose Allergen Immunotherapy: A Worldwide Data-Driven Cluster Analysis.
articles.journal: The journal of allergy and clinical immunology. In practice
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Most clinical data on allergen immunotherapy (AIT) focus on efficacy and safety, whereas limited information is available on the real-world clinical drivers guiding AIT prescribing.

OBJECTIVE: To identify the main drivers influencing AIT prescribing in routine practice.

METHODS: This prospective, multicenter, international observational study used a web-based survey conducted in 20 countries across 8 geographic regions. Two anonymous questionnaires were completed: one by participating physicians and one for each patient initiating subcutaneous or sublingual AIT (drops or tablets) according to local standards of care. Eligible patients had IgE-mediated respiratory allergy to pollens, house dust mite, animal dander, and/or molds. Data were collected centrally and analyzed by an independent third party using descriptive statistics and cluster analysis.

RESULTS: Questionnaires were obtained from 467 physicians and 11,550 patients. Physicians were predominantly allergists with substantial experience prescribing AIT. Most patients had allergic rhinitis (97.7%), and 35.6% had allergic asthma. Disease severity, patient preferences, biological activity (extract allergenic potency), and major allergen content were high-priority factors for AIT prescriptions. The most important reason for prescribing AIT was symptom reduction during treatment, followed by sustained efficacy after treatment discontinuation and, to a lesser extent, asthma prevention. Avoidance of new sensitizations was consistently rated as a low-priority factor. Cluster analysis identified six distinct prescribing patterns, highlighting marked heterogeneity in AIT selection across regions.

CONCLUSION: AIT prescribing in routine clinical practice is highly heterogeneous and influenced by regional and healthcare-related factors. These real-world data provide novel insights into AIT prescribing behaviour and support the development of regional-specific, context-sensitive, patient-centered guidance.

articles.title: Does critical care training explain higher survival after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest?, Letter to the Editor.
Reply to: Does critical care training explain higher survival after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest?
Factors Associated With a Severe Liver Phenotype in Patients With Autosomal Dominant Polycystic Kidney Disease.
articles.journal: American journal of kidney diseases : the official journal of the National Kidney Foundation
articles.abstract:
RATIONALE & OBJECTIVE: Polycystic liver disease (PLD) is the most common extra-renal manifestation of autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD). Severe PLD may require somatostatin analogs, cyst aspiration or fenestration, partial hepatectomy, and liver transplantation. This study evaluated factors associated with PLD severity, longitudinal total liver volume (TLV) growth, and treatment patterns in a large ADPKD cohort.

STUDY DESIGN: Retrospective cohort study.

SETTING & PARTICIPANTS: A single-center registry including 396 patients with ADPKD who underwent at least one TLV measurement between 2000 and 2023.

PREDICTORS: Demographic, clinical, imaging, genetic, and family history characteristics.

OUTCOMES: Severe PLD defined as height-adjusted TLV >1800 ml/m or receipt of PLD-specific therapies, and annual TLV growth rate.

ANALYTICAL APPROACH: Multivariable logistic regression with adjustment for intrafamilial clustering was used to identify factors associated with severe PLD. Longitudinal TLV growth was evaluated using a mixed-effects model.

RESULTS: Among 396 patients (mean age 45 years; 62% women; 88% White; 281 families; mean eGFR 82 ml/min/1.73m2), 115 (29%) had severe PLD. Factors independently associated with severe PLD included older age (P=0.01), female sex (P=0.007), family history of severe liver disease (P<0.001), and lower eGFR (P=0.01). Total kidney volume, genotype, and parity were not significantly associated with severe PLD. Among 195 patients with follow-up measures, the median annual TLV growth rate was 1.83%, with faster growth in women younger than 48 years than in older women (2.99% vs 1.60%, p=0.002). Among patients with severe PLD, 71% received therapy, including somatostatin analogs (48), cyst aspiration/fenestration (8), partial hepatectomy (8), and liver transplantation (44).

LIMITATIONS: Single-center retrospective study conducted in a tertiary referral center.

CONCLUSIONS: Older age, female sex, family history of a severe liver phenotype, and lower eGFR were independently associated with severe PLD in ADPKD. These findings may inform risk stratification and management of patients at risk for progressive PLD.

articles.title: MMP14 genetic variability may influence glycemic control and vascular complications in patients with type 2 diabetes.
articles.abstract: Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2D) is characterized by chronic hyperglycemia and progressive vascular complications driven by endothelial dysfunction, inflammation, and extracellular matrix (ECM) remodeling. Matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs), particularly MMP14 and MMP2, are key regulators of ECM homeostasis and may contribute to inter-individual susceptibility to diabetic complications. We performed a retrospective genetic association study including 207 patients with T2D. Six polymorphisms in MMP14 (rs1042703, rs1042704, rs743257) and MMP2 (rs243865, rs243849, rs7201) were genotyped using competitive allele-specific PCR. Associations with glycemic control, metabolic parameters, and diabetic complications were evaluated using non-parametric tests and logistic regression. Protein-protein interactions were analyzed using STRING. Carriers of at least one polymorphic MMP14 rs743257 allele were significantly less likely to experience microvascular complications (OR = 0.29 (0.13-0.66), P = 0.003), specifically retinopathy (OR = 0.23 (0.07-0.74), P = 0.013) and nephropathy (OR = 0.23 (0.09-0.60), P = 0.003) in univariable analysis.
